News.title: Spain and France wildfires live: 200,000 flee as flames scorch tourist areas
News.content:
Firefighters battle a wildfire in the Cebreros area, near Ávila, around 50 miles west of Madrid, on July 24

More than 200,000 people in France and Spain have been evacuated as wildfires continue to tear through vast areas of both countries

Huge wildfires are ravaging parts of south-west France and central Spain, forcing the evacuation of an estimated 200,000 people, including British tourists.

Around 141,000 people have been evacuated from their homes in France's Gironde and Landes departments, the French interior ministry said. Some residents and holidaymakers even fled by boat as flames swept through the popular tourist area of Cap Ferret on France's Atlantic coast.

In Spain, 60,000 have been forced to leave their homes in towns west of Madrid, the Spanish interior ministry said. Wildfires in the Madrid region and the nearby province of Ávila have prompted the government to declare a national emergency over wildfires for the first time.

Meanwhile, Police Scotland has declared a major incident as firefighters battle a huge wildfire in the Cairngorms National Park, with hundreds of people evacuated from homes in its path.

The force said strengthening winds have made the fire more unpredictable and caused it to spread towards Nethy Bridge, a small village in the Strathspey area of the park, prompting the decision to declare a major incident.

News.title: Essex explosion live: Inferno after huge blast as 100 firefighters tackle flames
News.content:
Aerial images show the scale of the blaze at a farm in Essex

More than 100 firefighters are tackling a massive fire at a farm off Southend Road between East Hanningfield and Rettendon in Essex

A massive explosion at a farm in Essex has shaken buildings up to 15 miles away, with footage showing an huge fireball erupting from the site.

Essex County Fire and Rescue Service said more than 100 firefighters worked to tackle a blaze involving industrial units at a farm off Southend Road, between East Hanningfield and Rettendon, near Chelmsford, on Friday evening.

The blaze, which is understood to be at Highlands Farm, has been declared a major incident due to its size. Around 50 firefighters will remain at the scene overnight and into the morning. Police have cordoned off a large area around the site.

"If you live or are travelling nearby, please continue to keep your windows and doors closed," the fire service said. "Please avoid the area while we deal with this incident."

News.title: Donald Trump defends ‘slave labour’ import tariff against UK amid court challenge
News.content:
Donald Trump defends ‘slave labour’ import tariff against UK amid court challenge

The White House justified the charges in law by claiming the economies targeted had failed to enforce bans on goods produced by slave labour - their imposition coincided with the expiry of a temporary 10% import levy

View 2 Images Mr Trump said: “We put the tariffs on. They’re very standard tariffs" (Image: AP Photo/Rod Lamkey)

Donald Trump has defended slapping fresh taxes on imports from the UK and dozens of other countries as a legal challenge was launched against the move.

‌



The US President slapped duties on 60 countries. They replace a previous set of tariffs that expired on Friday after the US Supreme Court ruled them illegal.

‌



Speaking in the Oval Office, the US president said the new levies were “very standard tariffs” that “follow the line”. The White House justified the charges in law by claiming the economies targeted had failed to enforce bans on goods produced by slave labour.

‌



View 2 Images In 2024, UK exports to the US were worth £66 billion, 17% of all UK goods exports. (Image: Getty Images)

Meghan Markle shares sweet holiday snaps of Archie and Lilibet visiting Diana's childhood home READ MORE :

Their imposition coincided with the expiry of a temporary 10% import levy, already faced by Britain, introduced after the Supreme Court ruled Mr Trump’s initial sweeping global tariffs, which he hailed at the time as “Liberation Day”, were unlawful.

Mr Trump said: “We put the tariffs on. They’re very standard tariffs. The other way was easier. I thought the decision by the Supreme Court was not a good one. But we have many forms of tariffs.”

‌



He was speaking after a legal campaign group brought a case on behalf of two small businesses in the US Court of International Trade in New York, opposing the latest import taxes.

The Liberty Justice Centre, which has successfully challenged Mr Trump’s previous tariffs, is seeking to overturn the replacement levies. Sara Albrecht, the group’s chairman, said: The administration allowed one global tariff to expire and immediately replaced it with another under a different statute.

“Changing the statute doesn’t change the law. Every tariff authority has limits, and every administration must respect them.”

‌



The centre’s senior lawyer Jeffrey Schwab said the legislative provision being relied on by the White House was “a targeted, country-specific and practice-specific remedial authority”.

He added: “It is not a freestanding authorisation to tax substantially all imports from substantially all countries at pre-established rates.”

The UK Government has pointed out there is no change to the tariff rate facing UK businesses as a result of the recent announcement, which would remain at 10%. The UK exports more to the US than to any other single country.

Article continues below

The Economic Prosperity Deal agreed between the two countries last year aimed to mitigate the impact of US tariffs on UK industries and deepen commercial ties.

Meanwhile, US import duties on Scotch whisky has now been lifted. The president announced in April that he would remove the whisky tariff, following the state visit by the King and Queen.

News.title: Twisted schoolboy, 14, who shot classmates and teachers in school rampage laughs as survivor reads statement
News.content:
Twisted schoolboy, 14, who shot classmates and teachers in school rampage laughs as survivor reads statement

Colt Gray was just 14 when he killed four and injured nine people in a horrific gun rampage at his own school - today the teen pleaded guilty in court

View 6 Images Colt Gray in court, in December (Image: AP Photo/Mike Stewart)

A teenager who unleashed a horror gun attack on his school, shooting dead two students and two teachers, laughed as a survivor spoke out to the court.

‌



Colt Gray, 16, killed four people and left nine injured after a gun attack at the Apalachee High School, in Georgia, when he was just 14 years old, in 2024. The trial for the deadly shooting saw survivors and families of victims share their statements to jurors. Survivor Natalie Griffith recalled her horror memories from the shooting but Gray was seen grinning and smiling as she spoke.

‌



On Friday, Gray formally pleaded guilty to all 55 charges against him, in relation to the school massacre. These included murder and aggravated assault.

‌



Calls for UK government to put pressure on Texas cops to re-open case of Brit shot dead by her dad READ MORE :

Coney Island horror mass shooting leaves eight injured including four children as cops swarm READ MORE :

View 6 Images Colt Gray in court on July 24 (Image: AP/YouTube)

Griffith was among the people injured in the school bloodbath and shared the heartbreaking impact the attack has had on her life nearly two years after the September 2024 incident.

The survivor told the court: "I got shot twice, once in my wrist and once in my upper arm. I lost the ability to use my left hand, but on some days it doesn't feel like that is the biggest thing I lost. After the shooting I lost my independence, I could not put on my own clothes or do my own hair, things that were easy for me became a challenge."

‌



View 6 Images Mugshot of Colt Gray after the September 2024 attack (Image: AP)

Griffith shared her story at a fast speed, prompting the judge to ask her to slow down. Several laughs were heard in the courtroom including from twisted Gray who was seen giggling.

Another survivor, Hayden Bowen, also tearfully shared a statement to the court, telling Gray: "I want to start off by saying I forgive you. Not for you, but for me and my peace."

‌



She added: "I have frequent panic attacks. I can't stay in places for too long. I can't go out anywhere. I can't even stay in my own bedroom without feeling fear. I'm not able to be a normal teenager anymore."

View 6 Images The four victims who died in the 2024 shooting (Image: Getty Images)

The four people who were killed in the 2024 shooting were pupils Mason Schermerhorn, 14, and Christian Angulo, 14, as well as two teachers Richard Aspinwall, 39, and Cristina Irimie, 53.

‌



Breanna Schermerhorn, whose 14-year-old son Mason Schermerhorn was shot dead, said her boy was "much more than a victim". She said: "Mason was kind, compassionate, funny and fiercely protective of others.

"As a child with exceptional needs, he understood what it felt like to struggle and be overlooked by others. Instead of becoming bitter, he became an advocate. He made people that were typically unseen feel seen, accepted and safe."

View 6 Images An attorney pointing to a weapon during the trial, in February (Image: AP)

‌



The mum added that Gray "knew that pulling that trigger was wrong, he knew that every choice he made that day would forever alter countless lives".

Gray agreed to a non-negotiated guilty plea, meaning the court will work to decide his sentence. The judge told the court that the minimum sentence is life with parole and the maximum is a life sentence without parole.

View 6 Images Mugshot of the killer teen's dad Colin Gray (Image: Barrow County Jail)

Article continues below

Ismael Angulo, the brother of Christian Angulo, asked the judge to put Gray in prison for life without the chance of parole, as "every day as a nightmare". The brother said: "The defendant's family will still get to see their son, talk to him and know he is breathing. My mother, my father don't get that privilege."

Gray was accused of carrying out the massacre with a rifle that his dad Colin Gray gifted the teen for Christmas. The dad was convicted, in March, of charged including second-degree murder. The court heard audio from Gray's arrest where he asked a police officer to share a message with his dad: "Tell him that it wasn't his fault and that I know he tried his hardest."

News.title: Sarah Ferguson's charity shuts down after scrutiny of links to paedophile Jeffrey Epstein
News.content:
Sarah Ferguson's charity shuts down after scrutiny of links to paedophile Jeffrey Epstein

Sarah's Trust, the charity belonging to Sarah Ferguson, has been shut and 'removed' from the charity regulator's website

View 3 Images Sarah Ferguson pictured in April 2025 (Image: UK Press via Getty Images)

Disgraced Sarah Ferguson has seen her charity wound up after her controversial links to convicted paedophile Jeffrey Epstein emerged.

The former-Duchess's Sarah's Trust charity had introduced philanthropists to good causes in need of funding, but was formally shut last month. It was first registered with the Charity Commission in 2018, but the regulator's website now lists the trust as being "removed", meaning it was no longer a registered charity. Sarah's Trust had also been listed at Companies House as a "charitable incorporated organisation" but its status is now "converted/closed".

Emails released by US officials, as part of the Epstein Files, revealed several emails between Fergie and Epstein and shed new light on their relationship. Ferguson has strongly denied all wrongdoing.

View 3 Images Sarah Ferguson and her ex-husband Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor in September 2025 (Image: UK Press via Getty Images)

The charity back in February said it would close "for the foreseeable future" just days after new revelations emerged after millions of documents were released in the Epstein Files.

At the time, a spokesperson for the charity said: "Our chair Sarah Ferguson and the board of trustees have agreed that with regret the charity will shortly close for the foreseeable future. This has been under discussion and in train for some months."

One of these included an email between Fergie and Epstein where she praised the sex offender and called him the "brother I have always wished for". Appearing in the Epstein Files does not indicate guilt or wrongdoing.

View 3 Images Sarah Ferguson smiling, in April 2025 (Image: Aaron Chown/PA Wire)

In another email, from 2010, the ex-Duchess wrote: "You are a legend. I really don't have the words to describe, my love, gratitude for your generosity and kindness," she writes. "Xx I am at your service . Just marry me."

Other publicly released files also showed that Fergie had invited Epstein to her 50th birthday party at St James's Palace in February 2010. This was after Epstein was released from prison in 2009, for soliciting prostitution of a minor.

Other charities associated with the former duchess also cut ties with Ferguson, including the Teenage Cancer Trust, which dropped her as patron after 35 years, Wiltshire and Dorset-based children’s hospice Julia's House, Prevent Breast Cancer, The Natasha Allergy Research Foundation and the National Foundation for Retired Service Animals.

Fergie's ex-husband Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor was stripped of his royal privileges and titles by the King because of "serious lapses of judgment" over his friendship with the late paedophile. Ferguson also lost her courtesy royal divorcee title and went back to her maiden name.

Article continues below

The Mirror has contacted Sarah Ferguson's representatives for comment.

News.title: Westminster Bridge: Four police officers seriously injured in horror Thames boat crash
News.content:
A police boat carrying armed cops has crashed near Westminster Bridge in central London, leaving four officers seriously injured after a number plunged into the River Thames.

Emergency services swarmed the scene in central London, with responders from the RNLI seen treating casualties on a boat at the pier.

A large number of police officers, fire crews and ambulances were also at the scene, with the bridge closed to traffic and the Underground also impacted.

Metropolitan Police Commander Nick John said: "Our thoughts are with all those involved, in particular our officers who were injured and those who responded in challenging circumstances.

"The four officers who remain in hospital have serious but non-life-threatening injuries. We will give them all every support as they recover."

News.title: RAF Typhoons scrambled to UK-bound Qatar Airways flight 'causing concern'
News.content:
RAF Typhoons scrambled to UK-bound Qatar Airways flight 'causing concern'

Flight QR23 from Doha to Manchester Airport caused 'concern to civil authorities' once it reached UK airspace, triggering a 'RAD Quick Reaction Alert'

View 2 Images The RAF launched Typhoons (Image: News Images/NurPhoto/Shutterstock)

Two RAF jets were scrambled to escort a Qatar Airways flight bound for Manchester from Doha tonight.

‌



The incident occurred as flight QR23 from the Qatari capital to Manchester Airport entered UK airspace. The RAF said in a statement that the aircraft was "causing concern to civil authorities", which triggered the "RAF Quick Reaction Alert".

‌



The jets were scrambled after ground controllers lost radio contact with the long-haul flight during its approach, according to Air Live. An unresponsive commercial aircraft constitutes a potential security threat and so the RAF Quick Reaction Alert protocol was launched.

‌



A spokesperson for the Ministry of Defence confirmed that the two Typhoons were deployed from RAF Coningsby in Lincolnshire. This was to make visual contact with the crew, Air Live reported.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



An RAF spokesperson said: "We can confirm that an RAF Quick Reaction Alert was launched for a Qatar Airways flight which was causing concern to civil authorities. The incident was resolved and the airliner landed safely at Manchester Airport."

The Mirror understands the Typhoons were stood down very quickly as no issue was identified. The aircraft was reportedly intercepted over Nottingham.

The seven-hour flight was operated on a Boeing 777 which can carry between 301 and 451 passengers depending on the configuration of the aircraft. It landed safely and on time at 7.45pm at Manchester Airport's Terminal 2.

Article continues below

View 2 Images The Qatar Airways flight landing at Manchester Airport on Friday evening (Image: Emily Brobyn/X)

The same aircraft is expected to take off soon from Manchester Airport to return to Hamad International Airport in Doha on flight QR24.

The flight was scheduled for 9.15pm but had not yet taken off as of 10.50pm. Qatar Airways has been approached for comment.

News.title: Andy Burnham rules out calling snap General Election and will plough on with Labour's manifesto
News.content:
Andy Burnham rules out calling snap General Election and will plough on with Labour's manifesto

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has ruled out a snap General Election, and said the government "needed to focus on making the country work" instead, claiming going to the polls would "postpone" that work

View 4 Images Andy Burnham during a meeting at No 10 North, in Manchester, on Friday (Image: Christopher Furlong/Pool Getty v)

Andy Burnham has shut down the idea of calling a snap election just days after he was sworn in as Prime Minister.

‌



Mr Burnham said he would push forward with Labour's election winning 2024 manifesto, while opening a new headquarters for the centre of Government in Manchester, dubbed the Number 10 North. The former Mayor of Manchester has become the seventh British Prime Minister in 10 years but has said no to another General Election anytime soon.

‌



When asked if he was considering calling a snap election for the country, Mr Burnham said: "No I'm not. I don't think that is right."

‌



Andy Burnham says rates cut is his way of backing venues he loved as youngster READ MORE :

View 4 Images Andy Burnham inside No 10 North on the opening day (Image: Christopher Furlong/PA Wire)

The new Prime Minister said the government's focus is currently on "making the country work".

The PM told the Manchester Evening News: "We live in a parliamentary democracy. There was a manifesto in 2024. I'm sticking to that manifesto. I'm bringing forward my version but it is still within that manifesto. I just think that we need to focus on making the country work.

‌



"That is the biggest priority right now. A general election would postpone that essential work. I'm also trying to do politics differently, as I did when I was mayor of Greater Manchester."

View 4 Images Andy Burnham and wife Marie-France van Heel pose for photos outside 10 Downing Street, on July 20 (Image: Dinendra Haria/SOPA Images/Shutterstock)

Before becoming PM, Burnham was asked if he would call an early election, while taking part in an Ask Me Anything (AMA) on Reddit. On July 3, the Makerfield MP also ruled this out and wrote: "No. As I said in my speech on Monday, I’m going to work to the 2024 manifesto."

‌



On Friday, Mr Burnham opened the No 10 North at Heron House in the centre of Manchester, where he is expected to work once a week during his premiership.

The Labour Party leader said his move to have a base in the north was about "rebalancing power in the country".

Mr Burnham was joined at the opening by Chancellor John Healey, First Secretary of State Louise Haigh, and the country’s top civil servant, Cabinet Secretary Antonia Romeo.

‌



View 4 Images Mr Burnham during a National Economic Council at No 10 North (Image: Christopher Furlong/Pool Getty v)

He later held a meeting with local leaders, including English regional mayors like Liverpool's Steve Rotheram and Greater Lincolnshire's Andrea Jenkyns. Mr Burnham argued the new northern headquarters would help save money.

The Prime Minister said: "Is it a gimmick? Well, the fact that I was there today with the Chancellor, the cabinet secretary, the First Secretary of State, the Transport Secretary - a large part of the government was there in Manchester with me today.

Article continues below

"And the fact of us being there, taking decisions there, just means that we're rebalancing power in the country aren't we? And the benefits that will fall to Manchester are massive. But it's about No 10 North taking power out of Whitehall and putting it into all parts of the country. That’s its job."

On Friday, Mr Burnham also revealed a separate, similar forum would be arranged with the leaders of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, which he described as a "different form of devolution".

Mr Burnham also revealed his feelings towards his new role saying: "I love the job". The Prime Minister said: "You can't ever prepare for it because you can't ever know what it's like until you do it, but... I'm getting used to it very quickly because you have to. So I'm in at the deep end, but I've started swimming and I've enjoyed it so far."

News.title: Law student is charged over intercepted bomb in car
News.content:
A 25-year-old law student has appeared in court charged over a bomb which was discovered in a car in the Republic of Ireland.

Isobella Perrie Sullivan, from Abbeylands Park in Clane, County Kildare, was charged with the possession of explosives.

It was alleged she was driving the car which was intercepted by gardaÃ­ (Irish police) near Carrickmacross, County Monaghan, on Wednesday.

A defence solicitor told the court his client had been asked to take a bag to Northern Ireland and had not been aware what was in it.

Earlier on Friday, gardaÃ­ (Irish police) told reporters their interception was part of an operation targeting dissident republican activity.

The accused, who was arrested on Wednesday, was brought before a special sitting of Trim District Court in County Meath on Friday evening.

A member of the Garda Special Detective Unit told the court the car she was driving was stopped by officers on N2 at Aclint, south of Carrickmacross.

News.title: Watch moment of explosion as huge fire breaks out in Essex
News.content:
A huge explosion triggered by a fire tore through an industrial unit in Essex on Friday, with more than 100 firefighters sent to tackle the massive fire.

Video posted on social media captured the moment the explosion rattled the surrounding area, with some people seen running from the blaze.

The Essex fire service declared a major incident due to the size of the fire, warning people to stay away from the area and keep doors and windows closed if they live nearby.

In an update on Friday evening, the fire brigade said the blaze was under control and there was no wider risk to the public.

News.title: Man describes trying to save mother and daughter who drowned off Essex beach
News.content:
A day-tripper has told the BBC how he dived into the sea in an attempt to save a mother and daughter who drowned off an Essex beach.

Craig Bowe, 42, battled the incoming tide at West Mersea, near Colchester, three times after hearing screams on Wednesday evening.

The kitchen fitter, who was on a day trip from Hertfordshire to celebrate his daughter's 10th birthday, managed to haul Shally and Samiha Rahman from the waves and also helped a seven-year-old boy onto a lifeboat.

Despite his efforts, the pair - aged 41 and 15 - died in the desperate attempt to bring the boy to shore.

The boy, who became stranded during a family day out from Barking, east London, was airlifted to hospital and remained there in a critical condition on Friday.

Three others were taken by ambulance to another hospital after the incident unfolded at about 17:35 BST.

News.title: Andy Burnham's first week pledges - how much do they add up to?
News.content:
Andy Burnham is ending his first week as prime minister by working out of Manchester in the new No 10 North for the first time.

He spent this week making a series of spending announcements mostly aimed at tackling the cost of living, including capping bus fares.

BBC Verify has looked at Burnham's first week of spending commitments, how much they cost and how the government says they will be paid for, which comes to about Â£1.5bn.

News.title: Heatwave reveals lost archaeological sites across Wales
News.content:
Lost archaeological sites have emerged in grasslands across Wales after a prolonged spell of hot and dry weather.

Wales has seen about 5% of the average rainfall for July, after a series of back-to-back heatwaves and a drier than usual April to June. A drought has also been triggered in parts of Wales.

Experts said these dry conditions have brought to light a range of hidden archaeological remains, including Roman buildings and practice trenches from World War One.

Many are only visible from the air as distinctive marks in crops and grass, with some not being seen for "two or three decades", according to the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales (RCAHMW).

News.title: Officers hurt as police boat hits Westminster Bridge
News.content:
Five Metropolitan Police officers have been injured after a police boat struck Westminster Bridge in central London.

The Met said the incident occurred at about 15:40 BST and involved a boat from the Marine Policing Unit which was carrying armed officers.

One officer has since been discharged from hospital and the others have serious but non-life-threatening injuries.

The police confirmed that no members of the public were involved or injured in the crash.

The police boat was responding to a report of a person in the water near Battersea.

The Met said in a statement: "As a result of the collision, three officers were thrown from the boat into the water. They were recovered by those on nearby boats.

"Additional officers responded alongside the London Ambulance Service and London Fire Brigade."

The Met's Cmdr Nick John thanked river users "who came to the aid of the officers, as well as other police and emergency service colleagues who immediately made their way to the scene to assist".

He added: "The quick-thinking and professionalism of all those involved undoubtedly prevented any further injuries."

News.title: Angela Rayner rules out rent controls in England
News.content:
Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has said Prime Minister Andy Burnham is not looking at bringing in rent controls in England.

She told BBC Breakfast that changes made through the Renters' Rights Act, which came into effect in May, were "already having a significant impact on the market".

She added that controls which had been implemented in some areas of the UK over the past few years had not "necessarily brought rents down".

In 2023 when he was the mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham called for freezes to private sector rents until the cost of living crisis was over.

But Rayner told the BBC on Friday: "I don't think that rent freezes, rent controls, is a way forward at the moment.

"Three years ago, Andy called for that because there was a significant crisis in the rental market.

"We implemented between then the Renters' Rights Act which is giving renters more power and control."

Temporary rent controls were introduced in Scotland in October 2022 but expired last year.

Under new legislation, ministers in Holyrood will be able to designate certain places in Scotland as rent control areas - expected to come in by 2027.

Councils will be able to cap rent increases on some properties at a maximum of 6%.

Green Party leader Zack Polanski has said he wants to see rent controls brought in for all rented property in England.

Responding to Rayner's interview, he described Burnham as "continuity Starmer", posting on X: "The new prime minister talks a lot of about helping with the cost of living crisis. This is the one single measure that would help the most and save billions. All talk."

Jeremy Corbyn, who pledged to bring in rent controls during the 2019 general election when he was the Labour leader, described Rayner's announcement as "extremely disappointing".

"There is no hope of ending homelessness if we do not stand up to vested interests and take action against extortionate private rents.

"We need rent controls, and we need them now."

Sir Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, has also long called on the government to implement a cap.

But Gareth Bacon, the Conservative's shadow housing minister, said rent controls would be "disastrous" and "intensify the damage done by Labour's agenda that has driven landlords from the market and reduced choice for renters".

"Labour are clearly divided. Burnham's pick for housing secretary has disowned a policy he himself has repeatedly backed," he said.

The term rent controls describes a range of measures a government can implement - from capping price increases to freezing them for a period of time.

Landlord groups say they may exacerbate the housing crisis by putting owners off renting out property.

The Renters' Rights Act was brought in to give more stability and security to the 11 million people who rent from private landlords.

Under the legislation, fixed-term tenancies have been banned and it is now significantly harder for landlords to evict tenants.

Rents can also only be increased once a year to the property's "open market rent".

News.title: NBA superstar LeBron James to join Philadelphia 76ers
News.content:
LeBron James has announced he will be joining the Philadelphia 76ers next season for what he says will be his final contract in the NBA.

The 41-year-old, the highest points scorer in the history of the league, left the Los Angeles Lakers after eight years last month.

The Cleveland Cavaliers, Golden State Warriors, Minnesota Timberwolves and Miami Heat were also rumoured to be in the running for the four-time NBA champion.

"I believe I can help make the Philadelphia 76ers a championship team and I am so excited to energise a new fanbase and start this incredible journey one last time," James said on X., external

James has won an NBA title with all three teams he previously played for. He won two with Miami, who earlier this week mistakenly posted a link to an 'introductory press conference' for James.

A Heat spokesperson told Reuters, external the video was posted in error by staff who were preparing for the possibility of James rejoining the team he played for between 2010 and 2014.

Either side of that Miami stint, James had two spells with Cleveland, who drafted James in 2003 and are based near his hometown of Akron, Ohio.

"Miami I'll forever love and Northeast Ohio will always [be] home," James added.

James helped the Cavs become NBA champions in 2016 and joined the Lakers in 2018, claiming another NBA title two years later.

He has been named the NBA's Most Valuable Player four times, all between 2009 and 2013, and has been an NBA All-Star the last 22 seasons running.

News.title: Huge explosion and fire rip through Essex industrial site
News.content:
A huge explosion triggered by a fire spreading to a store of fertiliser tore through an industrial unit in Essex on Friday, with more than 100 firefighters sent to tackle a massive fire and a "major incident" declared.

Footage which captured the moment of the explosion showed a ball of flames erupting into the air and people fleeing, while witnesses told BBC News the sound was "like a bomb" and as loud as a "sonic boom".

A number of buildings and vehicles on farmland were gutted by the fire, which was expected to keep burning into Saturday.

People living near the fire - which happened close to the village of Rettendon, south of Chelmsford - were urged to keep their windows closed as smoke spread.

News.title: Police declare 'major incident' as wind change increases Cairngorms wildfire risk
News.content:
Police Scotland has declared a major incident as emergency services continue to tackle a wildfire which has been burning in the Cairngorms National Park for 10 days.

The force said it followed "a significant change in weather conditions" which has increased the risk of fire spreading towards the village of Nethy Bridge.

All Nethy Bridge residents have been evacuated to allow emergency services to continue their response.

First Minister John Swinney said "all resources that can be deployed are being deployed".

Smoke from the wildfire can now be seen 59 miles away in Aberdeen following a change in wind direction.

Supt Judy Hill said: "The weather conditions experienced within the Cairngorms over the last 24 hours have added further complexities to this situation.

"With evidence suggesting the fire is spreading towards Nethy Bridge, the decision has been taken to declare a major incident and evacuate residents as a precaution.

"Additional police resources are being deployed to assist in contacting those who need to leave their properties and to maintain cordons around restricted areas while our fire service colleagues continue to tackle the wildfire."

News.title: Slapping therapist jailed over death 'released early'
News.content:
An alternative healer jailed over the death of a woman at one of his workshops has been released from prison just 18 months into a 10-year sentence, it is understood.

Hongchi Xiao, 63, from California, was convicted and sentenced in 2024 for the manslaughter by gross negligence of 71-year-old Danielle Carr-Gomm in 2016.

Carr-Gomm, who was diabetic, died while taking part in a therapy event in Wiltshire, which involved people being slapped or slapping themselves repeatedly.

On Friday, during a Court of Appeal hearing where an application to overturn his conviction was quashed, it emerged Xiao had been returned to the US and was believed to no longer be in custody.

In his judgment, Lord Justice Dingemans said it seemed Xiao had been returned to the US on 2 July through the Early Removal Scheme.

This enables eligible foreign national offenders to be deported from the UK once they have served the minimum required proportion of their sentence.

However, he added: "Other information suggests he was deported on 30 June 2026. It seems that Mr Xiao is not in custody in the USA."

A government spokesperson said: "Hongchi Xiao's crimes were terrible, and our thoughts remain with his victims.

"This government is deporting foreign national offenders at pace, with more than 5,000 deported last year, and Hongchi Xiao is prohibited from ever returning to the UK."

They added if Xiao were to return to the UK, he will be liable to serve the rest of his sentence from the point he was deported.

News.title: Southport killer Axel Rudakubana appears to be manipulating the system, families' lawyer says
News.content:
A lawyer for the families of the children murdered by Southport killer Axel Rudakubana has said his transfer from prison to a psychiatric hospital may be an attempt to "manipulate the system".

Rudakubana, 19, was given a life sentence for the murder of three children - Alice da Silva Aguiar, 9, Bebe King, 6, and Elsie Dot Stancombe, 7 - and attempted murder of eight other children and two adults.

On Thursday, he was moved from HMP Belmarsh to Broadmoor psychiatric hospital in Berkshire.

Prisoners who are considered to present a risk to staff, inmates or themselves because of mental disorders can be moved to hospital under the Mental Health Act.

Next Wednesday marks two years since Rudakubana carried out the attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class on 29 July 2024.

Lawyer Chris Walker, who represents the three bereaved families, said they "don't believe the merits" of the transfer on the basis of a mental health issue and is calling for more information from ministers.

"In my mind this is a new event, this is something which occurred whilst he was at prison, and we at this stage don't believe the merits of it in terms of him because I've seen no evidence at all until today which suggests he has a significant mental health disorder," Walker told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

He added: "We do have an evil person but being evil does not mean that you're suffering with psychosis of some sort.

"We need to know is this a single event, is this a recurring event, is this him playing the system and we need those answers."

The Prison Officers' Association told the BBC that Rudakubana was transferred due to a deterioration in his mental health.

Walker added in a separate statement that the news would "devastate" the families at any time but "the fact that this has occurred as we approach the second anniversary in our view is another move by AR who would appear to be attempting, once again, to manipulate the system".

He continued: "We have been given the barest of details and whilst we are supporting the families through this we are urgently seeking a meeting with the appropriate authorities to understand the situation before commenting further."

A lawyer for the families of the attack's survivors said they did not want to give "notoriety" to Rudakubana and that attention should be focused on supporting the children around the anniversary.

Nicola Ryan-Donnelly of Fletchers Solicitors said: "The focus of public outrage should not be on moves that this perpetrator has made, it should be examining how we are two years on from this attack and some of these girls are still not receiving the proper psychological care and support that they should be to recover from this."

Prior to Rudakubana's sentencing last year, his defence lawyer told the court no psychiatric evidence could suggest a mental disorder contributed to his actions.

The court also heard how Rudakubana presented as having high functioning autism and did not have any associated learning disabilities.

Stan Reiz KC added that his client had appeared to have been a "normal child" until he reached 13, adding: "However, he did make a transition from a normal, well-disciplined child to someone who was capable of committing acts of such shocking and senseless violence."

Rudakubana was deemed mentally fit to be detained, interviewed and stand trial. His late guilty plea meant his mental health was not discussed in detail in court during a trial.

He was given a 52-year prison sentence in January 2025 but the judge was unable to impose a whole life order due to Rudakubana being 17 when he carried out the attack. He will likely never be released.

News.title: Mega dinghy carries record 165 migrants to UK
News.content:
A record 165 migrants reached the UK in a single boat, the Home Office has confirmed.

The number broke the previous record from July, when 128 crossed the Channel from France in one vessel.

Border Security Command was pictured towing a mega dinghy - estimated to be the same size as a standard bus at 13m (42ft) long - when it arrived in Dover on Thursday afternoon.

A Home Office spokesperson said the crossing served as a "stark reminder that criminal gangs have no regard for the safety of those they claim to help".

"The reality is clear and lives are being lost in the Channel," they added.

A total of 162 people died, external in the busy waterway between 2018 and 2025, according to the University of Oxford's Migration Observatory.

This rises to 257 when considering other migration-related deaths in the area, such as accidents involving people trying to board lorries bound for the UK, it added.

News.title: Dad who murdered four-week-old son jailed for 18 years
News.content:
A man who murdered his four-week-old son after drinking up to nine pints of beer on a night out has been jailed for life with a minimum term of 18 years.

Tony Bartlett returned to the family home in Chard, Somerset, on 16 July 2022 and shook baby Atticus in what the sentencing judge described as "a sudden fit of anger".

The 39-year-old caused serious injuries to his son's spinal cord and ribs, as well as brain damage so severe he never regained consciousness or the ability to breathe independently. Atticus died seven days later.

Bartlett, who was convicted after a trial at Bristol Crown Court earlier this month, was jailed for life with a minimum term of 18 years.

Warning: This story contains details which readers may find distressing.

The trial heard the former postman, from Axminster in Devon, had gone to a pub and comedy club with his then-partner Evelyn Ballentyne on the night Atticus was fatally injured.

It was their first evening out since their son's birth.

After they returned home, Ballentyne went upstairs and left Bartlett alone to feed Atticus.

News.title: Fifty women tell BBC they were pressured into having sex with strangers
News.content:
Warning: This story contains details of sexual acts

Fifty women have told the BBC they were pressured or coerced by their partners into having sex with strangers.

They got in contact following an investigation which told the story of a woman who said she had been pressured into having sex with more than 100 people she did not know.

Many of the women who came forward said they had sex through swinging despite not wanting to, either because they feared the consequences of refusing or felt they had to keep their partners happy.

They spoke of deep, long-lasting trauma.

"I remember many nights of my partner keeping me up all night screaming at me, threatening me, and attempting to gaslight me into believing this was something I wanted," said one woman. "It was never what I wanted."

Another told us: "I felt like I had been given away. I felt used. I felt so dirty."

Most encounters were arranged via the website FabSwingers, say the women, which claims to have more than half a million UK active monthly accounts.

Six women told BBC News they had been raped by men met through the site.

One said her partner had forced her to have sex with more than 90 men through FabSwingers. On one occasion, he held her down by the ankles, she told us.

Sixteen said intimate photos of them had been uploaded to the website without their permission.

News.title: Sarah Ferguson's charity formally closes down
News.content:
Sarah Ferguson's charity, Sarah's Trust, has formally wound up and is marked as "removed" on the public register of charities.

The charity said in February it would close "for the foreseeable future" days after new details emerged about the former Duchess of York's friendship with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Among more than three million documents released by the US Department of Justice (DoJ) earlier this year were emails appearing to show Ferguson was in contact with Epstein while he was in prison for soliciting sex from a minor. Being named in the documents does not indicate wrongdoing.

The BBC has contacted Ferguson's representatives for comment on the closure of her charity.

Established in 2020, Sarah's Trust was "dedicated to supporting frontline, grassroots work to address the humanitarian and environmental crisis, the hunger crisis and issues perpetuating cycles of extreme poverty", according to its website.

In February, a spokesperson for the foundation said the decision to close had come after "some months" of discussion.

The foundation did not provide further details behind its decision to close at the time.

The massive drop of files by the DoJ earlier this year suggested Ferguson had been closer to Epstein than previously thought.

In the files, Ferguson was seen praising the late sex offender in 2009 as "the brother I have always wished for".

The emails also suggest she took her daughters along for lunch with him in Miami, days after his release from prison.

Ferguson's representatives have not responded to previous requests for comment on the documents.

The former duchess has already been dropped by multiple charities over her Epstein links.

In October, she lost her duchess title when her ex-husband, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, relinquished his Duke of York title over his links with Epstein, and she was also forced to move out of his Windsor mansion, Royal Lodge, where the couple lived together, despite having divorced in 1996.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention updated its official guidance regarding autism and vaccines, replacing long-standing assurances that immunizations do not cause autism with claims that scientific research has not definitively ruled out a connection.

But the website still suggests a link between vaccines and autism, after President Donald Trump’s Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. directed the agency to revise the website’s language last year to dispute long-held conclusions from large-scale medical studies.

The new changes appear to have been made to secure a crucial confirmation vote for Dr. Erica Schwartz, Trump’s nominee to lead the CDC.

Republican Senator Bill Cassidy, whose support is vital for moving health nominees through the Senate Health Committee, previously signaled that he needed assurances that the agency would uphold scientific integrity before advancing her nomination.

In a revision to its public guidance published July 22, the federal agency said previous statements denying a link between childhood immunizations and autism were not “evidence-based.” The site now notes that the Department of Health and Human Services is launching a comprehensive assessment to evaluate potential root causes of autism, including biological mechanisms and potential causal links.

open image in gallery The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention quietly updated its official guidance regarding autism and vaccines on July 22 after RFK Jr directed changes to challenge conclusions from medical researchers ( Reuters )

According to the updated CDC website, the revision was made pursuant to the Data Quality Act, a federal statute requiring government agencies to ensure the objectivity and integrity of information provided to the public.

The agency stated on the page that previous claims denying a link “have historically been disseminated by the CDC and other federal health agencies within HHS to prevent vaccine hesitancy.”

Sean Kaufman, Trump’s nominee to lead the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response, also appears to be facing hurdles from the Senate committee before a confirmation vote. “There are ongoing conversations with the administration on the path forward for Mr. Kaufman’s nomination,” according to a committee spokesperson.

Kaufman faced sharp questioning during confirmation hearings regarding his past anti-vaccine statements, including comments questioning the routine hepatitis B birth dose and opposing COVID-19 vaccines for healthy children. The agency oversees the nation’s readiness and response to pandemics, bioterrorism and other major public health emergencies.

open image in gallery The website changes appear to have been made so ensure Erica Schwartz, Trump’s nominee to lead the CDC, gets a confirmation vote from skeptical Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy ( AP )

The revised CDC language places particular emphasis on routine shots administered during a child’s first year of life, including immunizations for diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis, Hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type B, inactivated poliovirus and pneumococcal conjugate.

Federal reviews conducted over the last three decades by the Institute of Medicine and the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality found the available data was inconclusive, according to the CDC, which determined that evidence was “inadequate to accept or reject a causal relationship” between vaccines and autism.

The site also raises questions regarding aluminum adjuvants — additives used to boost immune response in several infant vaccines — citing cumulative exposure levels in early childhood to argue that potential links to chronic conditions warrant further scientific study.

Regarding the Measles, Mumps, and Rubella vaccine, the CDC acknowledges that prior reviews maintain a high strength of observational evidence showing no association with autism. The updated site claims most existing MMR studies are flawed because they rely on past population data, ignore potentially vulnerable children and fail to reflect the U.S. vaccination schedule.

HHS noted on the platform that its upcoming research initiatives would evaluate biological mechanisms such as neuroinflammation, aluminum exposure and potential risks for children with mitochondrial disorders.

The agency stated that the website will be updated as new evidence from its comprehensive autism assessment becomes available.

The Independent has contacted the CDC for comment.

British businesses have lost their advantage over the EU after Donald Trump’s latest wave of trade tariffs, experts have warned, despite the overall tariff for UK goods remaining the same.

The US president announced plans on Thursday to hit dozens of countries with renewed tariffs as time-limited levies, introduced in response to a Supreme Court defeat, expire on Friday.

However, while Britain and the EU will face the same 10 per cent tariffs, the bloc has been handed preferable terms thanks to differences between the two deals negotiated with Mr Trump.

The head of the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) said the UK had lost its comparative advantage against the European Union as a result of the new tariffs.

William Bain told the BBC: “There will be some concerns in the business community this morning about what the UK needs to do to get the same treatment the European Union has got here.”

Britain’s 10 per cent tariff remains the same while the EU’s has been reduced from 15 per cent to 10 per cent. However, the Turnberry deal, agreed between the EU and President Trump last year, meant no tariffs could be added to the 15 per cent blanket levy.

Now the tariff has been reduced to 10 per cent, it gives the bloc an edge over the UK for sectors not given specific carveouts in the deal Sir Keir Starmer agreed with the US last year, such as clothing, chemicals, beverages or bikes.

There was some good news for Britain, with a deal removing any tariffs on Scotch whisky announced on Friday, but critics have warned that Britain’s exit from the EU has left it exposed when it comes to trade.

Joe Meighan, policy advisor for the European Movement UK, said: “The UK’s much-vaunted tariff advantage over the European Union has evaporated overnight. It is a timely reminder that chasing preferential treatment from individual trading partners, particularly the US, is no substitute for being part of the world’s largest integrated market.

open image in gallery Donald Trump is now seeking a more durable system using a 1974 trade law after the court overturned his previous import tax regime in February ( AFP/Getty )

“Any limited gains from going it alone are dwarfed by the economic advantages of frictionless access to the European single market. At a time when global trade is becoming more protectionist and economic coercion is on the rise, there is real strength in standing together.

“The EU negotiates from a position of collective economic power that Britain simply cannot match on its own, and today’s tariffs underline why our long-term prosperity lies in rebuilding the closest possible economic relationship with Europe.”

Labour MP Stella Creasy, chair of the Labour Movement for Europe, added: “If we are to protect British business then we need to recognise that even more damaging for Britain than the precise rate of Trump’s tariffs is the fact that we’re out of the room when the EU – which represents five times our GDP – decides its response.

“As the steel tariffs saga has shown, Brexit left us adrift in the middle of a global trade war. If we want growth and security, our reset must do everything possible to address that.”

open image in gallery US trade representative Jamieson Greer pictured in Mexico on Thursday ( Reuters )

The US trade department said the tariffs are being imposed on countries it claims have not taken action to tackle the importing of goods made with forced labour.

The US administration said that the action followed investigations by the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR), which included public hearings, more than 2,100 public comments, and engagement with trading partners “to remedy these longstanding concerns”.

However, the USTR also said there would be product exemptions, where tariffs would lead to a shortage of raw materials domestically, cause economy-wide disruptions or where items cannot be grown or produced in sufficient quantity or at a reasonable price in the US.

There would also be an exemption for products from the UK and other named countries where “that would encourage these economies to fulfil commitments regarding forced labour import prohibitions or to enact and effectively enforce a forced labour import prohibition”.

open image in gallery The Supreme Court overturned Trump’s previous import tax regime in February ( AFP/Getty )

Tariffs are paid by companies in the US which import foreign products and usually move to pass along the cost by charging consumers higher prices.

Americans are already frustrated by the high cost of living, so the administration is taking a risk in rolling out new tariffs ahead of the critical midterm elections in November.

The UK exports more to the US than to any other single country.

In 2024, UK exports to the US were worth £66bn, 17 per cent of all UK goods exports.

The Economic Prosperity Deal agreed between the two countries last year aimed to mitigate the impact of US tariffs on UK industries and deepen commercial ties.

A government spokesperson said: “There is no change to the tariff rate facing UK businesses as a result of this announcement.

“The UK remains on a 10 per cent tariff rate and the preferential access secured under our agreement with the United States remains in place.

“We take forced labour very seriously and ensure that in global supply chains UK businesses are not complicit in forced labour and human rights violations.

“The US has recognised the steps the UK is taking, which is why there are no additional tariffs for the UK under this announcement.”

News.title: Law student charged in connection with ‘dissident republican bomb’ seized near Irish border
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

A law student has been charged after police intercepted a car bomb near the Irish border.

Isobella Perrie Sullivan, 25, of Clane in Co Kildare, appeared before a special sitting of Trim District Court in Co Meath on Friday evening.

Gardaí investigating the incident, which involved a suspected dissident republican bomb, arrested Ms Perrie Sullivan, who was the driver of the car.

In an intelligence-led swoop, members of the Garda’s Special Detective Unit stopped the vehicle travelling on the N2 south of Carrickmacross, Co Monaghan on Wednesday afternoon.

The Garda described the bomb seized from the vehicle as “extremely significant”. It is understood the device found contained suspected military-grade explosives.

Garda sources have described the bomb as “highly sophisticated” and “advanced”. Another suspect, a man aged in his 40s, remains in custody at a Garda station in the Dublin area.

open image in gallery Ireland’s Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan described the seizure as “very worrying” ( PA )

A court hearing heard that during a search of her vehicle, a bag was discovered in the rear seat that contained Semtex and a detonator, the court heard, prompting the area to be evacuated and Ms Perrie Sullivan was arrested.

The court heard that Ms Perrie Sullivan was studying for a law degree and wanted to become a barrister.

Gardaí objected to bail due to the seriousness of the offence.

Defence solicitor Gavin Booth, of Phoenix Law, said his client had been asked to take a bag to the north, and had not been aware what was in it, adding she had been “manipulated”.

Judge Raymond Finnegan agreed to allow bail.

It came with a number of conditions, which included an independent €15,000 surety, that she surrenders her passport, stays at an address approved by Gardaí, has a mobile phone number on which to be available 24/7, to sign in every day at Naas Garda Station and a curfew of 9pm to 7am.

Garda commissioner Justin Kelly confirmed details of the operation as he spoke to media at a Garda graduation event in Co Tipperary on Friday morning.

“To be clear, what we found was an extremely significant seizure,” he said. “So this was an explosive device.”

Commissioner Kelly added: “Any seizure of this nature is really concerning.

“However, we certainly know that there are a small minority of dissident republicans who did not agree with the Good Friday Agreement. They did not put weapons and explosives (out of use), they didn’t, you know, go through with the proper process in relation to decommissioning.

“So that is something that we continue to deal with.

“There’s a small minority of these individuals – I would describe them as radicalised republicans – and this is a threat that we’re going to continue to face for some time in An Garda Síochána.”

Ireland’s minister for justice Jim O’Callaghan described the seizure as “very worrying”.

“I think it evidences the fact that there is an ongoing threat in respect of dissident republican activity,” he said.

“But I also know that there’s been great cooperation between the PSNI and An Garda Síochána and, I think, I suppose the developments recently and the work of An Garda Síochána indicate the benefits of having that close co-operation between the PSNI and An Garda Síochána.”

PSNI assistant chief constable Davy Beck said police on both sides of the Irish border shared a “joint commitment” to tackle the dissident republican terror threat.

open image in gallery DUP leader Gavin Robinson described the development as ‘chilling’ ( PA )

“I very much welcome this significant seizure and the arrests made by our colleagues in An Garda Síochána, with whom we work very closely on a daily basis,” he said.

Northern Ireland secretary Sir Chris Bryant commended the Garda for thwarting a potential attack.

“Intercepting a dangerous device like this undoubtedly saved lives and kept communities safe on both sides of the border,” he said. “Strong cross-border security co-operation remains as vital as ever.”

DUP leader Gavin Robinson described the development as “chilling”.

The east Belfast MP questioned whether the Irish government needed to increase its focus on tackling dissident republicanism.

“All those involved in stopping this deserve enormous credit,” he said.

“Their actions may have prevented innocent families from suffering unimaginable tragedy.”

Sinn Féin Stormont assembly member Gerry Kelly described those responsible for the explosive device as “reckless”.

“Those responsible represent no one, are void of support and have nothing positive to offer our communities. Their actions are entirely reckless,” he said.

“Those involved should abandon their futile actions, leave the stage once and for all, and allow our communities to continue moving forward together in peace.”

A suspect in two stabbings on New York City streets was arrested Friday on attempted murder and other charges, including hate crime charges relating to one of the victims, a Jewish man, police said.

Raul Morales, 51, allegedly yelled the Arabic phrase “Allahu akbar” while attacking two men separately Thursday on Manhattan's Upper West Side, according to police accounts of what witnesses told them.

Police had no immediate comment Friday on how they decided that hate crime laws pertained to the Jewish victim but not the other, who is of Asian descent. Morales was awaiting arraignment, and prosecutors ultimately will decide what charges he faces in court.

As Morales was led out of a police station Friday evening, he shouted about seeking justice for someone. When reporters asked about the stabbings, he responded that he was “gonna talk about it” as he was ushered into a police car.

It wasn't immediately clear whether Morales has an attorney who could comment on the allegations.

The stabbings happened about two blocks apart Thursday afternoon, police said. Both victims were taken to a hospital and were expected to survive. Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said Thursday that there wasn’t any known link between Morales and the victims.

The Asian American Foundation, a New York-based advocacy group, said the attacks “underscore the persistent safety challenges” and mistreatment — from harassment to physical assault — facing Asian Americans in the city.

“We demand continued, meaningful investment in community safety and hate prevention that protects everyone,” the group said in a statement.

Hate crimes in New York City have been on the rise in recent years, while overall violent crime rates have dropped, according to police data. Tisch said in April that more than half of all confirmed hate crimes in the city so far this year targeted Jewish people.

Gov. Kathy Hochul said she was disgusted by Thursday's attacks and emphasized that New York stands with its Jewish and Asian communities.

“Asian New Yorkers, like Jewish New Yorkers, have endured waves of hate-fueled violence in recent years,” she said in a post on X. “Hate rarely stops with one group. New York will continue confronting it wherever it appears.”

A major incident was declared and over 100 firefighters called after fertiliser exploded during a blaze which engulfed insutrial units and a field in Essex.

Essex County Fire and Rescue Service said crews were called to farmland in Southend Road, between East Hanningfield and Rettendon, on Friday afternoon.

A number of industrial units and a field caught alight, and while fire crews were on scene fertiliser inside one of the units exploded – which people across the county reported hearing and seeing, area manager Dave Bond said.

Locals said an explosion shook houses and sent a huge mushroom cloud towering into the sky.

East of England Ambulance Service said they were responding to a "significant incident".

Pictures show large plumes of dark smoke in the air which can be seen for several miles.

According to the fire service’s call logs, the fire was first reported at 4:50pm and is ongoing, with firefighters expected to remain at the scene overnight.

Steven Whan, 58, from Bicknacre, near Danbury, told the BBC he thought he had heard a jet's sonic boom when the explosion occurred.

"Our house shook, the doorbell went off. I thought it was a sonic boom because we've experienced that before," he says.

Whan adds: "The police have blocked off everything. You can't get nowhere near it."

Another local, David Harris, who lives about six miles away from the blaze, said: "It sounded as though somebody dropped a sort of pallet of bricks or something just over the road, it was that loud, it was incredible."

The emergency services have advised local residents to keep their windows and doors shut, while roads in the surrounding area have been shut by police.

Mr Bond said: “This is a significant fire but we have it under control and there is no wider risk to members of the public.

“A number of industrial units have caught alight as well as a field and crews have been working to prevent the fire spreading to nearby houses.

“While on the scene, fertiliser inside one of the units exploded and residents across the county have reported hearing and feeling it.

“This is why we declared a major incidents and I want to reassure our residents that there is no wider risk to the public at this time.

“Everybody at the scene is safe, residents nearby have been evacuated while we put the fire out and Southend Road is currently closed to allow us more space to work safely.

“We expect to be at the scene throughout the night. It is producing lots of smoke so we recommended keeping your windows and doors shut if you live nearby.

“Roads will remain closed, please avoid the area and thanks for your patience.”

Brazil’s Ministry of Indigenous Peoples said Friday it has signed a memorandum of understanding with Peru’s Ministry of Culture to strengthen cooperation in protecting Indigenous territories, particularly those of isolated peoples along the border between the two countries.

The agreement, which the Brazilian government said is expected to be published in the coming weeks, has been under negotiation since 2024. It will establish a framework for sharing information and coordinating protection efforts, the ministry said.

The announcement comes after a group of Ashaninka Indigenous leaders began meetings with federal officials in Brasilia, Brazil's capital, seeking urgent protection for their territory.

Earlier this month, five armed men carrying machine guns invaded their land, threatened families and searched for their main leaders. The Ashaninka territory spans the Brazil-Peru border in the western Amazon.

The ministry said that safeguarding Indigenous territories and the communities living there requires a “coordinated response to shared threats, such as invasions, illegal activities and pressure on traditional lands.”

Peru’s Ministry of Culture could not immediately be reached for comment.

Gangs and drug traffickers are increasingly encroaching on Ashaninka land and using the rivers in the Amazon and adjacent land for drug routes. The recent invasion is part of a broad transformation of the Amazon border as criminal routes expand, through what experts call the Solimoes River route.

Indigenous territories are key to this route. Experts say protecting Indigenous land is one of the most effective ways to curb deforestation in the Amazon, the world’s largest rainforest and a key regulator of global climate. But the very forests these communities help protect leave them vulnerable: Dense tree cover in remote, hard-to-reach areas offers attractive hiding sites for drug traffickers.

The ministry also said the federal police opened an investigation into the attacks on Ashaninka territory. On Monday, they launched an operation in the region alongside state authorities.

“The operation aims to prevent and combat incursions into Indigenous territories, criminal organizations, drug trafficking, environmental crimes and other cross-border offenses,” it said.

In a separate statement, the Brazilian Army said it had reinforced its presence along the border by deploying about 30 troops to the area. Various Indigenous groups have previously criticized these deployments for being temporary while the threats remain permanent.

The Army said it continues to patrol the region and that preliminary information from Indigenous leaders and government agencies suggests the armed men were Peruvians who entered the Indigenous territory from across the border.

A federal judge in Virginia has declared illegal a requirement from President Joe Biden's administration that mandated special certification for doctors and pharmacies to prescribe the abortion medication mifepristone.

U.S. District Judge Robert Ballou, presiding in Charlottesville, Virginia, stated on Thursday that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) failed to justify the necessity of the 2023 requirements, especially given its repeated affirmations of mifepristone's safety and effectiveness.

"Nor does the FDA explain how, without these restrictions, prescribing the drug becomes an intolerable risk which would require withdrawal of the drug from the market," wrote Judge Ballou, a Biden appointee.

This ruling stems from a 2023 lawsuit filed by three abortion providers.

While Judge Ballou can compel the FDA to reconsider the rule, he noted federal law does not currently allow him to strike it down. He may, however, invalidate the rule later when addressing separate claims that it infringes upon the providers' constitutional rights. The FDA, which is conducting a broader safety review of mifepristone under President Donald Trump, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday.

The decision arrives amidst widespread efforts by Republican-led states and anti-abortion organizations to curtail access to mifepristone, a drug central to over 60% of U.S. abortions.

Abortion Pill Politics ( Copyright 2022 The Associated Press. All rights reserved )

Initially approved by the FDA in 2000, mifepristone's access has gradually expanded, including a separate Biden-era regulation permitting its prescription and dispensing via mail. The U.S. Supreme Court allowed this mail-order rule to remain in effect in May, pending a legal challenge paused until the FDA concludes its review.

Mifepristone, a component of a two-drug abortion regimen, has become a focal point in the abortion debate since the Supreme Court's 2022 decision overturning Roe v. Wade, which eliminated the constitutional right to abortion and empowered individual states to impose bans.

The Center for Reproductive Rights, an advocacy group representing the providers in the lawsuit, emphasized the significance of Judge Ballou's ruling. In a statement, they highlighted that it reinforces mifepristone's safety and efficacy at a time when its availability is under scrutiny.

Nancy Northup, the group's president, asserted: "The efforts to restrict it are not about science or safety — they are about making abortion harder to access."

Beijing announced Friday that China's top police chief and the director of the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation have committed to enhancing law enforcement cooperation following their meeting in the Chinese capital.

During talks with FBI Director Kash Patel, China's Minister of Public Security, Wang Xiaohong, stated that both sides should "engage in more constructive dialogue on the basis of mutual respect and deepen practical cooperation" against a range of criminal activities, an official Chinese summary showed.

Their meeting followed two recent repatriations of fugitives between China and the United States, which do not share an extradition treaty.

Patel said on X that he welcomed the direct engagements with Chinese public security officials, which he said has produced results in shutting off fentanyl precursor pipelines and expanding joint efforts on scam centers, violent crimes against children and a fugitive task force.

On Thursday, China's Public Security Ministry said it had handed over to U.S. law enforcement authorities a U.S. fugitive wanted for serious violent crimes, including the suspected murder of a spouse and the sexual assault of a young girl.

( Reuters )

Chinese and U.S. law enforcement agencies have recently carried out "a series of practical cooperation in areas such as counter-narcotics, repatriation of illegal immigrants, fugitive recovery, combating telecom and cyber fraud, and anti-money laundering", the ministry said.

It added that such cooperation was in line with a consensus reached between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Days earlier, the U.S. repatriated to Beijing a fugitive accused of kidnapping and killing Chinese citizens overseas, Chinese state media said. The repatriation was hailed by Beijing as "the latest achievement" in implementing the presidents' consensus.

The FBI's Patel visited Beijing in November 2025 to discuss fentanyl and law enforcement issues, following a summit in October of that year between Trump and Xi, when the two leaders agreed on cooperation to fight fentanyl trafficking, Reuters reported.

The two presidents are set to meet again in Washington in September, Trump has said.

News.title: Britain to pay higher Trump tariffs than EU
News.content:
Britain will pay higher tariffs than the EU after Donald Trump’s latest global trade onslaught.

Bosses in Britain have warned they will lose any competitive advantage over the bloc after the US President announced higher import taxes on goods from 60 trading partners.

The US administration imposed 10pc tariffs on both Britain and the EU to replace levies which expired overnight following a Supreme Court ruling earlier this year.

Britain must pay the import taxes on top of so-called Most Favoured Nation tariffs imposed on all members of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).

However, from Friday, the EU’s tariffs are inclusive of the WTO levies. The average WTO tariff rate is between 2.4pc to 3.5pc for non-agricultural food products.

William Bain, head of trade policy at the BCC, said: “There will be concerns about the loss of the UK’s competitive advantage over the EU and other countries which have secured a more favourable deal in other goods sectors.”

A government spokesman said: “There is no negative ‌change ‌to ⁠the tariff rate facing UK businesses as a result of this ⁠announcement.”

“Our agreement with the US remains in place, and today we see ​an improvement to our ‌trading terms with zero tariffs on whisky and medical technology.”

Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, said Scottish whisky distilleries would get a “boost” from the new tariff regime, which removes levies on scotch under a deal first announced during the King’s state visit to the US in April.

On Friday, Trump also threatened new tariffs on the European Union in response to billions worth of fines imposed on US tech giants by competition regulators.

In a post on his social media platform Truth Social, Trump said: “The United States of America is not a “PIGGYBANK” for Europe, nor will we allow it to be!”

The US president said he expected to impose “substantial tariffs” on the EU after the European Commission fined Google €890m (£760m) on Thursday.

UK and European stock markets shrugged off the latest tariffs, with the FTSE 100 up 0.9pc.

However, Wall Street was more mixed. The S&P 500 was roughly flat, while the Nasdaq Composite was down 1.1pc. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 0.3pc near the end of Friday’s trading session.

It followed dramatic falls in Asia overnight, with Japan’s Nikkei falling 2.7pc and South Korea’s Kospi down 5.7pc.

News.title: Mason Mount offering Michael Carrick a midfield solution which could have legs
News.content:
It is not uncommon to hear football club executives talking about the importance of the “money being on the pitch”.

In other words, managers having their best players fit and available most if not all of the time. Quality at the top level is essential but so is robustness. They go hand in hand.

Unfortunately for Manchester United, the money has not been on the pitch down the years nearly as much as the club would want or expect.

Bruno Fernandes stands out for what he does with the ball primarily, but also because he plays almost every minute of every game and, while his sheer indefatigability is extreme, United know they need more of his ilk.

This is why the forthcoming season is such a big one for Mason Mount. His quality has seldom been in doubt. The problem is he has rarely been on the pitch long or consistently enough to show it.

Indeed, the one-time England midfielder has started just 25 Premier League matches since his £60m move from Chelsea three years ago and that perennial unavailability is one of the reasons doubts were being cast about his Old Trafford future going into this summer.

Yet Michael Carrick was keen to keep Mount, United have rebuffed inquiries around him and intriguingly the 27-year-old could yet have an impact on what the club do during the remaining six weeks of the transfer window.

For the second time in the space of six days, Mount was deployed in a deeper midfield role alongside new £48m, signing Andrey Santos for Friday’s resounding 5-0 victory over Norwegian side Rosenborg in Trondheim, just as he had done against Wrexham last weekend.

News.title: Eleanor Cardwell: ‘Comfortable sportswear should not be expensive’
News.content:
What sports shoes do you recommend?

Robert, South West

The sports shoes that I’m currently wearing are from Puma. They’re very comfortable and have support. I actually wear a basketball shoe at the minute to have more support up the ankle.

A lot of the girls wear Asics as well, which I know is the netball shoe. I’ve worn Puma for the last four years, so I would recommend them.

But honestly, whatever works best for you, you have to try them out. Whatever is best for your instep and whatever is comfiest. And if you need more ankle support, you can put some ankle braces on.

How has playing for Manchester Thunder helped you develop as a player?

Jason, London

Manchester has massively helped me develop as a player. I’ve been playing here since 2012. As a young girl, it created me as a person, to be honest with you. It’s such a family environment that I think a lot of my values come from this club. So my family values, being connected, creating energy – all those things come rooted from this club, which is incredible.

I think whatever step you are in your career, whether you’re a young athlete or senior, they help you develop. Even now I’m 31, they’re still helping me learn new things on the court. The coaches are incredible, and I’m constantly learning and being inspired by them every single week.

Do players retire from elite netball quite young?

Helen, South West

I think it depends on the athlete. Some can retire at 40, and that’s because their bodies are so conditioned, and they might not have had any major injuries in their career. They’re able to continue to push themselves all the way until 40.

But I’d say the average is probably mid-30s. Now the Super League has become professional, the younger athletes are getting better training from a younger age. We want to keep pushing ourselves to play as long as possible.

How can netball get more coverage when women’s football is constantly pushed?

Sarah, South West

I think netball needs to have more sponsors to get more media coverage. Bigger sponsors.

Players need to put their personalities more out there on social media, so brands will want to work with us. Everyone’s got amazing personalities in netball. They [brands] should want to be a part of the netball players’ stories and the netball teams.

But it’s about getting as much exposure as possible, and making sure that everyone is going on YouTube or BBC, so more people are able to learn about the sport.

I loved netball at school. How do I get involved now in my 60s?

Sue, Yorkshire

Netball is for everyone. I personally love going to walking netball sessions and taking them through classes. You can go to the England Netball website and find out where you can play locally.

There’s also Back to Netball, depending on your ability and what you want to get out of it. Personally, I think walking netball is so much fun. The women who are in those sessions are a huge laugh, and I know when I retire, I’m going to be joining a group, for sure.

Apart from netball, what other hobbies do you have? How do they help you relieve the pressure of competition?

George, London

I feel like over the past few years I’ve really got into some new hobbies. I love reading. I love fantasy reading, like Throne of Glass. I love BookTok, so I’ve really got into that.

I’m also very crafty. I like making things – I’ve made little crochet bees for all the girls, and I like drawing, and painting occasionally – just wholesome activities to take me away from netball life. As soon as I zone in on an activity, I’m locked in and I have to complete it.
