World.title: Trump administration concedes that it canceled research grants in blue states
World.content:
The Trump administration admitted that it terminated nearly 300 federal research grants “solely because” the projects were connected to states that voted against President Donald Trump in 2024 and had two Democratic senators in office, according to court filings.

Subscribe to read this story ad-free Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

The administration made the admission in a court filing this month responding to a lawsuit brought by University of California researchers challenging the cancellation.

In the filing, the administration wrote as an undisputed statement of fact that on a list of more than 2,300 financial assistance awards across the Department of Energy, 624 grants on these lists were designated either “termination” or “cancel.”

Of those 624 grants, Jeff Novak, the principal deputy general counsel of the Department of Energy, wrote that in October 2025 the Office of Management and Budget identified 284 specific grants that were marked to be terminated.

Novak wrote that with one exception, “the 284 terminated grants had a recipient location and/or at least one place of performance in a state that awarded its electoral votes to Kamala Harris in the 2024 election and has two Democratic-caucusing Senators.”

Novak added that the remaining 340 grants proposed for termination were ultimately not canceled in October 2025 nor since then.

“All such grants had a recipient location and/or at least one place of performance in a state that awarded its electoral votes to President Trump in the 2024 election or has at least one Republican-caucusing Senator,” Novak wrote of the unterminated grants.

Novak wrote that the decision to cancel the grants listed in the October notice tranche — those 284 — was not “based on any programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction, or performance-based factor.”

“DOE accepts that the inclusion of grants in the October notice tranche was based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient’s state, i.e., whether the recipient’s location and/or place of performance was in a Blue State or a non-Blue State,” Novak wrote.

He added that the Department of Energy “will not contend that it looked beyond the prime grantee(s) to consider the political identity or geographic distribution of downstream beneficiaries of the grant funds.”

The New York Times first reported this filing.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Department of Energy argued in a statement Friday that court filings did not show that termination decisions were made on a political basis.

“That is a misrepresentation of the court filing and of Mr. Novak’s words,” Ben Dietderich, press secretary for the Energy Department, said in a statement. “None of the termination decisions were based on political considerations. Secretary Wright has explained this numerous times in briefings on Capitol Hill.”

In an appearance before the House Science, Space and Technology Committee in June, Energy Secretary Chris Wright denied that decisions made around grant cancellations were partisan.

“No decisions were made on politics. I keep hearing that charge. It’s bulls---t. We’re going to say it a million times,” Wright said.

In a social media post in October, when the 284 grants were canceled, OMB Director Russ Vought wrote, “Nearly $8 billion in Green New Scam funding to fuel the Left’s climate agenda is being cancelled.”

Vought listed 16 states where projects were canceled, including California, New York, Colorado, Vermont and New Jersey, among others.

The filing comes as the Office of Management and Budget proposed a new rule that would allow political appointees to gain unprecedented control over the $1 trillion per year that is provided by federal grants.

The office argues that the rule is meant to ensure that grants align with the sitting president’s priorities and to improve oversight. The rule proposes that political appointees screen grant applications to ensure they do not “promote anti-American values,” and they could terminate grants they saw as “no longer in the Federal Government’s interest.”

The 284 federal grants canceled by the Department of Energy are just one sect of funding that has been targeted by the Trump administration.

Since Trump began his second term, the administration has canceled grants for including mentions of DEI and has frozen research funding at universities like Harvard based on allegations of antisemitism.

Trump has also threatened to pull funding from states that do not conform to his policies. In January, he said he would deny federal funding to states that resisted his anti-immigration agenda and had so-called sanctuary cities.

World.title: Upper West Side double stabbing suspect facing hate crime charges
World.content:
The suspect in Thursday's double stabbing on New York City's Upper West Side has been charged with attempted murder as a hate crime, among other things.

The two stabbing victims come from two different communities that share a belief that something must change to keep people safe.

Charges in NYC double stabbing

Raul Morales, 51, has been charged with attempted murder as a hate crime, assault as a hate crime, and criminal possession of a weapon for stabbing Moshe Grunhaus, a 50-year-old Jewish man, police say.

For the stabbing attack on a 57-year-old Asian man, police say Morales has also been charged with criminal possession of a weapon, along with attempted murder and assault – but not as a hate crime for this instance.

Both victims are expected to survive.

Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch says the suspect allegedly yelled "Allahu Akbar" during both attacks.

Morales lives in an apartment building not far from where the attacks took place. Law enforcement executed a search warrant there Friday, and investigators were seen carrying out a laptop and a bag of books, including the Quran and a book about Che Guevara.

It's not clear if the items belong to Morales. We're told Morales lived in the apartment with other people.

One neighbor of Morales' told CBS News New York he never says a word to her, even when she says good morning.

Morales has no known mental health history with the NYPD, but Tisch says the initial investigation suggests mental health may have been a factor.

Police say Morales' prior criminal history includes two open drug arrests in 1991 and five sealed arrests.

"I am thankful that [Morales] is being held accountable and hope he will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. This kind of despicable violence is not who we are as a city," Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement, in part. "Every New Yorker deserves to be safe, regardless of their religion or race. Our administration will always stand against bigotry and do everything in our power to root out antisemitism, racism, and hateful acts of all kinds."

"It can't go on like this"

Rabbi Yosie Levine, of the Jewish Center, said he has known Grunhaus for the past decade, and that he is devoted to the Jewish community.

Levine said Grunhaus had been praying at his synagogue Thursday moments before he was stabbed.

"Moshe had just gotten up to leave at around 1:30 after having spent the whole morning and beginning of the afternoon with us, and for this to happen 200 feet from our synagogue is just, it's almost hard to believe," he said.

Levine visited Grunhaus at the hospital Friday morning and said he was released later that afternoon.

"I was happy to see him. I was very relieved to see him alert and in relatively good spirits, all things considered," Levine said. "He was surrounded by good friends and family."

He added, "I would say in the 22 years that I've been serving as a rabbi in this community, I never visited with a stab victim in the hospital, and I never visited with a victim of a hate crime in the hospital ... There's a real person whose whole life is turned upside down because of this. It can't go on like this. It's intolerable."

The rabbi said Grunhaus recently moved to Florida and was just back in town for a couple days to tie up loose ends when this happened.

The second stabbing victim remains in the hospital but is doing well, according to a spokesperson for the Mount Sinai Health System.

World.title: South Carolina on cusp of being first 2028 Democratic presidential primary state
World.content:
South Carolina is one step away from becoming the first-in-the-nation Democratic presidential primary state for 2028, after the Democratic National Committee's Rules and Bylaws Committee voted to recommend it at a meeting Friday.

The proposed calendar will be voted on by the full DNC at its summer meeting next month in Austin, Texas.

The other top contender was Nevada, and the panel grappled with whether the party should prioritize its most consistent voting bloc or the fastest-growing demographic group in the country.

In its presentation before the bylaws committee in May, South Carolina representatives argued that it should remain the first primary state in light of the Supreme Court decision on the Voting Rights Act and its impact on Black representation in the South. The Palmetto State also held the first Democratic presidential primary in 2024.

South Carolina advocates have said that removing its status as the first primary contest now would be a "slap in the face" to the Democratic Party's Black voter base.

"This decision is bigger than South Carolina. It's about whether the Democratic Party will stand with the voters who have stood with the party through everything," South Carolina Democratic Party Chair Christale Spain said in May. "Will Democrats meet this moment by supporting the communities on the front lines of defending democracy, or will the Democratic Party tell their most faithful voters they no longer deserve to lead the primary process?"

Advocates for Nevada argued it should be first to weigh in on the presidential nominee because it most closely represents a coalition Democrats need to win nationally. Nevada, they said, includes groups whose support for Democrats has been eroding, like working-class voters, Latinos, Asian American Pacific Islanders, men and low-propensity voters.

Nevada Democratic Party Chair Daniele Monroe-Moreno echoed this sentiment Friday during the debate over the proposed calendar order.

"Nonpartisan voter registration is the largest voter registration bloc in America now. Why? Because people are mad at both sides of the aisle," Monroe-Moreno said.

And as Democrats consider their nomination calendar, she told the committee, "My state, the state of Nevada, is that coalition that we need to win back."

The committee also voted on the other states that will hold the earliest presidential nomination contests in 2028, settling on these states and dates:

South Carolina: Jan. 22, 2028

Nevada: Feb. 1, 2028

New Mexico: Feb. 15, 2028

Michigan: Feb. 22, 2028

Virginia: Feb. 29, 2028

Super Tuesday: March 7, 2028

Spain told CBS News in an interview after Friday's meeting that the calendar gives significant weight to Latinos and expands the party's reach.

"What we did also is expand our map in a way that I don't think we've ever even imagined that we could by adding New Mexico," Spain said. It "adds a plethora of opportunities to engage with the Latino community," she added.

DNC Chairman Ken Martin has sought to ensure that the calendar selection process has been as democratic as possible.

In remarks Thursday, Martin said that he and the Rules and Bylaws Committee had taken pains to avoid repeating the 2024 selection process, and he criticized former President Biden for cutting the party out of the decision-making.

In 2022, Biden sent a letter to DNC leaders, urging them to make South Carolina the first nominating contest in 2024. The letter upended the debate in the Rules and Bylaws Committee about the order of the nominating contests, and the party ultimately complied with his request. In 2020, Biden had lost the earliest contests in Iowa, New Hampshire and Nevada, and it was his overwhelming victory in South Carolina that salvaged his candidacy.

Martin said Biden's push to make South Carolina the first primary created "an unfortunate ending" to the selection process, and the party "had the outcome dictated to us."

But a president running for reelection, as Biden was in 2024, is the de facto head of the party and wields significant power over the nomination process and the party platform and messaging.

This year, Martin said the committee is trying to set a calendar that ensures a rigorous process that will battle-test presidential candidates and will not be too costly ahead of the general campaign.

"What we did was about making sure we're in the best possible position to win. But it's also setting down a marker of where our values are, what our party stands for, and most importantly, who we're fighting for," Martin said.

World.title: Paramount says it will pause its Warner acquisition while legal challenges play out
World.content:
Paramount says it will pause its Warner acquisition while legal challenges play out

Jae C. Hong/Associated Press



The blockbuster merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery is on hold — possibly for many months — as two legal challenges to the $111 billion deal play out in court.

In a legal filing in federal court in California on Friday, Paramount says it has agreed not to take any steps to acquire Warner until June 1, 2027, or five days after the lawsuits are resolved, if that comes first.

The proposed deal would unite Paramount and Warner's film studios, streamers Paramount+ and HBO, and dozens of cable channels, along with CBS and CNN.

Sponsor Message

But Paramount is battling a pair of lawsuits filed by a consortium of 12 states and from the Writers Guild of America, which represents many entertainment professionals who work in Hollywood.

The Democratic attorneys general and the Writers Guild allege that Paramount's purchase of Warner Bros. would reduce competition, hurting filmgoers along with TV and news consumers and especially those who create entertainment programming and the news content that the public relies on.

Earlier this week, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín granted a temporary restraining order to pause the acquisition. Martínez-Olguín has yet to sign the agreement filed Friday.

In a statement, New York Attorney General Leticia James wrote, "Halting this merger while our case proceeds is a critical victory in our efforts to uphold the law and protect the film and television industries."

"Our argument against this illegal merger is straightforward: When too few corporations have too much power in markets central to American life, it makes things more expensive, and it makes things worse," said California Attorney General Rob Bonta.

The delay will have huge financial costs for Paramount. Starting Oct. 1, Paramount has to pay Warner shareholders a "ticking consideration" of roughly $650 million for every 90 days the deal is set back. If the deal is not closed by June 4, 2027, Paramount would have to pay Warner $7 billion according to the terms of the deal that Warner shareholders approved.

Sponsor Message

A Paramount spokesperson confirmed those fees are not affected by the latest development.

Paramount said in a statement that the company looks forward to going to trial.

"Today's agreement is a significant win because the result is exactly what we have sought from the outset: a direct path to a trial based on the evidence," the statement said. "This is the fastest and clearest way to prove that this transaction is good for competition, good for consumers, and good for creators, a conclusion dozens of competition authorities around the world have already reached."

The proposed deal has gotten scrutiny outside Hollywood for the relationship between Paramount's controlling family and President Trump — especially because two major newsrooms would be under that family's control.

The merger is largely bankrolled by Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, the father of Paramount CEO David Ellison and a close ally of Trump. Trump has long accused CNN of being "fake news" and has publicly mused about what he'd like to do to the cable news giant.

World.title: Democrats approve new primary election calendar, putting South Carolina first
World.content:
Democrats approve new primary election calendar, putting South Carolina first

toggle caption Sean Rayford/Getty Images/Getty Images North America

South Carolina was chosen to hold the first Democratic presidential primary in 2028 after a panel voted on the calendar Friday afternoon. The move was pushed by key Democrats to prioritize Black voters, a reliable and influential voting bloc for the party.

The Democratic National Committee's Rules and Bylaws panel recommended South Carolina vote first over Nevada, New Hampshire and Iowa, who had each been seeking the first spot. Only six states will be permitted to hold primaries before Super Tuesday on March 7, 2028.

The order recommended by the panel is South Carolina's primary, to be held on Jan. 22, 2028, followed by Nevada and New Hampshire, which are typically early voting states. New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia would also be permitted to hold early contests. This calendar will be presented to the full DNC in August, to be voted on and finalized.

Sponsor Message

South Carolina and the other five states could now hold early nominating contests, a play they have been pushing for since the start of this year.

During the committee meeting Friday some states' party leaders and allies were making cases for why their state should go early.

"The place to start is in the West," said David McDonald, a member of the committee, "The place to start is in Nevada, which offers the best combination of diversity, certainty and opportunity."

McDonald was likely referring to Nevada's diverse population of Latino, Black, Asian American and Pacific Islander, Native American and working class voters.

Nevada was considered alongside South Carolina because the party also wants to prioritize Latino voters, a voting group that had a significant election impact in 2024 when President Trump won reelection. Because 2028 is an open primary, advocates for these two states argue they give candidates the best chance to be tested by influential voting blocs. At the end, some members raised concerns about Nevada being able to rapidly process election results.

South Carolina previously led the Democratic presidential primary in 2024 — the first time the process didn't start with the Iowa caucuses and New Hampshire's primary election. Some members of the panel spoke about the southern state's role in former President Joe Biden's 2020 nomination. Biden picked up his first early state victory in South Carolina that year, before winning other southern states on Super Tuesday.

Sponsor Message

Nearly one in four registered voters in South Carolina is Black, according to state voting data. According to AP Vote Cast, 83% of Black voters nationwide backed former Vice President Kamala Harris in the last presidential election.

"The South is not the past, we are the future," said Christale Spain, chair of the South Carolina Democratic Party. "And if we are serious about changing this country, Democrats have to start winning in the South."

Spain said Democrats need to demonstrate that they are serious about making the investment in the South, adding that South Carolina has a lot of flexibility for its election dates and two weeks of early voting.

South Carolina allies said that the party should show that Black voters are a priority for them in a year when the Supreme Court's Voting Rights Act decision led to multiple states drawing new Congressional boundaries in districts that had previously ruled in violation of that law.

The six states picked to be first together tell the story of who the Democratic party is, said Debbie Dingell, a congresswoman from Michigan, urging members to not read too much into who was given the first slot. Michigan will also vote early in the current plan.

World.title: ICC member states vote to remove chief prosecutor Karim Khan
World.content:
ICC member states vote to remove chief prosecutor Karim Khan

toggle caption Peter Dejong/AP

UNITED NATIONS — The International Criminal Court voted to remove the global tribunal's chief prosecutor on Friday, nearly two years after sexual misconduct allegations against him first emerged, the court's oversight body announced.

British barrister Karim Khan was accused of sexual misconduct with a female aide, as outlined by The Associated Press in a series of stories, allegations which he has steadfastly denied.

By a large majority, the ICC's 125-member states ousted Khan from his position, the first time a chief prosecutor has ever been removed from office.

The court's oversight body, the Assembly of States Parties, concluded that Khan had committed "serious misconduct and serious breach of duty," said Päivi Kaukoranta, the body's president.

Sponsor Message

The 56-year-old Khan was temporarily removed from his duties at the ICC in June, pending Friday's vote, after a report by the executive committee of the court's oversight body found he had committed "serious misconduct." According to documents seen by the AP, Khan engaged in a sexual relationship with the woman and tried to prevent her from pursuing her allegations. Khan disputes those findings.

Early in the session, a motion brought by Sierra Leone that would have made it harder to oust Khan failed and diplomats quickly moved forward to vote on removal, several hours ahead of schedule, according to three diplomats familiar with the proceedings.

The lengthy and complicated process has pitted human rights advocates, staff and member states against one another at a time when the court is already facing daunting challenges, including a campaign by the United States to "dismantle" the ICC, which was established to prosecute people responsible for humanity's worst crimes.

In a statement last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. was launching a "sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court to U.S. sovereignty."

Rubio said he will pressure member states to withdraw from the institution, sanction organizations that work with the court and ban staff from traveling to the United States. Countries that "enjoy the benefits of the U.S. security umbrella" will be called upon to reject the court's jurisdiction over U.S. citizens.

Sponsor Message

Hours after the vote, Venezuela announced it would withdraw from the court. "Venezuela considers that the Court's actions reflect a demonstrated geographical bias, which has disproportionately concentrated its work on African and Latin American countries, to the detriment of the Global South," Félix Plasencia, the country's foreign affairs minister announced in a statement. Earlier this year, prosecutors at the court announced they were dropping an investigation into whether U.S. sanctions against Venezuela qualified as crimes against humanity, citing a lack of evidence. A separate investigation into possible crimes committed by Venezuelan security forces under former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro will continue.

Trump's administration already has brought sanctions against Khan and a dozen other ICC staff in retaliation for warrants the court has issued for top Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, over the war in Gaza and investigations into U.S. personnel in Afghanistan.

"Karim Khan believed that by launching a political witch hunt against Israel and issuing a politically motivated arrest warrant against Prime Minister Netanyahu, the world would ignore the grave sexual misconduct allegations against him. He was wrong," Israel's ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, said in a statement.

The allegations have become entwined with the court's investigation into the war in Gaza, experts said.

"Political considerations have been folded into this, especially as it is the first time a prosecutor has pursued warrants against a Western ally," Iva Vukusic, a researcher at Utrecht University who has been following the process, told the AP.

Khan's removal will have no immediate impact on the arrest warrants in 2024 for Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for crimes against humanity, which can only be withdrawn by ICC judges.

World.title: How The Illharmonic's mix of hip-hop and classical builds community, one show at a time
World.content:
How The Illharmonic's mix of hip-hop and classical builds community, one show at a time

toggle caption Brianna Scott/NPR

Vocalist and composer Jeffrey McNeill says it was back in 1987, when he was still a kid, when he first started hearing the links between hip-hop and classical music.

"I was put in flute and piano lessons as a child, and my father introduced me to The Sugarhill Gang, 'Rapper's Delight,'" McNeill explained in an interview with All Things Considered. "One day, my brother brought home the Beastie Boys' 'Paul Revere,' and to me, it sounded like it went perfectly with Beethoven's 5th Symphony."

Nearly 40 years later, the marriage of those two genres — as well as McNeill's literal marriage to fellow artist Andrea Coln McNeill — are manifest in The Illharmonic Orchestra, which has booked shows in major concert venues across the country over the last two decades.

Sponsor Message

McNeill — who performs as "Thee Phantom" — and Coln McNeill — who is also known as "The Phoenix" — blend hip-hop and R&B vocals with live horns, woodwinds, strings and percussion, performed by all-Black orchestral ensembles. That representation in classical music performance is a key goal for the group's leaders.

"It was really important for us to show that these two genres are not as completely different as people think they are," Coln McNeill told NPR's Juana Summers during a visit to NPR headquarters.

"Even in 2026, some of the major symphony orchestras still are really lacking in diversity. But there's clearly a reflection that those individuals exist. We play with them all the time," she explained. "Folks who look like us, who play these instruments, who have the training, who have been to the conservatory, who have the Ph.D.s, or self-taught — we know that that talent level exists within the folks that look like us."

And for many of their audiences, the experience can be transformative, said McNeill — on top of being a lot of fun.

"It's a house party in a concert hall. It's a community experience," he said. "And it has helped the performances so much that the people actually get it, and they connect with the music and they connect with us, and they see us on stage and they see themselves in us on stage. And that's really kind of what's kept us going for this long."

Sponsor Message

Ahead of a performance at the Lincoln Theater in Washington, D.C., The Illharmonic Orchestra stopped by NPR to offer a special performance.

Listen to the full interview and their performance by clicking on the blue button above, and you can find their performance schedule here .

Audio for this performance chat was engineered by Andie Huether and Tiffany Vera Castro.

World.title: A former nun explains why she ran away from her 'Cloistered' life

World.title: Oil surges to $100 per barrel. And, Trump imposes a new round of tariffs
World.content:
Oil surges to $100 per barrel. And, Trump imposes a new round of tariffs

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

The House yesterday approved a resolution to remove U.S. forces from the war in Iran as the conflict continues to escalate in the Middle East. The non-binding resolution reflects lawmakers' disapproval of a war they did not vote to authorize. It marked the second such rebuke passed by the House since the war began. Soon after the House vote, Senate Democrats attempted to advance their own war powers resolution, but it failed 47 to 49. In the past two weeks of renewed fighting, the U.S. has launched strikes on Iran, while Iran has targeted American bases in the Gulf and Jordan, impacting global energy markets.

toggle caption J. Scott Applewhite/AP

🎧 Brent crude oil reached its highest level since May yesterday when it surged more than 6% to $100 a barrel, NPR's Hadeel Al-Shalchi tells Up First. The spike will impact everyday people, increasing costs for school supplies and fresh food. Shipping companies like UPS are tacking on fuel surcharges. Prices rose after Iran-backed Yemeni Houthis attacked two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they got involved in the war to retaliate against Saudi Arabia for its siege on Yemen and assaults on the capital's international airport. Earlier this week, the rebel group also threatened to blockade the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The strait is another crucial chokepoint for oil and fuel transport, in addition to the Strait of Hormuz, which the U.S. and Iran have been fighting for control over. The ongoing conflict has also led some foreign missions to reduce their presence in Iran, according to Al-Shalchi.

Sponsor Message

The Trump administration announced overnight that it is imposing tariffs on 59 countries and the European Union. The new tariffs have two tiers — 10% and 12.5% — and went into effect at midnight, at the same time as when a 10% global tariff struck down by the Supreme Court earlier this year expired. The administration said it imposed these new tariffs because these countries are importing goods made with forced labor. The tariffs cover more than 99% of imports to the United States. Major categories like energy and many foods will remain exempt. Earlier this week, President Trump also signed proclamations to impose 50% tariffs on a selection of Canadian goods.



🎧 Polls show that Americans largely disapprove of tariffs and that their approval of Trump's handling of the economy has declined, NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben says. Despite public opinion, she says Trump views tariffs as a tool to pressure other countries into making concessions on things like trade deals. As the midterm elections approach, the administration continues to assert that its tariff policies will yield long-term economic benefits. Some economists caution that it is risky to ask voters to back a potentially unpopular approach, given the uncertainty of future outcomes.

A vigil last night in Madison, Wisconsin, drew hundreds of people mourning 38-year-old Corey Ruiz, a man shot and killed by police on Wednesday. Madison Police Chief John Patterson said that officers responded to a call about a man checking cars. When they arrived, Ruiz fled on his bike. When officers attempted to arrest him, he produced a knife and injured one officer, according to the police chief. Four officers were involved in the incident. The officer who was injured was the one who shot Ruiz. Authorities have not yet released his name. The four officers have been placed on administrative leave.



Sponsor Message

🎧 Emotions are running high in the city since the shooting, says Sarah Lehr of NPR network station Wisconsin Public Radio. The community is particularly raw to this incident, having experienced two other deadly shootings by police in the same neighborhood since 2012, Lehr adds. The Wisconsin Division of Criminal Investigation is looking into the shooting. The officers involved in the incident were not wearing body cameras, as the Madison police don't have them department-wide. Madison police do have dashboard cameras, and there are multiple bystander videos circulating of the incident, Lehr says.

Living better

toggle caption fcafotodigital/Getty Images

Living Better is a special series about what it takes to stay healthy in America.

A growing number of consumers are interested in avocado oil's purported health benefits. But some people might not be getting what they think they're buying. A new study finds that consumers paying a premium for foods advertised as containing avocado oil are probably not receiving it, highlighting ongoing authenticity issues in the industry. Selina Wang, the lead author of the study, says the findings are particularly disheartening, as avocado oil products are often much more expensive than those made with olive or other vegetable oils. Here's what we know:

🥑 In a study, researchers conducted a chemical analysis of 54 products that listed only avocado oil. They found that 89% were adulterated with cheaper oils like soybean.

🥑 In comparison, researchers found that, out of 20 packaged foods made with olive oil tested, only one showed signs of adulteration.

🥑 Some see avocado oil as a healthier alternative to seed oils like canola and soybean. According to Sarah Berry, a nutrition professor at King's College London, there's limited direct evidence supporting its health benefits compared to data about eating avocados.

🥑 Avocado oil costs more largely because avocados are costly and produce a limited amount of oil.

Weekend picks

Check out what NPR is watching, reading and listening to this weekend:

🍿 Movies: Can't get to Broadway? Don't worry! Catch the film adaptation of Hadestown: The Musical, a retelling of the Greek tragedy of Orpheus and Eurydice. The show is in theaters for a limited time.

Sponsor Message

📺 TV: Netflix's new series The Hawk stars Will Ferrell as a past-his-prime golfer. In the show, he reunites with some former collaborators, including Molly Shannon, Luke Wilson and Chris Parnell.

📚 Books: Grace Farris' graphic memoir See One, Do One, Teach One gives readers an insider's look at medical school, including the stresses of student loans, friendships built under pressure and the impossible pursuit of work-life balance.

🎵 Music: NPR's New Music Friday is breaking down the best new albums out today, and Charli xcx, Tyla and Shania Twain are on that list. Check out the other albums that made the cut and listen to a playlist of new songs.

🕹️ Gaming: Discover the best games of 2026 so far as NPR staff members spotlight some of their favorites with this interactive list.

❓Quiz: This week's quiz features a variety of topics, from a deformed yet adorable animal to international politics. Fortunately, the Up First newsletter answered several questions throughout the week.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption Natosha Via for NPR

Theresa Aletheia and Danielle Lussier, two Catholic sisters in Kentucky, are seeking to establish a new official order in the Catholic Church dedicated to helping survivors of clergy abuse. Wang Hong was awarded the Fields Medal yesterday, making her the first Chinese woman to win the world's most prestigious mathematics prize. More than 1,000 people in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo have now died from the Ebola outbreak. Officials say that the virus is spreading at the fastest rate on record.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: Trump threatens a major escalation in Iran after 13 straight nights of strikes
World.content:
Trump threatens a major escalation in Iran after 13 straight nights of strikes

toggle caption AFP via Getty Images

AMMAN, Jordan — The U.S. continued airstrikes in Iran on Friday while Tehran launched retaliatory attacks on U.S. targets in the Gulf as the region braced itself after President Trump said he was close to deciding whether to launch the biggest offensive of the war.

"I am considering a massive attack. Bigger than ever before. I am close to making a decision," Trump told the Axios news outlet.

The U.S. military later said it conducted its 13th consecutive night of strikes against Iran in attacks aimed at degrading Iran's ability to threaten maritime traffic.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi was quoted by state media as saying "Iran has shown that it will not bow to U.S. bullying and will under no circumstances respond to the language of force, pressure and threats." He also said he had "detailed" talks with the foreign ministers of Russia and China.

Sponsor Message

The standoff continues over the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway between Iran and Oman, with Iran asserting its control and the U.S. imposing a blockade on Iranian ports. The conflict on Thursday pushed global benchmark oil prices to over $100 per barrel, their highest level since May. The price has since fallen below $92 a barrel Friday. The national average price for regular gasoline in the U.S. continued to climb to $4.10 per gallon — up more than 17 cents from a month ago, according to AAA.

Loading...

Iranian state media reported explosions overnight, including along the Strait of Hormuz in Qeshm and Bandar Abbas.

United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres told the U.N. Security Council that the Middle East was "teetering on the edge of [the] unimaginable."

"The situation is getting out of control," Guterres said. "The region is being pulled into an ever-widening circle of confrontation. One crisis feeds another. One escalation triggers the next."

The collapse of the ceasefire has brought Yemen's Houthi rebels, a key Iranian ally, further into the conflict. The Houthis this week attacked Saudi tankers in the Red Sea near Bab el-Mandeb. The Houthis control that waterway, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and is vital to global container traffic moving through the Suez Canal.

Trump threatened "major military punishment" against the Houthis if the attacks continue. Saudi Arabia backs an internationally recognized Yemeni government that controls the north of Yemen. The Houthis blame Saudi Arabia for an attack on the airport in the Yemeni capital last week.

In the Kurdistan region of Iraq, security forces shot down explosive-laden drones near the regional capital Irbil's international airport. The airport director said it had closed temporarily but was operating normally again later Friday morning.

toggle caption AFP via Getty Images

Iran did not issue claims of responsibility for the strikes in the Iraqi Kurdish region where the U.S. has a military presence. Armed Kurdish-Iranian opposition bases in the Kurdish region have been a frequent target of Iranian and Iranian-backed attacks.

Sponsor Message

Newly appointed Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said after a visit Thursday to Iran he had promised not to allow attacks on Iran from Iraqi soil. Zaidi met President Trump this week in Washington, where he promised to intensify efforts to rein in Iran-backed Iraqi militias that have attacked U.S. forces.

In response to the increased tension, the United Kingdom announced it was temporarily withdrawing diplomatic staff from Iran. Some airlines began canceling flights to the region. Qatar Airways, a major regional carrier, announced it would suspend flights to Bahrain, Kuwait and Irbil until the end of July.

World.title: U.S. allies hit with new tariffs object to Trump's forced labor allegations
World.content:
U.S. allies hit with new tariffs object to Trump's forced labor allegations

toggle caption Mark Schiefelbein/AP

Many of America's key allies on Friday criticized the U.S. administration's new tariffs against them, after President Trump renewed the tax on imports from more than 60 countries just as the previous tariffs expired.

The U.S. Supreme Court had ruled earlier this year that many of the tariffs imposed under emergency powers were unconstitutional.

The president cited lax enforcement of a ban on the use of forced labor to produce goods as his reason for renewing the tariffs, an allegation Australia and the European Union vehemently rejected.

🎧 Listen to NPR's State of the World podcast, a human perspective on global stories in just a few minutes, every weekday.

Those targeted with the latest penalties face between 10% and 12.5% on many of their exports to the U.S., although various countries have trade deal exemptions for certain sectors.

Sponsor Message

"Trading partners that have made commitments to adopt, and effectively enforce, forced labor import prohibitions will have a 10% tariff, and trading partners that have failed to adopt a forced labor import prohibition will have a 12.5% tariff rate," according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative.

Here are some reactions from around the world:

Australia and New Zealand

Australian Trade Minister Don Farrell said the 12.5% tariffs on his country's exports to the U.S. were "unjustified" and called it "an extremely disappointing decision."

"We believe we do take the issue of modern slavery seriously. We have some of the most progressive legislation anywhere in the world. We say that these tariffs are unjustified and we call on the United States government to reverse them," Farrell said to Sky News.

In New Zealand, Prime Minister Christopher Luxon called the tariffs "extremely disappointing."

"The U.S. investigation did not provide meaningful evidence to support claims in relation to forced labour. Tariffs are not the way — they drive up costs and uncertainty for businesses," he said online.

European Union and the United Kingdom

The EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, also questioned Trump's rationale for the new tariffs.

"If you compare our labor laws to the ones of the United States, I mean, we have, people have paid vacations, we have very good conditions, labor conditions, for our employees, so it's not really grounded," she told Reuters.

toggle caption Ng Han Guan/AP

The British government said Trump's latest 10% tariffs will amount to "no negative change" for British exports. Former Prime Minister Keir Starmer was able to strike a better U.S. trade deal than many other countries, with lower tariff rates. And King Charles III got the U.S. tariff on Scotch whisky reduced to zero when he visited the White House in April.

Sponsor Message

But the British government said in a statement: "We take forced labour very seriously to ensure that in global supply chains U.K. businesses are not complicit."

Asia

The world's second-largest economy, China, was hit with 12.5% new tariffs and the Foreign Ministry condemned the move.

"Tariff wars and trade wars do not serve any parties' interests," ministry spokesman Lin Jian told a regular press conference on Friday.

Japan will also see 12.5% tariffs on exports to the U.S. Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said his country had been reassured by the Trump administration that its goods would not be slapped with more tariffs.

"It is regrettable that the measure imposes tariffs on the grounds of nonexistence of measures banning imports of goods made by forced labor, even though Japan's industry and trade are in line with international rules," he said.

Latin America

Trump's latest tariffs stacked a 12.5% duty on many imports from Brazil — just days after putting 25% tariffs on Brazilian goods.

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva said in a statement that his government "rejects" the measure, saying the U.S. "manipulated" human rights issues to support a "protectionist trade policy." He said Brazil has ratified dozens more international labor treaties than the United States has.

Trump has often tussled with Brazil's left-wing government. But other South American countries with more pro-Trump presidents, including Chile, also got the higher 12.5% tariff.

The U.S. slapped a 10% tariff on its top trading partner Mexico. But Mexican Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard said his country will see no change since there has already been a 10% tariff, and more than 80% of Mexico's exports to the U.S. enter duty free under the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement.

Lauren Frayer contributed to this story from London, Kristina Kukolja contributed from Melbourne, Australia, and Catherine Osborn contributed from Rio de Janeiro.

World.title: Gordie Howe International Bridge open to vehicle traffic 'as early as 12 p.m.' Monday, officials say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Vehicles can begin crossing the Gordie Howe International Bridge “as early as 12 p.m.” on Monday, bridge officials revealed on Friday.

And people can begin using the pedestrian and cycling path on Aug. 5 at 8 a.m. ET.

The news came at a ribbon-cutting ceremony and celebratory hockey game in Windsor ahead of the long-awaited opening of the crossing connecting Ontario and Michigan.

The Windsor-Detroit Bridge Authority "began its journey in 2014, when this bridge existed as an idea, a vision and a promise,” Chuck Andary, interim CEO of the organization that oversees the bridge, said in his remarks to the crowd.

“Today, it stands as a remarkable accomplishment that will serve Canadians for generations to come.”

The event, featuring speeches from politicians and family of the late hockey legend Howe, was held near the customs booths on the Canadian side of the bridge.

It was originally set to be a joint celebration with U.S. officials, but was hastily reduced to a Canada-only event after U.S. President Donald Trump announced new tariffs targeting an estimated $28 billion in Canadian exports.

Mayor hopes for future cross-border celebration

Before the ceremony started, Windsor Mayor Drew Dilkens spoke to CBC Windsor Morning.

“ I'm really hopeful that one day in the future we'll be able to close the bridge for a couple of hours and actually have the proper type of ceremony in the middle of the bridge with our American friends to sort of reset and to celebrate this binational relationship, and to celebrate not just the construction and what it took to get us here, but also to celebrate the man after whom the bridge is named,” Dilkens said.

Trump’s tariff threats and tensions over the toll-sharing deal between Canada and the U.S. to secure the bridge's opening were evident at the event Friday. Reporters questioned Dilkens and federal Infrastructure Minister Gregor Robertson about the new bridge deal and about the owners of the Ambassador Bridge who have fought to block the Gordie Howe crossing's construction.

But officials focused their attention on the benefits of the bridge, including its economic impacts.

"When you look at the Gordie Howe bridge, when you see how iconic it is on the landscape and when you think long game here, it's easy to get caught up in Donald Trump and his latest tweet of the day. But … this bridge is going to be here for over 100 years," Dilkens told Windsor Morning.

The family of the late pro hockey legend Howe, who was born in Saskatchewan and played most of his career with the NHL's Detroit Red Wings, were front and centre at the bridge celebration on Friday. (Emma Loop/CBC)

On the Michigan side of the border, four women rolled out massive signs about six metres long that read, “Canada, we’re sorry. Michigan.”

Miranda King, who lives in Detroit, said she came to show her support for Canadians after the U.S. threatened more trade action earlier this week.

“There are people over here who understand and sympathize with them, and we’re sorry for the way things are going,” King said.

“We hope we can be great friends again."

Two Michigan Democrats issued statements ahead of the opening ceremony.

"Canada is our neighbor, friend, and indispensable partner," Rep. Debbie Dingell wrote on X.

"This opening serves as a lasting reminder of the ties that unite us."

Sen. Elissa Slotkin referred to Canada as "one of America's most critical allies" and criticized Trump's latest tariff threat.

The Detroit council member in whose district the bridge is located said she wished the two countries could celebrate together.

“While I cannot speak to the irrational actions of the Trump administration, what I do know is Canada has always been one of our closest allies and I could not be prouder to have this new linkage between our countries right here in Detroit,” Gabriela Santiago-Romero said in a statement sent to CBC Windsor.

“I remain optimistic that ties between Detroit and Windsor will only strengthen with this long-awaited opening.”

Howe's son lauds Red Wings star born in Canada

Howe’s son, Murray Howe, spoke at the ceremony about his family’s history with the Windsor-Detroit area, starting when his mother moved to Windsor from Germany in 1912.

She subsequently moved to Saskatchewan and married, but a teenage Gordie returned to the city in 1944 to try out for the Detroit Red Wings.

After meeting and marrying his wife, the couple settled in Detroit.

Murray talked of delivering the news to his father about the naming of the bridge.

“ As a family, we are so grateful that our father was able to experience such a profound expression of love, reverence and gratitude in the twilight of his life."

Born in Floral, Sask., the hockey superstar and Hockey Hall of Fame inductee played 25 of his 26 years in the NHL with the Red Wings. He died in 2016 at age 88.

World.title: Trump vows tariffs to come for Canada over wildfire smoke that has drifted to U.S.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump returned to making tariff-related threats against Canada on Friday afternoon, restating his intent to impose tariffs in retaliation for wildfire smoke drifting across the border into the United States.

"We're going to put a big tariff on Canada because of the smoke," Trump told reporters, when speaking in the Oval Office following an announcement relating to American nuclear energy.

Trump, who made a similar threat a week ago, did not provide any detail on how the tariffs would be implemented.

In the Oval Office, Trump also said he had "told Canada they have to do something about it," which he'd also previously stated doing.

Trump isn't the only U.S. lawmaker who has criticized Canada over the fallout from wildfires this summer.

A handful of members of the U.S. Congress wrote to Prime Minister Mark Carney, accusing Canada of failing to conduct adequate forest maintenance to reduce the risk of wildfires. However, a U.S. senator this week suggested recent statements from U.S. Republicans criticizing Canada for its wildfire management are insulting and ridiculous.

Trump administration favours use of tariffs

Trump is an avowed fan of tariffs. His administration has favoured the use of tariffs during his second presidency — even after running into court-related setbacks in terms of how the U.S. government is able to wield them.

Earlier this week, Trump separately threatened to impose 50 per cent tariffs on billions of dollars' worth of Canadian goods effective Aug. 19.

Carney has said Ottawa will consider retaliatory measures if the federal government is unable to reach a deal with the Americans before Trump's threatened tariffs come into effect.

World.title: Wildfires near Boston Bar, B.C., merge as district says some residents still refusing to evacuate
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Two of the three out-of-control wildfires threatening Boston Bar, B.C., and surrounding communities have merged.

In a Thursday night update, the B.C. Wildfire Service said the Anderson Creek fire, which broke out Tuesday, had grown to merge with the southern edge of the massive Ainslie Creek fire.

The two covered an area of more than 264.1 square kilometres as of Friday morning.

“This really has not changed our response, it just means they’ve merged together into one incident," B.C. Wildfire Service fire information officer Jean Strong said.

The Brunswick Creek wildfire also continues to burn out of control, at 72 square kilometres, on the other side of the Fraser River, leaving the community essentially encircled by fires.

Together, the trio make up the Brunswick wildfire complex.

The Brunswick Creek wildfire is seen burning near Boston Bar, B.C., on July 6. (B.C. Wildfire Service)

Highway 1 remains closed between Spuzzum Creek Road and the Jackass Summit, and more than 450 properties in the area are under evacuation orders.

The Fraser Valley Regional District (FVRD), however, said some residents have refused to leave.

"We understand evacuation reluctance, however, these individuals are violating the law. This action leaves them at risk," the district said in a statement.

"With the rapidly changing weather and wildfire behaviour, it significantly increases the risk of not knowing, before it is too late to leave the area, or before exit access is cut off. Leaving the area is for their protection and the protection of first responders."

Boston Bar evacuee Kyle Wood said he saw the Anderson Creek wildfire grow rapidly on Tuesday. (CBC News)

Boston Bar evacuee Kyle Wood watched how quickly the Anderson Creek wildfire grew on Tuesday.

“The trees were candling right beside the road," he said.

“By the time I got to my dad’s, I just looked over and half the mountain was on fire," he added.

“So we went back to my place, packed up and got out. And by the time we got out we could see the red of the flames coming up over the hill closer to Boston Bar."

The B.C. Wildfire Service said its number one priority in the area remains protecting the community, and that crews are on the ground "actively defending structures around Boston Bar, the Boston Bar First Nation and Canyon Alpine."

Personnel are on the ground patrolling for hotspots and maintaining sprinkler systems, the service said.

More than 100 active wildfires across B.C.

The fires around Boston Bar are among 103 burning across British Columbia on Friday, more than half of them out of control.

Most of the fires are burning in the southern half of the province.

“The Cariboo Fire Centre has seen a lot of activity in the last 24 hours and we expect that will continue. There are wildfires in the areas near Williams Lake and Clinton we’re continuing to respond to," Smart said.

“We expect we will continue to see that aggressive fire behaviour in the coming days, as we continue to see that hot, dry weather continue, we’ll keep seeing those gusty winds."

The wildfire service said the Fiftynine Creek wildfire northwest of Clinton has grown to more than 167 square kilometres, triggering an evacuation order and alerts.

Overnight, the Thompson-Nicola Regional District expanded an evacuation order south of Clinton, due to the Pear Lake fire.

“We expect we will cibntnue ot see that aggressive fire behavour in the coming days, as we continue to see that hot, dry weather continue, we’ll keep seeing those gusty winds.

The Fiftynine Creek fire is seen burning on July 21. (B.C. Wildfire Service)

On Thursday, TNRD community and emergency services manager Kevin Skrepnek confirmed that structures on about 20 properties in the region were "impacted" by the fires, with the damage ranging from melted siding to a complete burn-down.

In B.C.'s southeast, the entire city of Kimberley remains under an evacuation alert due to the nearby Bootleg complex of wildfires, including a cluster of wildfires burning west of the city.

Hugh Murdoch, incident commander on the complex, said there are seven fires that firefighters are closely watching in the region, and he is happy to share that the fire behaviour "has been held in check for the most part."

But Murdoch said the weather forecast was "far from favourable," with "no rain in sight" and above-seasonal temperatures expected for the foreseeable future.

B.C. Hydro said Friday that some customers were experiencing flickering lights as a result of wildfire activity.

"This is a result of smoke and ash from wildfires in the BC Southern Interior in proximity to our powerlines resulting in short and temporary interruptions in the flow of electricity on the impacted powerline," spokesperson Susie Rieder said in an email.

Rieder said the grid was performing as expected under challenging conditions, and that the system was capable of self correcting after a fault due to branches on power lines, lightning strikes or smoke or debris.

Scientists say human-caused climate change plays a key role in the province's worsening wildfire seasons, as B.C. grapples with drought, drier forests and more days with hotter temperatures.

World.title: Heated Rivalry thirst traps: The Canadian export that won't quit
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

First it was Hudson Williams for Peloton.

Now it's François Arnaud for Under Armour.

It seems U.S. fitness brands can't get enough of the Canadian actors who portray the beloved fictional hockey players in Heated Rivalry ... and the internet is eating it up.

Both campaigns bear certain hallmarks that push them from equipment and sportswear  into clear thirst-trap territory: close-ups on chiselled abs, artistic beads of sweat and coquettish looks into the camera.

Everyone involved understands two things: Sex sells, and these particular stars are used to being objectified by men and women of all ages, in countries around the world.

Part ad, part advocacy

François Arnaud is openly bisexual, and the Under Armour  alludes to that by depicting both a man and a woman growing increasingly agitated as they not-so-subtly watch him work out.

"The ad is bisexual," said Joe Recupero, an associate professor of sports media at Toronto Metropolitan University. "I thought this is a really cool ad because when do you ever see ads directed at the bisexual community?"

He also commended Under Armour for releasing the ad after Pride month, at the risk of perhaps turning off some of its target demographic.

"It's very cheeky ... because it's subtle, but it's not so subtle."

Arnaud came out as bisexual in a social media post in September 2020, just before Bi Visibility Day. (Chris Pizzello/The Associated Press)

Under Armour is also clear about wanting Arnaud not just for his talent and looks but for what his Heated Rivalry character represents.

"The character he portrays ultimately finds his greatest success when he stops trying to fit someone else's mould and embraces who he truly is. That's a lesson that resonates deeply with us," Matt Dornic, the company's chief communications officer, said in a statement.

Peloton's message was more focused on self-love when it launched the Hudson Williams campaign in April.

"Our goal with this campaign was to capture that feeling of total freedom," chief marketing officer Megan Imbres said in a news release.

Captivated audience

The Peloton campaign — which featured Williams half-dancing and half-walking on a treadmill, lifting weights and working out with a trainer — quickly went viral. Heated Rivalry superfans made pilgrimages to downtown Toronto to see the ad on the big screen over Sankofa Square.

Arnaud's Under Armour ad is receiving a similarly enthusiastic response, garnering nearly 75,000 likes on its Instagram post during its first day online.

" Finally, the bisexual deities have answered our prayers," said one top commenter. "Oh, I love the way he holds up our flag," said another.

One self-declared bookstagrammer said, "I would like to personally thank all the marketing teams across the country."

Overexposure?

It has been eight months since Heated Rivalry premiered on Crave, and the stars of the show are still a favourite subject of gossip blogs, fan accounts and traditional media stories.

Season 2 isn't scheduled to air until April 2027. Until then, the most devoted fans are "reheating" or rewatching the series multiple times.

WATCH | Heated Rivalry's creator says show is about celebration: Why Heated Rivalry is hopecore coded | Duration 1:42 Heated Rivalry creator Jacob Tierney tells The National's Ian Hanomansing he wanted the show to be a celebration of queer joy when audiences are more used to seeing punishment in storylines involving queer love and sex.

But Recupero said he doesn't think the public is anywhere close to reaching Heated Rivalry fatigue.

"I keep waiting for the bottom to drop out and the fandom to cool down and for oversaturation," he said. "I think this is going to be something people are really looking at and studying about when is the oversaturation point? And I don't believe we've hit it yet."

World.title: Wildberries is the Amazon of Russia. Ukraine is trying to destroy it
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

For a week now, Ukrainian drones have been attacking vast warehouses that are a crucial part of Russia's biggest online retailer, Wildberries.

Logistics hubs in St. Petersburg were hit overnight Thursday. Video verified by CBC News and Reuters show multiple drones exploding as they crash into the facilities, leading to fires that appear to have totally destroyed the warehouses. It's estimated that billions of dollars worth of goods have gone up in flames.

The attacks started last weekend, one in the town of Kotovsk, some 360 kilometres from the border with Ukraine, and another in the city of Elektrostal, about 50 kilometres east of Moscow. Nine people were killed and 80 others wounded.

More attacks happened early Wednesday. Ukrainian drones struck Wildberries warehouses in Krasnodar and Stavropol. Verified video of those incidents spread widely on social media.

WATCH | Ukraine's strikes on Wildberries : The facts about Ukraine striking Wildberries, Russia’s Amazon | Duration 1:36 Ukraine has been hitting warehouses for the online shopping giant Wildberries in Russia. The drone strikes have killed night shift workers and destroyed the merchandise of many sellers. Here are the facts about Wildberries — and why Ukraine is targeting these sites.

The strikes on Wildberries warehouses were confirmed by company founder Tatyana Kim in statements after the attacks, as well as Russian officials.

At least seven warehouses have been struck so far.

What is Wildberries?

Wildberries is often referred to as the equivalent of Amazon in Russia. By some estimates, it accounts for half of all online sales in the country.

Wildberries was launched in 2004 by Kim, a teacher and a young mother at the time, focused, at first, on selling clothes.

Since then, the platform has become an industry leader and household name, allowing big and small businesses alike to sell their goods to customers across the country by storing, shipping and delivering their inventory. In April, Forbes Russia estimated Kim's fortune at $8.1 billion US.

Kim has said that last year, the company had more than 200 logistics facilities totaling over 5.2 million square metres, with plans to build new warehouses this year in Belarus and Kazakhstan, where Wildberries operates as well. It also operates in Russian-held Crimea.

Smoke billows from a warehouse after deadly Ukrainian drone attacks in Elektrostal, Russia. The image, from social media, was verified by Reuters using satellite imagery. (Social media/Reuters)

Does Wildberries supply military equipment?

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy did not name Wildberries directly, but he said the facilities his country attacked were involved in supplying gear and various technical components to the Russian military.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Tuesday that "it is not the case" and accused Kyiv of continuing to "strike civilian targets."

Searches of the Wildberries website show it sells some products that could be used by the military, such as body armour, helmets and radios. But the site also sells a wide range of consumer products in virtually every category, including books, clothes, cosmetics, toys, appliances, sports equipment, household goods, pharmaceutical drugs and more.

Smoke billows from a burning Wildberries warehouse in St. Petersburg, Russia, after a Ukrainian drone attack on July 24. (Reuters)

Some sellers have suffered huge losses

It's not clear how many sellers there are on Wildberries, but estimates are that it is in the range of 500,000 to 800,000.

Russian fashion designer Viktoria Terekhova says she shipped virtually her entire summer collection of children's clothes last week to the giant warehouse in Elektrostal, east of Moscow.

Within a couple of days, it was destroyed in the Ukrainian drone strike. Terekhova says she lost 12,000 items, amounting to about 45 per cent of her company's total inventory, and another 4,000 items in attacks on Wildberries hubs in southern Russia.

Oleg Kondratyev, co-founder of the clothing brand Airbase that manufactures mostly women's tracksuits, said he had lost about five million roubles ($90,000) of stock in the warehouse attacks.

That has placed him in a dire financial position, he said.

"For today, we cannot pay our loans because sales through Wildberries have stopped. Tax payments are not due yet, but they will be soon, and most likely we will not be able to pay those either," Kondratyev said.

World.title: Elections Alberta verifies signatures for petition calling for independence referendum
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Elections Alberta says it has verified that a citizen initiative petition looking to force a vote on the province separating from Canada was able to surpass the number of signatures it required.

But the future of the petition remains on hold, Elections Alberta said in a news release on Friday afternoon.

The verification process was conducted between July 6 and July 23, and has now been completed, the non-partisan office said.

Gordon McClure, the province's chief electoral officer, determined that while requirements have been met, any further steps in the citizen initiative process are stayed pending direction from the Court of Appeal of Alberta.

Stay Free Alberta, the group behind the petition, previously said almost 302,000 signatures had been collected, far more than the nearly 178,000 needed under provincial legislation.

Elections Alberta said the total number of valid signatures counted was 279,337 and using random statistical sampling, the office said it found 222,597 verified signatures.

Elections Alberta said the most frequent reasons signatures were rejected during the validation phase included incomplete addresses, electors not completing their declarations that they were eligible electors, canvassers signing their witness declarations before electors signed the petition, and electors providing a mailing address instead of the required physical residential address.

The petition was submitted in early May, but just two weeks later, a Court of King's Bench ruling quashed it. The judge ruled McClure made an error in law to approve the second citizen initiative petition and failed to consider an earlier court decision that said separation would violate Indigenous people's treaty rights.

But last month, Stay Free Alberta earned a partial win in court when another judge ruled the signature verification process should take place while the original ruling is appealed.

Premier Danielle Smith has called a referendum for Oct. 19, when Albertans will be asked a number of questions, including if they want to remain in Canada or start the process of having a second, binding vote on separation.

More to come.

World.title: Paramount agrees to delay closing Warner Bros. buyout for months while judge considers states' challenge
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Paramount on Friday agreed to delay closing its $81 billion US buyout of Warner Bros. Discovery well into next year, as a judge continues to consider a challenge from 12 states seeking to block the deal altogether.

In a court filing, Paramount said it wouldn't close the merger until either June 1, 2027, or whenever a court ruling is made on the merits of the states' lawsuit.

The move comes just days after U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin granted a temporary restraining order to freeze the transaction for several weeks, ruling that the states had raised some "serious questions" and a strong case about the merger's potential to "substantially lessen competition."

Paramount called Friday's agreement a "significant win because the result is exactly what we have sought from the outset: a direct path to a trial based on the evidence."

The company, which was bought by Skydance just last year, added that this was the "fastest and clearest way" to prove its merger was good for competition and the wider industry.

WATCH | Paramount challenges Netflix bid to buy Warner Bros. Discovery: Paramount challenges Netflix bid to buy Warner Bros. Discovery | Duration 1:40 Just days after Netflix seemingly won a bidding war to take over Warner Bros.-Discovery, Paramount Skydance has launched its own hostile takeover bid worth $108.4 billion US.

Twelve states, led by California, sued to block Paramount's pending buyout of Warner last month — alleging that such a merger would instead "extinguish competition" in Hollywood and lead to fewer choices for consumers, particularly moviegoers and cable customers.

"From the workers and artists who bring stories to life, to the families who buy tickets at the box office, Paramount's illegal takeover of Warner Bros. is a bad deal for all those who count on a competitive entertainment industry," New York Attorney General Letitia James, who is among those suing to block the merger, said Friday.

She called the agreement to halt the deal a "critical victory."

A Warner Bros.-Paramount merger would bring together two of the five last legacy studios in Hollywood — as well as host of TV networks, titles filling streaming libraries and news operations.

That would include Warner Bros.' HBO Max. Crave, the Bell Media-owned streamer currently holds exclusive rights to HBO in Canada.

In statements to Broadcast Dialogue and The Hollywood Reporter in March, Bell Media said its deal with Warner Bros. Discovery would see HBO and HBO Max programming on Crave "for the foreseeable future."

World.title: Doctors are using a regulatory gap to prescribe an unauthorized peptide
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Despite Health Canada's warnings against the use of unauthorized peptides as a health and fitness shortcut, a CBC News investigation uncovered doctors using a regulatory loophole to prescribe one of the unproven products to patients.

The popularity of peptides has surged as fitness influencers endorse them to build muscle, reverse the signs of aging and lose weight.

Peptides are short amino acid chains naturally produced by the body that act as building blocks of larger proteins that support growth, metabolism and healing.

But unlike approved peptides used in medicine, such as insulin and GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic, Health Canada tells CBC "unauthorized peptide products sold for wellness purposes have not been assessed for safety, quality, or effectiveness."

And yet, CBC News found doctors promoting and prescribing a popular unauthorized peptide called Body Protection Compound-157 (BPC-157) that is touted to help accelerate muscle growth and tissue repair.

That's because the same regulator prohibiting BPC-157’s sale as an injectable drug or a licensed natural health product says it can be compounded as a pill by pharmacies — with a doctor's prescription.

"It's maddening," said Timothy Caulfield, a professor in the faculty of law and the school of public health and research director of the Health Law Institute at the University of Alberta.

Doctors should be "warning their patients about these products, not providing them," he said.

Hidden camera claims

CBC News journalists armed with hidden cameras visited two doctors — at clinics in Ontario and B.C. — that advertised unauthorized peptides to hear the health claims offered to patients.

"I'm on some peptides myself," said Dr. Shawn Seit, speaking to an undercover CBC journalist at his Rejuuv Medi Spa in Markham, Ont. "So, that's how safe I feel they are."

In a recorded one-on-one consultation, Seit said that BPC-157 "really helps in terms of healing and inflammation."

WATCH | Getting peptides through a loophole: How Canadians are getting unauthorized peptides | Duration 10:00 A CBC News hidden-camera investigation uncovers unauthorized peptides, such as BPC-157, being promoted across Canada. For The National, CBC’s Idil Mussa breaks down what the team uncovered and how the findings sparked a series of new investigations by Health Canada.

In B.C., Dr. Charles Jiang claimed, until recently, on his Richmond Anti-Aging Clinic website that BPC-157 can be used for "musculoskeletal and gut lining repair." He also told a CBC journalist during an in-person visit that unlike peptides sold online, the ones he prescribes are safe.

"When you order online, you never know what is the truth behind it," said Jiang. "If you come to us we are professional doctors."

Caulfield says physicians that prescribe unauthorized peptides are capitalizing on a fad that could be risky.

They're "leveraging a longevity wellness trend," he said. "Despite the fact there's no evidence and real potential harm."

Jiang did not respond to CBC's repeated requests for comment.

In emailed statements, Seit said his aim is "always directed at optimizing my patients' care and treatment” and that he is permitted to compound BPC-157 as a natural health product (NHP), which Health Canada confirmed. The same is true of any doctor in the country.

Timothy Caulfield, a professor in the faculty of law and the school of public health and research director of the Health Law Institute at the University of Alberta, says doctors should be warning their patients about these products. (Curtis Trent)

Compounding BPC-157: A regulatory loophole

In a statement, Health Canada said "BPC‑157 has not been authorized, its safety, efficacy, and quality have not been assessed … and there is limited scientific evidence to support its use, including a lack of established human dosing protocols."

In addition, the regulator says BPC-157 is not approved for use in any NHPs in any form, including oral and injectable, but it can still be compounded for topical use or oral administration as an NHP.

That means doctors can prescribe BPC-157 to patients and compounding pharmacies — that mix custom medications — can formulate them.

"Nobody's minding the store," said Stuart Phillips, a professor of kinesiology at McMaster University in Hamilton.

"Health Canada won't approve it as a drug, but it slips through as a compounded natural health product, where the federal safety check basically doesn't happen."

Health Canada considers NHP compounding within a practitioner-patient relationship distinct from manufacturing and not subject to the same regulatory oversight.

"The practitioner-patient relationship is supposed to be where evidence gets turned into advice. But you can't practise evidence-based medicine on a substance that has no evidence," said Phillips.

The federal agency says compounding must not be used to circumvent the federal drug review and approval process, but Caulfield says that appears to be the case.

Stuart Phillips, a kinesiology professor at McMaster University, says when it comes to unauthorized peptides, there should be greater regulation and oversight. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

"BPC-157 is not an NHP," he said.

"Compounding is not meant to be a strategy that allows consumers to go around regulatory oversight, which seems to be what is happening here if they allow the application of NHP rules."



Seit said the prescriptions he provides "do not circumvent regulatory oversight." The regulatory bodies to which Jiang, Seit and those pharmacies belong had various responses.

In a statement to CBC News, the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario said the information physicians provide to patients or the public about treatments should be accurate and informed by evidence.

The College of Physicians and Surgeons of British Columbia said it doesn't have specific guidance on prescribing oral BPC-157, but expects "licensees to exercise professional judgment to ensure they are providing safe and appropriate patient care."

The Ontario College of Pharmacists says compounding an NHP using ingredients unauthorized by Health Canada could be investigated as a breach of professional conduct.

The College of Pharmacists of British Columbia states it "cannot be determined in general terms" whether a pharmacy has violated its standards.

Health Canada says it is illegal to promote health products that have not been authorized for sale, including compounded products tailored to individual patients.

After CBC News asked the department about the websites advertising BPC-157, it said it was investigating whether those activities complied with the Food and Drugs Act.

The mention of peptide therapy and BPC-157 was also taken down on Seit's and Jiang's websites after CBC News contacted them for comment.

All hype, no research

During CBC's undercover consultation, Seit admitted there was a lack of clinical human studies on BPC-157.

"A lot of these studies are based on animal models," he said. "They're not based on human models."

In an email to CBC News, he stated he was candid with his patients about the current research regarding BPC-157.

Jiang's clinic website also stated that BPC-157 had "limited human trial data."

Phillips, at McMaster University, says the lack of human trials raises serious questions about BPC-157's potential health risks.

"There are basically no published human efficacy trials for BPC-157."

Phillips says all he can find is one small safety study from a decade ago, and a trial that only started enrolling participants this past February.

Patricia Brubaker’s work helped pave the way for approved peptide medications like Ozempic. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

"Almost everything else is rodent work."

Patricia Brubaker, a professor emeritus of physiology at the University of Toronto, has taken a hard look at the research and has come to a similar conclusion about BPC-157's alleged benefits.

"Animal models do not always translate into humans. Dosing doesn't translate into humans. Safety doesn't translate into humans necessarily," said Brubaker.

Brubaker says drugs need to be carefully tested in stages before they are approved for use in people.

"It's really important that scientific discoveries are translated from the bench cells, animals into humans through a series of clinical trials that prove at every step, with increasing numbers of subjects, that this product is effective, that it's safe, and that you know how much of it to administer."
