“To ensure the security of Latvian society… and to provide general support to Ukrainian society, the importation of certain industrial goods into the Republic of Latvia from the Russian Federation and the Republic of Belarus is prohibited,” the amendments to Latvia's law (link in Latvian language) on Support for the Civilian Population of Ukraine read.

The tweaked law prohibits imports of goods originating in Russia and Belarus that are not already subject to EU sanctions, tariffs or other trade restrictions — in what appears to be one of the first national bans in the EU on a broad range of Russian and Belarusian consumer goods beyond the bloc's sanctions regime. The restrictions will also apply to goods imported via third countries if their country of origin is Russia or Belarus.

The ban, which was approved on the same day as the EU agreed its latest sanction package, covers products that lawmakers say can be used to spread propaganda and disinformation, including books, newspapers and video games, as well as sporting goods, toys, clothing and footwear.

"These amendments are the latest tool to systematically reduce economic ties with Russia and Belarus while maintaining our unwavering support for Ukraine in its fight for freedom and independence,” said Raimonds Bergmanis, Chairman of the Defense, Internal Affairs and Corruption Prevention Committee responsible for the progress of the bill in the Latvian Parliament.

Imports of the newly targeted goods from Russia and Belarus totalled €12.5 million in 2025, accounting for 6.5% of Latvia's remaining imports from the two countries and just 0.05% of Latvia's total imports.

Cutting the last ties

The proposal was drafted by Latvia's Foreign Ministry and fast-tracked through parliament as part of the government's broader effort to eliminate remaining trade links with Russia.

"Latvia has already significantly reduced economic ties with Russia, but our goal should be a complete policy of refusal with regard to the goods of the aggressor state,” Minister of Economy Viktors Valainis said at the end of May, following the ministers' meeting on restricting trade with Russia. At that meeting, the Foreign Ministry was instructed to prepare the legislation approved by parliament this week.

The final list of products covered by the ban will be adopted by the Cabinet of Ministers. The law will enter into force the day after it is promulgated, with the import restrictions set to remain in place until 1 July 2027.

Foreign Minister Baiba Braže has repeatedly argued that Latvia should end its remaining economic ties with Russia by the end of 2026 and has called on other EU member states to adopt similar measures.

World.title: Countdown to the ballot: Zambia gears up for August elections
World.content:
This week on Spotlight on Africa, we're heading to Zambia, where general elections are set to take place on the 13th August. Voters will go to the polls to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs. Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema has already picked up endorsements from within his own camp, the UPND Alliance, the coalition that's held power since 2021. So what's at stake, and who's in the running?

Advertising

This week on the podcast, we're heading to Zambia, which is gearing up for elections next month and is now in full campaign mode. Two of our RFI colleagues, Yang Mei and Igor Strauss, travelled to Zambia recently for in-depth reporting on four years of Hakainde Hichilema's rule, and his chances of re-election.

In power since August 2021, "HH", as he's most often called, is a businessman, farmer and politician, and the seventh president of Zambia.

General elections are due to be held in the country on 13 August 2026 to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs.

The year ahead for African democracy: who is going to the polls in 2026?

Hichilema has received endorsements from some members of the UPND Alliance, including from the leaders of the Party of National Unity and Progress and the Movement for Multi-Party Democracy.

According to an opinion poll conducted by a University of Zambia demographer, Hichilema is set to be re-elected, leading with 60 percent of the vote, while the combined opposition would take 35 percent.

Zambia's Hichilema sworn in, becoming rare opposition president in southern Africa

Our colleagues Yang Mei and Igor Strauss bring us some of the interviews they gathered on the ground, so join us as we hear from ordinary Zambians, as well as from leading journalist Joseph Mwenda, editor-in-chief at News Diggers, who has led multiple investigations into the current government's relations with China; and from Robert Mwale, an economist and Lead Public Finance and Economic Governance Researcher at the Centre for Trade Policy and Development (CTPD).

Among the issues at stake are a lack of freedom of expression, but also a legacy of economic growth, driven in no small part by China's heavy involvement in the economy.

Thanks to our reporters, Igor Strauss and Yang Mei, for their work and insight, and thank you for listening.

This is the last episode of the 2025–26 season. We'll be back in September with another one.

Spotlight on Africa is produced by RFI's English language service. This episode was mixed by Erwan Rome.

World.title: ICC votes to dismiss Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan
World.content:
Members of the International Criminal Court have voted to remove Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan amid allegations of sexual misconduct. Khan has denied the accusations.

International Criminal Court members voted on Friday to dismiss Karim Khan as prosecutor ​following allegations ​of sexual misconduct.

The ICC's oversight body, the Assembly of States Parties (ASP), found that Khan had committed "serious misconduct and serious breach of duty," ASP President Paivi Kaukoranta said.

What do we know about the Khan allegations?

A British barrister, Khan was accused of sexual misconduct by a female aide, allegations which he has repeatedly denied.

He had been temporarily removed from his duties at the ICC in June, following a report by the executive committee of the court's oversight body that found he had committed "serious misconduct."

In all, 82 of the court's ​125 member states voted in favor of Khan's removal, while 13 voted against and 15 countries abstained.

Khan, 56, made headlines in 2024 when he successfully applied for arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over the Gaza war, as well as leading members of the Hamas militant group who have since been killed. Hamas carried out the October 7, 2023 terror attacks on Israel.

All active ICC warrants will remain in place despite Khan's dismissal, because only ICC judges have the authority to withdraw warrants.

What were the reactions to Khan's dismissal?

Khan's lawyer, Tayab Ali, said Khan would challenge his dismissal.

"Mr. Khan will challenge the lawfulness and fairness of the decision, though all available legal mechanisms," Ali wrote in a post on X.

Kenneth Roth, the former executive director of Human Rights Watch and now a visiting professor at Princeton University, wrote on X that the ICC states did "the right thing" by removing Khan.

Israel's Ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, criticized Khan, suggesting the barrister had thought that the arrest warrants against Israeli officials, which Danon called a "political witch hunt," would "distract from serious sexual misconduct allegations."

"He was wrong," Danon said.

ICC prosecutor suspended: can the court still serve justice? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Khan suspension comes as Trump administration wants to 'dismantle' ICC

The move to dismiss Khan also comes at a time when the US President Donald Trump's administration is seeking to weaken and undermine the ICC. The court, based in the Dutch city of The Hague, investigates and prosecutes individuals for genocide and other crimes against humanity.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently said that the US had begun a "sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court to US sovereignty."

The State Department said countries that enjoy the benefits of the US security umbrella are "called upon to reject the ICC's purported authority to prosecute American officials and servicemen." The State Department is also mulling "visa revocations and travel bans for ICC personnel" along with "increased sanctions against the ICC and affiliated organizations."

Neither the United States nor Israel is a member of the ICC.

Venezuela announces it will withdraw from ICC

Meanwhile, Venezuela said it would withdraw from the ICC on Friday. The move comes after Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro was abducted and overthrown by the US earlier this year and replaced by interim leader Delcy Rodriguez, who has been willing to comply with the Trump administration's demands.

Notes from Caracas — Venezuela and the US intervention To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Venezuelan Foreign Minister Felix Plasencia said the "court's actions reflect a demonstrated geographical bias, which disproportionately concentrated its work on African and Latin American countries, to the detriment of the Global South."

Plasencia said the withdrawal was at the instruction of Delcy Rodriguez.

World.title: Poland's main opposition collapses over far-right slide
World.content:
A power struggle within Poland's main opposition force has come to a head. But a move to expel former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki may greatly weaken the right-wing party's popularity.

"Over 30 delegates of our group have effectively forfeited their membership," Jaroslaw Kaczynski, the head of the Law and Justice (PiS) party, said on Friday. He's accusing Poland's former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki, as well as dozens of his followers, of attempting to split the party.

"We couldn't accept that," Kaczynski continued. "It's all done." For their part, the rebels alleged they have not resigned but been "expelled."

A three-hour "last chance" talk between Kaczynski and Morawiecki ended on Thursday without results. "We were looking for understanding, but couldn't accept subjugation," Piotr Mueller, an EU delegate close to Morawiecki, later said about the talks on X.

The ultimatum that Kacynski had placed on rebel party members ended at midnight. By then, they were expected to deliver a written declaration that they would refrain from activities in the Rozwoj Plus (Development Plus) association led by Morawiecki. In Kaczynski's view, the breakaway association has undermined his party's primacy.

"I'm not signing any loyalty pledge," Morawiecki told the Polish television station TVN. "That's something one might have required of me in the 1980s," he added, alluding to his persecution for his father's prominent opposition to the regime at the time.

Poland swings back to the right after presidential vote To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For a quarter of a century, Kaczynski and his PiS party have dominated the right wing of Poland's party landscape. Any attempt to establish a new, more radical right was successfully quashed. Since 2001, PiS has been in power twice, from 2005-2007 and again from 2015-2023, and has occupied the office of state president with Kaczynski's twin brother, Lech, then Andrzej Duda and — since mid-2025 — Karol Nawrocki.

Greatest crisis since party's founding

Just over a year before the next parliamentary election, the party is facing its greatest crisis since it got its start in 2001.

By now, two parties have established themselves to the right of PiS: the far-right nationalist and libertarian alliance Confederation Liberty and Independence (KWIN), and the extreme right-wing, ultranationalist, traditionalist Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP). Taken together, they enjoy more support in the polls than the PiS party alone. Kaczynski's party has lost many voters to these two radical groups.

To win them back, Kaczynski has pushed his party ever further to the right. In March, he nominated Przemyslaw Czarnek, the ultraconservative, ultra-Catholic former minister of education and science, as the party's lead candidate for the 2027 parliamentary election. Morawiecki and his followers have called the move a fundamental mistake.

Two lungs or one fist?

Czarnek is trying to outflank the two confederation parties from the right with verbal attacks against the EU and Ukraine. In the recent Polish-Ukrainian dispute over unresolved historical issues, Czarnek called for all military aid to Ukraine to be halted until Kyiv changed its position. Supporters of this hard line have said the party should act "like a fist."

Morawiecki has dismissed Kaczynski's ultimatum to assure adherence to the PiS party line: 'I'm not signing any loyalty pledge' Image: Klaudia Radecka/IMAGO

Morawiecki responded to his party's shift to the right by launching the political association Development Plus. He's invited 1,000 guests from various political backgrounds to a policy event in late July, where they can discuss the country's future over a barbecue.

The former prime minister has been traveling up and down the country to speak with local politicians and businesses. As early as April, he clashed with Kaczynski, who accused him of threatening the party's unity. At the time, however, the party head gone along with Morawiecki's efforts and spoke of "two lungs" within the PiS party. That compromise did not hold long.

Reaching out to new voters

At public appearances, Morawiecki has repeatedly emphasized that he intends to remain within the PiS party. His goal, he said, was to open the party to new voters, to ensure that right-wing conservatives returned to power in 2027.

Just a few days ago, Morawiecki could count on the support of 40 members of Poland's lower house of parliament, the Sejm, and several EU delegates. But it's currently unclear whether all will be able to withstand Kaczynski's pressure.

Opinion polls conducted by Opinia24 for the Polish channels TVN and TVN24 on July 22 gave Morawiecki 6.2% of the vote, while support for PiS dropped to 17.7%. In the 2023 parliamentary election, the PiS party under Kaczynski won 35% of the vote.

Where do Europe's far-right parties differ? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Out of all of Kaczynski's longtime associates who have worked with him since the 1990s, Morawiecki is still considered an outsider. Following Poland's democratic transition, the trained historian held leading positions in several banks before joining the PiS party in 2016.

Under PiS party rule he served as development minister and finance minister, and finally prime minister. Morawiecki and his associates have accused their opponents of orchestrating a plot against them.

Gloating among the governing coalition

The center-right governing coalition under current Prime Minister Donald Tusk has made no secret of its amusement with the PiS party's current predicament. "I love PiS so much, I'd love to have two of them," Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski joked when he heard the news..

Political scientist Danuta Plecka said Friday that the situation was like "a gift" to the ruling government. "All the scandals of recent months are now fading into the background," she explained. "Tusk doesn't have to do anything, he can just sit by the riverbank and wait for the bodies to float by."

However, University of Gdansk researcher believes the conflict between Kaczynski and Morawiecki may be a staged performance. "There are hardly and programmatic differences between the two," she told TVN. "The main difference between them is in the language and political tactics."

She believes Morawiecki is meant to win over voters who lean more toward the political center. Then, after the election, both groups could work together, Plecka predicted.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Trump threatens EU with tariff probe over Google, tech fines
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has said he will initiate a tariff investigation against the EU in response to fines against US tech companies. He cited the latest case that Google lost on Thursday, as well as others.

US President Donald Trump on Friday threatened to launch a tariff investigation against the EU in response to the bloc's anti-competition fines and other penalties levied against US tech giants like Google, Apple, Amazon and Meta.

In particular, he cited Thursday's latest fine of €890 million (roughly $1 billion) issued against Google for allegedly giving unfair preference to its own search engine and its Play app.

Trump's threats come just a few hours after his administration imposed its latest tariffs on the EU, and many other countries, for supposedly not doing enough to prevent imports made using forced labor from their supply chains.

US trading partners and allies like the EU, Japan and Australia have responded to these with a mixture of outrage and bafflement at the new tariffs.

What did Trump say online?

Trump issued the warning in a lengthy post on his Truth Social online platform.

"The European Union is at it again and, as usual, taking direct aim at GREAT American Companies!," he wrote.

He then listed a series of fines — or cumulative totals of supposed fines — against various tech companies, which he falsely alleged were issued "for no reason at all" and "without explanation."

He mentioned the latest penalty to hit Google, and claimed this took the total of their fines to "over 18 Billion Dollars!" without specifying a timeframe or evidence of any sort.

EU courts did recently uphold a record fine of over $4 billion for Google — in a process that had been under review for almost eight years — in one case among several in recent years.

"The United States of America is not a 'PIGGYBANK' for Europe, nor will we allow it to be! Please let this TRUTH serve to represent that we will immediately initiate a 301 Investigation in the practice of 'ROBBING' American Companies and, in turn, the American Taxpayer," Trump wrote.

What is a 301 Investigation?

The 301 Investigations are the new means Trump relies on to impose tariffs, after the Supreme Court declared he had overstepped his authority with the near-global levies he imposed on what he called "Liberation Day" in 2025.

The so-called investigation relies on the US internally demonstrating what it deems to be unfair trade practices against it in order to issue retaliatory sanctions and refers to Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. Dozens of such investigations are in the pipeline.

"The European Union will pay a very big price for this illegal and highly unethical conduct, which I have consistently warned them about," Trump wrote. "The penalties will be entirely reveresed and, we anticipate, a substantial TARIFF to be placed on them at the earlier moment. Stay tuned!"

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer had already criticized the decision on Thursday, saying the EU's enforcement action undermined "constructive dialogue" and posed a "real risk" to transatlantic trade stability.

The EU and US have been bickering over the terms of their fragile trade agreement reached last year amid Trump's Liberation Day tariff frenzy. The slow ratification process across the EU's 27-plus member states and the institutions in Brussels has frustrated the Trump White House.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

World.title: Russia hits drone demonstration near Kyiv, killing 10
World.content:
Ukraine says 10 were killed and around 100 injured in the strike, a day after Zelenskyy met with officials from US arms giant Raytheon. Meanwhile, in St. Petersburg, another Wildberries warehouse came under drone fire.

Russia struck various sites in Ukraine on Friday, including a defense event on the outskirts of Kyiv thought to be showcasing aerial defense technologies like drones.

Sometimes fatal attacks elsewhere in the country disrupted power supplies in five separate regions.

Meanwhile, Ukraine again struck facilities belonging to Russia's largest online retailer, Wildberries, this time in President Vladimir Putin's hometown of St. Petersburg.

And in the skies over Romania, NATO jets downed a stray drone on Friday morning, with no immediate reports of casualties or damage.

Across the Atlantic, the White House said President Donald Trump and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy would hold talks on Tuesday of next week, almost four and a half years after Russia's full scale invasion.

The strikes came soon after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held talks with representatives of US weapons manufacturer Raytheon, which makes the mobile Patriot missile interceptor SAMs Image: State Emergency Service of Ukraine

What happened in Ukraine?

Acting regional military administration head Ruslan Oliinyk said the strike hit the grounds of a privately operated military training site that was hosting an event at the time. The site is some 20-30 kilometers (12-18 miles) from central Kyiv, in the Bucha district.

Attorney General Ruslan Kravchenko called the attack a war crime, saying that 10 people were killed and around 100 more were injured.

The surrounding area was also struck repeatedly, with Zelenskyy posting images of destruction and rescue efforts from the wider Kyiv region.

He said, "Interceptors for Patriot systems are the number one priority," a reference to the air defense systems made by US arms giant Raytheon, which had sent a delegation to Kyiv on Thursday.

Russia's Defense Ministry also acknowledged the attack online, saying it had used "high-precision long-range weapons" to target "a demonstration of unmanned aerial vehicles [UAVs or drones], including promising ones, of Ukrainian and foreign production, used to strike civilian targets in Russia."

Russia's Defense Ministry claimed that at the time of the strike, leading defense industry officials and Ukrainian military members were at the site, saying these people were "directly planning and carrying out strikes on Russian territory."

Five people were reported killed in the eastern region of Slovyansk on Friday. The EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, bemoaned one such strike that she said hit "Latvia's Honorary Consulate" in Slovyansk, saying, "We will summon Russia's envoy to the EU over today's strikes," and thatshe would propose further EU sanctions to target Russia's "military-industrial complex."

Ukraine's energy company Ukrenergo reported damage to power plants in five separate regions, saying around 150,000 people were left without power in the Chernihiv region alone after an attack on a facility there.

Smoke billowed over Vladimir Putin's hometown St. Petersburg on Friday after the latest strike on Wildberries online retail warehouses Image: REUTERS

What happened in Russia?

The latest Ukrainian drone strikes to target warehouses of the online retail giant Wildberries struck in St. Petersburg, Vladimir Putin's powerbase for decades, on Friday.

Company founder Tatyana Kim said facilities came under attack in St. Petersburg, in the adjacent Leningrad region, and also in occupied Ukraine in Simferopol, a city in illegally annexed Crimea.

Large plumes of smoke were visible rising over central St. Petersburg on Friday morning.

Ukraine has struck a series of Wildberries facilities in recent days, causing large fires. It describes the sites as logistics hubs and says it provides components that Russia uses for military equipment like drones. Analysts also speculate that it might be an attempt to make ordinary Russians feel the consequences of the war and sense that their government cannot safeguard their interests.

Wildberries facilities have been repeatedly struck on an almost daily basis this week Image: AFP

What happened in Romania?

Romania's Defense Ministry and later NATO also said on Friday that Alliance aircraft had shot down a stray drone that had entered Romanian airspace.

Bucharest's Defense Ministry said a Romanian F-16 fighter engaged the drone and neutralized it "over an unpopulated area in the vicinity of Padina, Buzau County."

It described a flight path entering its airspace around Sulina, a town bordering the southwestern tip of Ukraine, across the Black Sea from occupied Crimea. It headed west and inland, approaching Buzau. After tracking the drone for a little over an hour, a Romanian Air Force jet shot it down just after 11 a.m. local time, the ministry said.

Several incidents of stray drones straying into NATO members, more typically in the Baltic but also sometimes further south, have taken place this year. Ukraine tends to blame Russia for scrambling the drones' navigation systems and causing them to encroach on other countries' airspace.

World.content:
07/24/2026 July 24, 2026 Netanyahu vows to 'act with full force' after fatal West Bank clashes

The incident occurred near the Israeli settlement of Havat Gilad in the occupied West Bank Image: Hilel Ben Or/JNA/ZUMA/picture alliance

The Israeli military killed four Palestinians near an Israeli settlement in the occupied West Bank on Friday, while two Israelis were also killed in the clashes.

Israeli media reports and local Palestinian officials suggested that a group of Israeli settlers, some of whom were armed, entered the Palestinian village of Tell, southwest of Nablus, on Friday morning. The settlers were met by residents of the Palestinian village who were fearful of an attack.

Footage of the incident that was confirmed by the Israeli military and shared online by the military correspondent for Israel's Army Radio showed two armed men in civilian clothing, as well as at least one Israeli soldier, pointing their weapons at a group of Palestinians who had gathered in a field.

"Villagers came out to defend their homes and property. Clashes and physical altercations broke out between the residents and the settlers," the head of the village council in Tell, Walid Zidan, told the AFP news agency.

"Israeli soldiers were present and together with the settlers began opening fire ... it was the settlers who stormed the village, with the intention of killing, vandalizing and setting property on fire."

Mobile phone footage showed parts of the incident Image: REUTERS

The Israeli military said it has received reports that Israeli civilians were hiking in the area and had been attacked by Palestinians.

In response to the incident, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed to "act with full force against the terrorists and those who orchestrate and sponsor them."

The Israeli military subsequently set up roadblocks near Tell and Nablus and announced a widespread operation in the occupied West Bank.

"Following the terror attack earlier today in the area of Tell, IDF soldiers are preparing for extensive counterterrorism operational activity in the sector," the military said.

World.title: US floats AI 'kill switch' to stop rogue AI models
World.content:
A rogue AI agent has sent a "wake-up call" about the perils of the fast-evolving technology, sparking calls to provide a US government kill switch. But what exactly does that mean, and what are the issues with it?

Lawmakers in the US have called for an AI kill switch after an Open AI agent in testing went rogue and hacked a tech startup earlier this week.

Congressman Ted Lieu, a Democrat, and Congressman Nathaniel Moran, a Republican, introduced a bill named the "AI Kill Switch Act" on Thursday.

The move came a day after Open AI CEO Sam Altman admitted to a "significant security incident" in which an Open AI agent had escaped its testing environment, reached the internet and broke into tech startup Hugging Face to try to fulfill its task. In other words, Open AI lost control.

Hugging Face is an open-source repository for sharing AI models used largely by developers and researchers. The company's co-founder, Thomas Wolf, called the incident a "wake-up call” and "very different" from the usual cyberattacks.

"This will be one of the most common types of cyberattacks we see", he told the BBC, adding that most firms are not aware that the "game has changed."

Can Germany and Europe hold their own in AI race? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In the wake of the attack there were some unsubstantiated claims that the incident was a PR stunt to raise the profile of Hugging Face. Regardless of the truth of the matter, the incident has brought into even sharper focus the threat posed by AI without clear guardrails.

What is an AI kill switch?

There are different types and levels of kill switch, according to what's gone wrong. What politicians Lieu and Moran want is to ensure the US Department of Homeland Security has the authority to order a private company to shut down an AI model or tool in an incident like what happened this week, when control is lost.

"It is imperative that these AI systems have kill switches so we can keep this technology from causing catastrophic harm, and that the federal government has the clear authority and process to shut down rogue AI models," said Lieu.

Rather than a physical switch, this would involve any compromised AI company disabling or throttling a number of technical processes to shut a rogue agent, or program, down.

The US government has generally welcomed AI advances. The Pentagon said earlier this year that the US military is fast becoming an "AI-first fighting force," after signing new and expanded contracts with many of the sector's biggest names. In 2025, the Trump administration launched an"‘AI Action Plan" which he said would "remove red tape and onerous regulation" around AI development.

Why is an AI kill switch needed?

Companies including Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic and Samsung have already agreed to show US authorities new AI tools and capabilities before release. In theory, this should mean that a kill switch is not needed in products released to the public.

But the commitment is voluntary and does not mandate a kill switch. Neither would that mechanism stop a product in testing, like OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol, which was involved in this week's incident.

The rapid rise of AI has posed serious questions over its regulation, with technology able to move much faster than lawmakers. There are also concerns that models may, at some point, become sophisticated enough to bypass a kill switch.

How the US is merging artificial intelligence and warfare To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The bill in the US is an attempt for a government to take some form of control over a largely unregulated technology in which power is largely concentrated in a few private companies. However, even if the AI Kill Switch Act is successful, it will still rely on the cooperation of profit-driven private companies.

What other AI safeguards are US authorities now considering?

As well as the kill switch capability, the proposal in the US seeks "incident reporting and [to] preserve forensic records so we actually learn from failures instead of only hearing about them after the fact."

At the same time, but separately to the kill switch act, a bipartisan group of six US lawmakers has proposed legislation that ​would require developers of the most powerful AI models to submit them for independent security audits. The auditors would be overseen by a new role in the US Department of Commerce, which would also accredit the auditors.

World.title: Europe wildfires: Thousands flee by boat as fires spread, merge
World.content:
Tens of thousands hopped onto cars and boats to escape wildfires raging in southwestern France. In Spain's Madrid region, authorities declared a national emergency after at least two fires merged.

Wildfires continued to rage through parts of France and Spain on Friday, forcing tens of thousands to evacuate and authorities to ask European Union neighbors for help.

French authorities ordered the total evacuation of the tourist Cap Ferret peninsula off the Atlantic coast, with many boarding boats to flee.

In Spain, two fires converged near the capital, Madrid, with authorities declaring a national emergency, the first ever due to a wildfire.

Wildfires in southern Europe cause mass evacuations To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What do we know about France's Cap Ferret fire?

Over 60,000 people evacuated the area in and around Cap Ferret as the blaze consumed some 100 square kilometers (38 square miles) of land.

Authorities sent boats to help with the evacuation, with many others using small water taxis.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told local television that a fire that erupted in Saumos, north of Cap Ferret, was the largest so far this season in France. It was threatening to cut off the only road out of the peninsula.

"It's quite impressive and even frightening," the Associated Press quoted Laurent Moretti, a resident in the town of Ares, as saying. "An evacuation on this scale has never happened before. All we really hope is that the firefighters can quickly get it under control."

Tens of thousands had to evacuate the tourist area of Cap Ferret as wildfires continued to rage Image: Stephane Mahe/REUTERS

Some 1,500 of those who fled the peninsula arrived in the city of Arcachon by sea. They were met with coffee, fruit and water in a reception area prepared by town officials.

In the Gironde department, Nunez said 40,000 people have been evacuated, with 23,000 more in the Landes department.

French President Emmanuel Macron said the country will receive EU reinforcements to help put out the blaze, after calling for the neighbors' help.

Madrid blaze 'beyond firefighters' capacity' as 2 fires merge

As Spanish authorities declared a national emergency over the wildfires, two fires converged despite the deployment of over 2,000 personnel and 10 aircraft in an effort to control the blaze, according to Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska.

Some 40,000 people evacuated or confined due to Madrid region wildfires, officials have said. Over 19,000 people were ordered to evacuate from towns in the mountains west of Madrid, where many of the capital's residents sport second homes. The area is densely populated.

The fire outside the Spanish capital is "at its peak" and out of control, said Carlos Novillo, the Madrid regional government's emergency management chief.

Heat waves fuel wildfires across southern Europe To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The wildfire is at its peak and is currently beyond the capacity of firefighters to contain," he told reporters on Friday.

Only emergency vehicles were allowed on roads near the blaze, the AFP news agency reported. Police set up checkpoints to prevent unauthorized access.

Nicanor Sen, the government representative for the Castile and Leon region, told reporters a third fire in nearby Avila province was about to also merge with the other fires, or may have already done so.

Residents had to flee to shelters in the area west of Madrid to escape the fires Image: Pierre-Philippe Marcou/AFP

"I've lived here for 36 years and I've never seen anything like it. ​Nor did I expect it. I thought they were going to get it under control last night, but it was already late, and it was all out of control," local resident Javier Martin told Reuters.

Spanish authorities declared a national emergency on Thursday in the Madrid region and the province of Avila.

"We are experiencing a dramatic situation, not just in several Spanish regions but also in neighboring countries," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez wrote on X.

Edited by: Sean Sinico and Karl Sexton

World.title: Niger still seeks stability, after 3 years of military rule
World.content:
The military government in Niger had promised social, security and economic improvements when it took power in 2023. Three years down the line, there are mixed reviews on its performance.

The military seized power in Niger on July 26, 2023. General Abdourahamane Tchiani , who became head of state, justified the coup by citing the poor security situation, which he said persisted despite international support.

In the weeks that followed, the military government announced a transitional period that was to last a maximum of three years.

However, the political promises made upon taking office have not been fulfilled. The transitional government continues to hold all the reins, and the security situation in the Sahel country remains fragile.

In the Tillabery region in southwestern Niger, attacks by jihadists are on the rise. Thousands of people have been forced to flee their villages, plunging the region into a severe humanitarian crisis.

Niger's military government has struggled to end an Islamist insurgency despite promises to do so Image: Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty Images

"Today, attacks on the armed forces and the civilian population are significantly more frequent and violent than they were three years ago," Maiga, a resident of the city of Tera, which has a population of 30,000, told DW. Maiga wished to remain anonymous for security reasons.

"Life used to be better despite the insecurity; the weekly markets operated normally and supplies arrived regularly," he said, adding that at the moment entire villages had fled and schools are closed.

The independent conflict monitor ACLED has also said the the security situation has deteriorated since the 2023 coup.

According to the organization, the Tillaberi region remains the main hot spot for clashes between two rival Islamist groups, Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin and the so-called Islamic State in the Sahel Province (formerly ISGS). This rivalry has resulted in numerous casualties among soldiers and civilians.

In 2025, nearly 1,200 deaths were recorded in the region. For Heni Nsaibia, a staff member at ACLED, these figures attest to the scale of the security crisis affecting Niger.

The most recent major attack, on July 17, claimed the lives of at least 16 soldiers, according to Niger's state media, ANP. Fifteen terrorists were killed in that attack, ANP said.

"The situation in Niger has worsened, particularly in the Tillaberi region, where the death toll is the highest in the central Sahel," Nsaibia told DW.

Insecurity taking a toll on civilians

"We live in makeshift shelters and are defenseless against the elements; we take on small odd jobs to survive," a woman told DW.

"I used to be able to live with dignity from my work, but right now it's very difficult; even [portable] drinking water is a problem for us," added a local herder.

Young Nigeriens are torn between disappointment and optimism: In the youth assemblies, known as "Fadas," the topic continues to spark discussion. Some — like Fadila — believe that the situation is gradually stabilizing after the turmoil of the first few years.

There was much optimism in Niger after the military took over power three years ago Image: AFP/Getty Images

"For a while, it wasn't easy at all: Salaries weren't paid on time, food supplies… that wasn't easy. But for some time now, things have been going pretty well overall," Fadila told DW.

General Tchiani has emphasized that young people can once again participate in politics. "Before the coup, young people were excluded from decision-making bodies." But in the meantime, he said, an advisory commission has been established that includes young people. "So that means the concerns of young people are now being taken into account in decision-making bodies."

Just two days after the ouster of President Mohamed Bazoumin 2023, junta leader Tchiani announced plans to combat corruption and boost the economy.

But three years later, the people of Niger are no better off, noted Tahirou Garka, a close ally of Bazoum. He is the spokesperson for the G25, a movement advocating for a return to constitutional order in Niger.

"They have failed economically and socially," he said, referring to the military government. "People are struggling to find drinking water; there is no water, no electricity, no fuel."

What is the Alliance of Democrats for the Sahel? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, Hamani Oumarou of LASDEL, a social sciences research institute based in Niamey, takes a different view. According to him, the socioeconomic situation has improved for a large portion of Niger's population, especially for those who are not part of the middle class or the elite.

"Households with low incomes have more money left over to feed their families," Oumarou told DW. However, Niger is also forced to import food at certain times of the year, which leads to a sharp rise in prices.

Rebuilding ties with ECOWAS

Along with Mali and Burkina Faso, Niger is a founding member of the lliance of Sahel States (AES), which was formed in 2023 after all the three countries withdrew from the West African regional organization ECOWAS.

The AES has distanced itself from Western partners and is seeking closer ties with Russia.

Pape Ibrahima Kane, an expert on international organizations, now hopes for a rapprochement between the AES member states and their longtime allies in West Africa.

The military leaders of the Sahel Alliance support one another militarily and economically, but still face political sanctions by the African Union Image: Mahamadou Hamidou/REUTERS

He sees a positive sign in the fact that former Guinean Prime Minister Lansana Kouyate was elected chief negotiator for ECOWAS a few days ago. According to Kane, Kouyate seems to have been accepted by the AES.

"We are at the beginning of a promising process, as both sides are truly on the same page when it comes to starting talks," he told DW.

For him, economic negotiations should also play a role. Niger depends on access to the port of Benin and on its electricity supply from Nigeria and Benin, both of which are ECOWAS member states.

Reliou Koubakin and Ali Abdou contributed to this article.

This article was originally written in German.

Correction, July 24, 2026: A previous version of this article stated that Lansana Kouyate is Guinea's current prime minister. This has been corrected, and DW apologizes for the error.

World.title: Última hora de los incendios forestales, en directo | Más de 60.000 afectados por el fuego voraz en Madrid y Ávila
World.content:
El delegado del Gobierno de Madrid considera que esta noche "se abre una verdadera oportunidad" para hacer frente al fuego

El delegado del Gobierno en Madrid, Francisco Martín, ha señalado a las 23.30 que “tras haber pasado una tarde verdaderamente complicada, ahora se abre una verdadera oportunidad para hacer frente a este incendio con garantías de éxito”.

Tras la última reunión del Cecopi, Martín ha indicado que las condiciones han mejorado respecto a esta tarde: ha bajado la temperatura, se ha frenado el viento y ha aumentado la humedad relativa. “Por tanto, se dan las condiciones precisas para que todos los esfuerzos de extinción se desarrollen en cada uno de los flancos y podamos controlarlo. Esa oportunidad la vamos a aprovechar”.

Las labores de extinción con medios terrestres continuarán toda la noche y por la mañana se incorporarán los medios aéreos. Confían en poder utilizar las condiciones de la noche para lograr perimetrarlo, algo que ha sido complicado durante el día, sobre todo debido al viento y el “voraz” avance de las llamas.

“Por la mañana se prevé que vuelva a levantarse el viento, además con rachas un tanto erráticas y, por tanto, las condiciones que se puedan desarrollar a lo largo de mañana serán complejas. Por eso es tan importante que aprovechemos esta noche para tratar de controlar el incendio todo lo que podamos”, ha apuntado desde el puesto de mando en el municipio madrileño de Cenicientos. También ha añadido, respecto al avance hacia El Escorial, que “el frente se mantiene suficientemente lejos para que no tengan que tomar medidas adicionales [ya se han evacuado 5.000 personas de un camping]”.

World.title: La moderación del precio del petróleo levanta el castigo al mercado de deuda
World.content:
El barril de ‘brent’ baja hasta los 95 dólares y diluye el temor a un repunte de la inflación. El Ibex ha liderado el viernes las ganancias en Europa con una subida del 1,6%

Las Bolsas cierran la semana con alivio después de que el petróleo frenara su escalada y remitiera la presión sobre la deuda soberana. El brent, que el jueves llegó a superar los 100 dólares por barril, se ha alejado de esos máximos y ha favorecido un rebote de la renta variable y de los bonos. Con el retroceso de la tensión energética, los inversores han rebajado parte de las expectativas de inflación que amenazaban con lastrar el crecimiento económico. El Ibex ha recuperado el viernes un 1,6%, hasta los 19.585 puntos, con un avance semanal del 1,9%.

El crudo de referencia en Europa ha corregido este viernes más del 5% y vuelve a situarse en los 95 dólares por barril, pese a los ataques por parte de la milicia hutí, aliada de Irán, a barcos que transportaban petróleo de Arabia Saudí por el mar Rojo. Un recrudecimiento de las tensiones en la región que hace temer por el destino de la que ha sido en los últimos meses la principal vía de salida de la producción de combustibles del reino saudí tras el cierre del estrecho de Ormuz y que complica aún más el transporte de petróleo, gas natural y sus derivados. Por el momento, las amenazas de represalia del presidente estadounidense, Donald Trump, que ha asegurado estar “considerando un ataque masivo”, no se han traducido en un nuevo repunte de los precios de la energía.

Los inversores optan por la cautela y aguardan a conocer la respuesta de Washington durante el fin de semana. Desde el inicio del conflicto, el mercado se ha acostumbrado a una secuencia en la que la Casa Blanca eleva el tono al cierre de la semana para moderarlo al comienzo de la siguiente, una pauta que ha llevado a muchos operadores a evitar reaccionar de forma precipitada a cada declaración.

El baño de realidad que ha supuesto el repunte del crudo —el brent en lo que va de mes sube casi un 40%— supone una clara advertencia para unos inversores que habían desplazado el foco de atención a la evolución de los resultados trimestrales y que habían dejado en un segundo plano la inestabilidad geopolítica. “Los mercados están evaluando si el brent debería mantenerse en el nivel de 100 dólares por barril, ya que están aumentando las preocupaciones sobre la demanda”, ha reconocido a Bloomberg June Goh, analista sénior del mercado petrolero en Sparta Commodities. En su opinión, “desde la perspectiva de la oferta, estamos claramente en una situación de déficit, con el estrecho de Ormuz y Bab el-Mandeb prácticamente bloqueados y la producción del oleoducto del Caspio [en Kazajistán] limitada”.

Un contexto que, según los analistas de RBC BlueBay, puede desencadenar nuevos episodios de elevada volatilidad, ya que ni Washington ni Teherán parecen dispuestos a dar su brazo a torcer. El escenario que recuerda al denominado “juego de la gallina”, en el que el riesgo de un error de cálculo aumenta a medida que ambas partes elevan la presión.

La moderación del petróleo ha tenido además efecto calmante en el mercado de bonos, penalizado por la perspectiva de que un precio del petróleo más elevado provoque un alza de la inflación. Aun así, el rendimiento del índice de Bloomberg que recoge los bonos soberanos de países con calificación de grado de inversión se ha disparado hasta el 3,68%, su nivel más alto en tres años, solo superado por el alcanzado durante la crisis financiera de 2008. El temor a que el shock energético derive en un repunte sostenido de la inflación, algo que por ahora se ha evitado, se ha dejado sentir como una losa en la deuda soberana esta semana. La rentabilidad del bono de Estados Unidos a diez años ha llegado a dispararse hasta el 4,7%, máximos desde 2024. Un castigo que también se ha visualizado con virulencia en Europa, donde el rendimiento de la deuda alemana a una década ha llegado a alcanzar el 3,2%, récord desde 2011. En el caso del bono español, ha llegado a tocar el 3,7%, su máximo en los dos últimos años.

El repunte del petróleo vuelve a poner a prueba a los bancos centrales en su lucha contra la inflación. El Consejo de Gobierno del Banco Central Europeo optó esta semana por mantener sin cambios los tipos de interés y dejó abierta la puerta a una subida en septiembre. No obstante, la institución evitó comprometerse con un movimiento concreto y supeditó cualquier decisión al comportamiento de la inflación y la actividad económica durante los próximos meses. La próxima semana será el turno de la Reserva Federal, el Banco de Japón y el Banco de Inglaterra. Mientras tanto, el encarecimiento de la energía ha reactivado las expectativas de una política monetaria más restrictiva en Estados Unidos. El mercado descuenta con una probabilidad creciente una subida de tipos en septiembre allí, y ya empieza a contemplar un segundo incremento antes de finales de año.

El alivio por la moderación del petróleo devuelve el apetito por el riesgo a las Bolsas europeas. El Euro Stoxx 50 ha avanzado un 1,2% y el Ibex 35 se anota un 1,65%, suficiente para recuperar los 19.500 puntos y borrar las pérdidas sufridas en la sesión anterior. La temporada de resultados vuelve a marcar el paso del mercado: Acerinox se ha disparado este viernes un 10,7% tras regresar a beneficios y Sabadell, un 3,4%, después de rendir cuentas al mercado. Entre los valores más castigados figura Mapfre, que ha retrocedido un 4,7% un día, después de anunciar la adquisición de Safety Insurance por 1.542 millones de dólares.

Aunque la temporada de resultados sigue respaldando el optimismo de los inversores, el entusiasmo no se reparte por igual. Después de meses, e incluso años, de fuertes subidas entre las grandes tecnológicas, las dudas sobre la sostenibilidad de sus multimillonarios planes de inversión en inteligencia artificial empiezan a pesar más en la valoración de algunas compañías. “Los inversores ya se muestran cada vez más nerviosos respecto a la sostenibilidad del repunte de la IA”, afirmó a Bloomberg Gerald Gan, director de inversiones de Reed Capital en Singapur. “Dicho esto, es probable que cualquier corrección a corto plazo vuelva a atraer a los compradores que aprovechan las caídas. Por ahora, la música no se ha detenido”, añadió.

De puntillas ha pasado el mercado por la nueva oleada de aranceles anunciada por Donald Trump. El mandatario ha impuesto gravámenes de entre el 10% y el 12,5% a 60 socios comerciales clave de Estados Unidos, entre ellos Reino Unido, China, Japón e India, al considerar insuficientes sus esfuerzos para combatir el trabajo forzado. Los inversores, sin embargo, han relegado esta amenaza a un segundo plano, más pendientes de la evolución del petróleo, la inflación y sus posibles consecuencias para la política monetaria.

El retroceso del petróleo ha dado un respiro temporal a los mercados, pero no ha despejado las incógnitas. La posibilidad de nuevas interrupciones en el suministro energético, el riesgo de un repunte de la inflación y la perspectiva de unos tipos de interés más elevados amenazan con devolver la volatilidad a los activos financieros. Por ahora, los inversores celebran la tregua del crudo, aunque son conscientes de que la calma depende de factores que escapan al control de los mercados.

World.title: El Corte Inglés aprueba un nuevo dividendo récord: abonará en torno a 250 millones de euros
World.content:
De izquierda a derecha, el secretario del consejo de El Corte Inglés, José Ramón de Hoces; Cristina Álvarez, presidenta; y el consejero delegado, Javier Catena, en la junta de accionistas celebrada este viernes.

El Corte Inglés vuelve a batir un nuevo récord en el reparto de dividendos. La compañía de distribución, que este viernes ha celebrado su junta de accionistas anual, ha aprobado el reparto de un dividendo de en torno a 250 millones de euros, según ha podido saber este periódico. Una cifra que supera los 225 millones del año pasado, que ya marcaron el techo histórico en esta variable, y que confirman la política al alza en la retribución al accionista.

Esos 250 millones equivalen a casi la mitad del beneficio neto recurrente que El Corte Inglés alcanzó el año pasado, de 522 millones, un 11% más que en el anterior. Una proporción de las ganancias, o payout en la jerga financiera, que viene dedicando a este fin en los últimos años. El beneficio neto consolidado, contando también elementos extraordinarios, fue de 628 millones, resultado que también ha sido aprobado en junta, al igual que el nombramiento de Javier Catena como nuevo consejero delegado. El mismo fue anunciado el pasado 19 de junio.

Esta ha sido la primera junta de El Corte Inglés presidida por Cristina Álvarez, en el cargo desde enero. En su discurso a los accionistas, esta ha confirmado que la compañía aprobará el próximo mes de septiembre una actualización del plan estratégico que tiene en marcha, que contempla un mayor nivel de inversiones y que se centrará en el crecimiento del negocio, la mejora de la logística y las nuevas capacidades tecnológicas.

Álvarez no ha detallado el nivel de inversiones que se sumarán al actual plan estratégico, que contemplaba un volumen de 3.000 millones de euros hasta 2030 en iniciativas como la renovación de las tiendas. Sí ha puesto el foco en el ámbito logístico, al que pone el objetivo de “crecer y dar un mejor servicio a nuestras tiendas y clientes”. También lo ha hecho sobre la implementación de la inteligencia artificial, que debe “ayudar a personalizar la experiencia de compra, optimizar la disponibilidad de productos, agilizar la atención y sobre todo interpretar mejor las necesidades de nuestros clientes”. Para este ejercicio, la inversión está fijada en 650 millones.

Las nuevas líneas maestras del grupo, que deberán ser ratificadas por el consejo de administración a la vuelta de verano, vienen a actualizar el plan que fue presentado, precisamente, en la junta de accionistas de hace un año, cuando Marta Álvarez era presidenta del grupo y Gastón Bottazzini, su consejero delegado.

En estos últimos 12 meses, los cambios no han dejado de sucederse en la cúpula de la compañía: Bottazzini fue despedido en octubre; Marta Álvarez comunicó un mes después que dejaba la presidencia en manos de su hermana Cristina, con efectos a partir de enero; y ya bajo el mandato de esta, la compañía ha recuperado a Javier Catena como consejero delegado, tras salir de la misma meses antes, lo que a su vez ha provocado la salida de su ya ex director general, Santiago Bau.

La de hoy, por tanto, ha sido la primera vez que Cristina Álvarez se ha dirigido a los accionistas de El Corte Inglés. Según un comunicado enviado por la compañía, esta ha puesto el foco relevancia del servicio al cliente, de la tienda física y en la excelencia en el producto como aspectos estratégicos.

“La tienda física es, hoy más que nunca, un entorno de experiencias donde se genera la interacción humana, donde tenemos la oportunidad de construir marca, más allá de una pura transacción económica”, ha dicho Álvarez, quien ha defendido el establecimiento físico como un “valor diferencial para el grupo”, así como “un activo esencial para conectar con nuestros clientes”.

Esta también ha destacado el canal online “gana peso día a día”. “Nuestra web y nuestra app se han convertido en la puerta de entrada de muchos clientes. Debemos seguir impulsándolas, mejorando la experiencia digital y la personalización, porque son uno de nuestros grandes motores de crecimiento y de captación de nuevos clientes", ha añadido. En paralelo, ha reafirmado a El Corte Inglés como “la casa de las marcas”, y como una compañía capaz de “ofrecer a nuestros clientes productos exclusivos, curados, novedosos, y adaptados a la realidad de cada una de nuestras diferentes tiendas y canales”.

Resultados y apuesta por los viajes

La presidenta de El Corte Inglés ha valorado los resultados cosechados por la compañía el año pasado, en un contexto comercial marcado “por cambios estructurales, incertidumbres, aceleración tecnológica y evolución de las expectativas del consumidor”. En este sentido, ha destacado que el grupo “ha demostrado una gran capacidad de adaptación y de fortaleza”, y que los resultados “son la expresión financiera de la confianza que nuestros clientes han depositado en nosotros”.

La cifra de negocios de El Corte Inglés alcanzó los 14.988 millones de euros, un incremento interanual del 1,4%, porcentaje que sube al 2% a superficie comparable. El volumen total de transacciones alcanzó los 17.247 millones de euros, un 1,1% más, aunque esta cifra incluye servicios de intermediación que presta su agencia de viajes que no se incluyen en la cuenta de resultados.

Precisamente, sobre la agencia de viajes ha destacado que se trata de un servicio “que lleva nuestro sello, que genera confianza, y que refuerza el vínculo con nuestros clientes”. Y añadió que “es nuestra obligación seguir apostando con fuerza por este negocio”. En las últimas semanas, Viajes El Corte Inglés se ha hecho con un contrato para ser la agencia de Aena durante los próximos dos años, valorado en 27 millones por ese periodo, lo que le permite reforzarse en el ámbito corporativo.

Álvarez culminó su discurso asegurando que El Corte Inglés cuenta, en estos momentos, “con el mejor equipo, con una estrategia sólida, y con una marca que ocupa un lugar único en el corazón de millones de personas. El futuro no se improvisa. Se construye cada día con trabajo, con humildad, con capacidad de escuchar, y con voluntad permanente de mejor”.

World.title: El fabricante suizo de chocolate Lindt se enfrenta a una demanda en EE UU por presunto uso de trabajo infantil
World.content:
La compañía suiza de chocolate Lindt & Sprüngli ha sido demandada ante un tribunal federal de Washington D.C. por su supuesto uso de trabajo infantil en la producción de cacao en Ghana y Costa de Marfil, pese a que la empresa asegura públicamente estar comprometida con un abastecimiento responsable de sus materias primas.

Según la demanda, presentada el martes ante la justicia estadounidense, Lindt estaría ofreciendo a los consumidores información engañosa al afirmar que trabaja para erradicar el trabajo infantil de su cadena de suministro y que mantiene un firme compromiso con los derechos de la infancia y los derechos humanos. Los demandantes sostienen además que la empresa conoce desde hace más de dos décadas que parte del cacao que utiliza se produce con mano de obra infantil y que obtiene beneficios de esa práctica.

“La persona consumidora razonable no esperaría que una empresa comprometida con el respeto de los derechos humanos y con una actividad empresarial ética, legal, ambiental y socialmente responsable recurriera a una cadena de suministro del cacao en la que el trabajo infantil está ampliamente extendido”, señala el escrito de la demanda.

De acuerdo con la denuncia, Lindt obtiene el 100% de los granos de cacao de calidad para consumo procedentes de Ghana y adquiere manteca de cacao en Costa de Marfil. La demanda ha sido presentada por International Rights Advocates, un despacho de interés público que anteriormente también ha impulsado acciones legales contra fabricantes de chocolate como Mars, Mondelez y Nestlé por presunta dependencia del trabajo infantil.

Por su parte, Lindt rechazó las acusaciones. En declaraciones remitidas por correo electrónico, un portavoz de la compañía afirmó que la empresa se toma “muy en serio” la cuestión del trabajo infantil, condena “enérgicamente todas sus formas” y niega las acusaciones recogidas en la demanda. “Contamos con protocolos para nuestros proveedores e investigamos de forma sistemática los casos sospechosos de trabajo infantil en nuestra cadena de suministro”, aseguró la compañía.

La empresa, con sede en Kilchberg (Suiza), incluye en su página web un Plan de Sostenibilidad 2030 en el que detalla iniciativas destinadas a apoyar a los productores de cacao de África occidental y reducir los riesgos asociados al trabajo infantil. Asimismo, publica una declaración sobre esclavitud moderna en la que expone una estrategia específica para mitigar estos riesgos, entre otras medidas, mediante el cumplimiento de los estándares de certificación de Rainforest Alliance para las prácticas agrícolas.

La demanda busca poner fin a lo que describe como una conducta ilegal dirigida a los consumidores del Distrito de Columbia, aunque no reclama compensaciones económicas. El director ejecutivo de International Rights Advocates, Terry Collingsworth, sostuvo que las investigaciones de la organización confirman que Lindt, al igual que otras grandes compañías del sector del cacao, dispone de “excelentes políticas sobre el papel”, pero presenta una aplicación “prácticamente inexistente”, especialmente en lo relativo al trabajo infantil.

El despacho también ha presentado demandas contra empresas como Apple, Cargill y Starbucks por presuntas prácticas de trabajo forzoso en sus cadenas de suministro.

World.title: Blood on Her Tongue: A modern vampire tale not for the squeamish
World.content:
Johanna van Veen’s gothic horror Blood on Her Tongue offers up a classic vampire tale with some modern contemplations.

The book follows Lucy Goedhart as she is called to the ominously named Zwartwater (black water) estate, where her sister has taken ill. In 1887, there isn’t much in the way of medical treatment, but Lucy’s sister Sarah isn’t fighting off a regular illness.

Sarah has become obsessed with a body found in the bog of the vast estate and since interacting with the 300-year-old corpse she has become increasingly incoherent, struggles with taking care of herself and has developed an insatiable hunger.

As Lucy tries desperately to save her sister, she finds that her sister’s husband, her sister’s doctor and childhood friend, and several other characters who are present at the remote manor house all have their own interests and motivations – some as dangerous as whatever condition is plaguing Sarah.

The book is not for those easily bothered by gore. The title – Blood on Her Tongue – is a pretty good indication of what is to come. Van Veen does not shy away from the horror elements, including two separate scenes of eyeball gouging.

Like any good horror novel, the macabre monster is not the scariest part. The threats Lucy faces are from the men surrounding her sister. Her brother-in-law attempts to seduce Lucy while badgering her to send Sarah away to an asylum.

Sarah’s doctor expresses his own interest in Lucy, pushing his vision of the future while supposedly devoting himself to his patient. The mores of 19th-century upper-class society may be the biggest piece of villainy of all.

In the tradition of Dracula, Blood on Her Tongue tells its story through letters, journal entries and newspaper clippings. The personal correspondence adds to the claustrophobia of the work, with everyone limited to an isolated house, but the media reports remind the reader that the world outside does exist.

The work is the second book from Dutch author Johanna van Veen. It was published in 2025 in English and became a USA Today bestseller. Her first book, My Darling Dreadful Thing, was nominated for the Bram Stoker Award for best horror novel. Van Veen grew up in the Netherlands as a triplet, something that influenced her writing about the sisters Lucy and Sarah.

If horror is your thing, Blood on Her Tongue will creep you out and keep you turning the pages.

You can get your copy at the American Book Center.

World.title: Thousands cross finishing line as Nijmegen Vierdaagse ends
World.content:
The 108th edition of the Nijmegense Vierdaagse (four-day march) ended on Friday, with tens of thousands of walkers being welcomed with flowers by well-wishers.

British walker Simon Brownlee crossed the finishing line ahead of the rest of the walkers for the 27th time, local media reported. Brownlee, who completed the distance before 10am, told local broadcaster Omroep Gelderland that the walk “felt like home”. “I’m happy it is over and I can now relax,” he said.

Wheelchair participant Ronald van Dort was the very first person to finish, picking up his seventh medal for completing the event.

Over 45,000 walkers from 70 countries took part in this year’s series, which is proving increasingly popular among the young. Ten years ago, 7.5% of the walkers were aged 21 to 30, but this year their number rose to over 20%.

This year the event was marred by a fatal shooting just outside the area where the Vierdaagsefeesten, the street festivities accompanying the annual four-day marches, were taking place. One man has been arrested.

The shooting, and other crowd problems, led the organisers to cancel performances by urban scene artists such as Ronnie Flex and Lil’ Kleine because their presence was “attracting the wrong sort of people”, the AD reported.

World.title: Dozens of women forced into prostitution by Romanian gang
World.content:
Dozens of women may have been forced into working as prostitutes in Amsterdam’s red light district by a Romanian gang, Dutch police confirmed on Friday.

The statement follows a joint Dutch and Romanian campaign against human trafficking in the area earlier this month. Seven men were arrested during a string of raids on July 14 – four in the Netherlands and three in Romania. All were Romanian nationals.

Shortly after the arrests, police issued a video interview with one of the victims speaking Romanian, which has led more women to come forward and has resulted in other information reaching the police, the statement said.

Police now say they have spoken to several victims and say they believe more women have been trafficked. They too are said to be Romanian.

The women were lured to Amsterdam with the promise of high earnings but found themselves forced into working in brothels and handing over their earnings to the gang. They were also forced to pay “rent” for their rooms.

None of the men had jobs but were big spenders, buying expensive clothes and cars and gambling heavily, the statement said. The gang also treated part of the red light district as their “personal kingdom”.

Four men remain in custody in the Netherlands, one of whom was extradited from Romania. Another man may also be extradited soon, RTL said. They are all suspected of human trafficking and forming a criminal organisation.

According to the Parool, two of the suspects are half brothers aged 44 and 45 who have earlier convictions for trafficking in women in Romania.

More arrests have not been ruled out.

A year ago, Dutch and Romanian police arrested 13 people in a joint investigation into human trafficking and the forced prostitution of Romanian women, mainly in and around Amsterdam.

World.title: Singer Sophie Straat cleared of discrimination over mosh pit
World.content:
Discrimination hotlines in both the Netherlands and Belgium have concluded that Dutch singer Sophie Straat did not discriminate when she asked “all white men to step back” during two of her recent performances.

Last month at the Best Kept Secret festival in Beekse Bergen, Straat — real name Sophie Schwartz — asked for space for women, queer people and people of colour in the “mosh pit”, an area in front of the stage where fans dance chaotically.

She made the same request on Monday during a performance in Ghent, Belgium.

The Dutch discrimination hotline Discriminatie.nl said it received hundreds of complaints but maintains that Straat’s comments do not amount to discrimination against white men based on their colour or gender.

“The call only concerned one short, one-off mosh pit for these groups,” said the hotline. “Therefore, visitors were not refused entry to the concert.”

Belgian authorities reached the same conclusion after receiving some 200 complaints following her performance in Ghent.

“Although the statement may be perceived as polarizing or offensive, in this context it must be seen as a symbolic and artistic expression,” a spokesperson for the Belgian discrimination hotline Unia told the Flemish broadcaster VRT.

“According to the case law of the European Court of Human Rights, artistic and political expressions enjoy broad protection under freedom of expression, even when they provoke, shock or offend.”

Hate messages and death threats

Straat wrote on Instagram earlier this month that she has received “a wave of sexist, antisemitic hate messages and (death) threats, some more explicit and creative than others”.

She has also questioned where the left-wing media has been in all this, saying the public narrative is being controlled by the right.

The singer, who was raised in a Jewish home in Amsterdam’s de Pijp neighbourhood and is known for her protest songs, has said she never wanted to exclude anyone but rather wanted to make room for people who feel unsafe in a mosh pit.

World.title: Youngster arrested for participating in sadistic online network
World.content:
Police have arrested a young man from Noord Holland who they suspect of being part of the sadistic online Com network “764”.

The public prosecution department reported the arrest on Thursday, saying the suspect encouraged underage girls to cut themselves and write his online name on a wall with their own blood—so-called “bloodsigns”.

He also is said to have prompted them to write his name on their bodies with a marker, known as“fansigns”. Both are practices within the Com movement—short for The Community—for members to gain prestige.

The suspect himself, who was also charged with aggravated assault, exploitation of underage girls and possession of images of sexual child abuse, was a minor at the time of the alleged crimes. Because of that, no further details are being released.

The Com network consists of various chat groups where members recruit vulnerable young people and force them to commit acts including assault, sexual abuse and murder.

The members, from all corners of the globe, then share images of these acts online in private chat groups, using such platforms as Telegram and Discord.

According to NOS, at least 70 Dutch people are involved in this movement known as “nihilistic extremism” because the incitement to commit such extreme violence doesn’t have a clear ideological motive.

The phenomenon is especially attractive to young men.

World.title: Dangerous drivers face extra surveillance under points system
World.content:
The police and justice ministry officials are working on a system which would see traffic offenders being given points for dangerous driving – which will lead to persistent offenders coming under extra surveillance.

Motorists who have collected six points for using a mobile phone while driving or not wearing a seatbelt would come under the tougher regime, RTL Nieuws reported on Friday. No start date has yet been set.

The points will be awarded in addition to regular fines. The number of points will depend on the seriousness of the offences and speeding tickets recorded by camera will not be included.

The new system is being devised in an effort to tackle persistent offenders who do not change their behaviour despite being fined multiple times, RTL said. Last year, almost 30,000 people would have had at least six points if the new system had been in existence.

“Research shows that people who don’t stick to the rules are often responsible for accidents,” Achilles Damen from the public prosecution department told the broadcaster.

The privacy implications of monitoring specific individuals are still being assessed, RTL said.

World.title: Ajax beat Vojvodina in Conference League qualifier, Twente lose
World.content:
Ajax kicked off their European football campaign with a 4-1 win over Serbian club Vojvodina in the second qualification round of the Conference League competition in Novi Sad on Thursday evening.

The simple win sets the Amsterdammers up in a strong position ahead of the return match next week. If Ajax win again, they will meet either Irish side Shelbourne FC or Estonian club Nõmme Kalju in the third qualification round for the third-tier European competition.

The Amsterdam goal total included one for 16-year-old debutant Mohamed Abdalla, who became the youngest player to score for a Dutch club in Europe.

There was disappointment for FC Twente, who are hoping to qualify for the group stage of the Europa League. They lost 1-2 at home to Hungarian side Ferencváros and will have to pull out all the stops during the away leg next week to remain in the competition.

If they do lose, Twente will move down to the qualification rounds of the Conference League.

PSV Eindhoven and Feyenoord have qualified directly for the Champions League while NEC is taking part in the qualification competition. AZ, as winners of the KNVB Cup last season, will take part in the Europa League competition.

World.title: Unilever backs London for food division secondary listing
World.content:
Unilever’s food division, which is being sold to US sauce and spice producer McCormick, will have a secondary listing on the London stock exchange, despite an intensive lobbying campaign to list in Amsterdam.

Unilever itself has been based in London, and listed there, since 2020.

Unilever said in a statement that the secondary listing is separate to McCormick’s plans to establish an international headquarters in the Netherlands and maintain Unilever Food’s R&D facilities and operations in Wageningen.

This “reflects its commitment to the European market and the critical role the Netherlands will continue to play in the combined company”, the statement said.

Economic affairs minister Heleen Herbert said in a reaction to the sale when it was announced in March that the cabinet had already discussed developments with Unilever and would talk to the new owner “such as about a listing on the Amsterdam stock exchange”.

Unilever’s ice cream arm, spun off in 2024, is listed on the Amsterdam stock exchange as the Magnum Ice Cream Company and is headquartered in the Dutch capital.

The sale of the food arm means there is nothing left of the original Dutch part of Unilever, which was set up in 1930 through the merger of the Dutch Margarine Unie and British soap maker Lever Brothers. Unilever now focuses on personal care and household cleaning products.

World.title: Poland bans chaining of dogs and cats

Keeping dogs and cats chained up at home will be banned in Poland from next year, after President Karol Nawrocki signed into law a bill prohibiting the practice. His decision ends a long-running dispute over the issue, after Nawrocki last year vetoed a previous proposal to ban chaining because it also included what he argued were excessive and unrealistic additional measures on minimum kennel sizes for dogs. Zawetowana w listopadzie 2025 r. ustawa łańcuchowa była źle przygotowana i przeregulowana, ponieważ nakładała na obywateli obowiązki, których wielu nie byłoby w stanie spełnić. Dzisiaj otrzymujemy ustawę lepszą, z pozytywnym głosem takich podmiotów jak rolniczy samorząd.… pic.twitter.com/h7kIAI77KR — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) July 24, 2026 The new law bans owners from tethering dogs and cats at home. Animals must be kept either inside the house, in a fenced garden or, if that is not possible, in a kennel “large enough for the animal to move freely and satisfy its natural needs”. Dogs kept in kennels must be provided with daily exercise outside of it. Dogs and cats can still be put on leashes in certain situations, such as when they are being walked, but also during transport, while participating in shows, performances or training, if they are at vets or groomers, or if they represent a danger to humans or other animals. Now that the bill has been signed by Nawrocki, it will be published in the official Journal of Laws (Dziennik Ustaw), after which it goes into force 12 months later. The new measures represent a successful second attempt to introduce a leashing ban. A previous bill was approved by parliament last September. However, in December, Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, announced that he was vetoing it. The president argued that, “although the intention – protecting animals – is just and noble, the law itself was poorly drafted”. In particular, he said that elements introducing minimum sizes for dog kennels were unrealistic and would “harm farmers, breeders and ordinary rural households”. After an attempt by parliament to overturn the veto failed, legislators went back to the drawing board and, following discussions with the president’s chancellery and animal rights groups, drafted a compromise bill that was approved by parliament earlier this month. The bill received support from the current ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, as well as most MPs from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the main opposition party. The far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) voted against it. Thousands of people have protested in Warsaw against President @NawrockiKn's veto of a law that would have banned the chaining up of dogs Parliament will vote on Wednesday on whether to overturn Nawrocki's veto, which would require a three-fifths majority https://t.co/0GRup2sppb — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 15, 2025 “We now have a better law, with positive feedback from entities such as the agricultural chamber,” said Nawrocki today. “It demonstrates that the pressure of the presidential veto makes sense. My previous decision to refuse to sign this bill forced the government and parliament to work harder.” However, although Nawrocki said the new law would no longer entail “rigid and costly requirements” for kennels, his office noted in a separate statement that the legislation requires the agriculture minister to issue a regulation establishing “minimum kennel area, taking into account the dog’s size”. It remains unclear if and how that would differ from the requirements Nawrocki previously vetoed. The presidential chancellery also noted that the law itself already outlines that kennels must be made of “wood or wood-like material with thermal insulation”, must be insulated from the ground, and must have openings on at least two sides to allow light and air to enter. World.title: Police and park rangers step up joint patrols in Poland’s Tatras after series of tourist offences
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
