World.title: Armenia’s labour market trends: Social media replaces employment agencies as jobs and wages grow
World.content:
Analysis of labour market trends in Armenia

Armenia‘s unemployment rate fell only slightly in 2025, declining to 11.8% from 13.3% in 2024. At the same time, according to the country’s Statistical Committee, wages continued to rise, with the average monthly salary increasing by 5.6% over the same period to 303,140 drams ($828).

Compared with 2021, the average nominal monthly salary has increased by 48.6%, the number of employees has grown by 22.4%, and the unemployment rate has fallen by 2.7 percentage points.

Employment remains highest in the wholesale and retail trade sectors, as well as in education and manufacturing. By contrast, employment is lower in the arts and culture, scientific research, and real estate sectors.

An analysis of online job platforms shows that employers are currently seeking couriers, waiters, accountants, assistants, sales and marketing specialists, and fundraising professionals.

At the same time, job seekers are increasingly drawn to international, foreign, and joint ventures, attracted by both higher salaries and better working environments.

“The labour market has become more coordinated”

Until 2016, Naira Piloyan ran an employment agency that helped many people find jobs and earned a reputation as a reliable partner for local organisations. Over the past decade, however, she says the labour market has changed. Employers now search for candidates through online platforms, using their own social media pages and job websites. As a result, she had to close her agency. She now works as a human resources specialist at a pharmaceutical company.

She says every medium-sized and large company in Armenia now employs HR specialists. They use online platforms and professional networks to find qualified candidates.

“I closely follow developments in the labour market. From my own experience, I can say that local professionals have become much better at presenting themselves during the hiring process. Employers have also become more selective when recruiting staff. The whole process is now far more streamlined and coordinated,” she says.

At the same time, she notes that personal connections and recommendations from friends or acquaintances still influence hiring decisions.

However, serious companies have realised that hiring unqualified staff creates a “time bomb” for their future development.

Instead, they rely on candidates’ experience, references from previous employers and personal interviews.

“Over the past few years, salaries at our company have increased by around 30% on average. Higher levels of professionalism among staff have largely driven that increase. Every employee takes professional development courses or retrains in a new field. As people gain knowledge and experience, they expect higher pay. If they don’t receive the salary they believe they deserve, they start looking for another job. That staff turnover has become a major challenge for large companies,” the HR specialist explains.

She says employers have also started investing more in their employees’ skills. Many companies now pay for foreign language courses, mainly English, as well as training abroad in manufacturing, technology and other fields.

She believes this growing coordination has improved the quality of Armenia’s labour market. When someone from another company applies for a job with her employer, she can now openly discuss the candidate’s abilities and professional qualities with HR managers at their previous workplace.

“In the past, asking someone for an opinion about a job applicant felt awkward. Now I simply send an email and receive a reply within a few days. The only real difficulty today is finding highly specialised professionals and technical staff. Problems usually arise when we urgently need to hire someone like a driver, security guard or cleaner. Candidates for these jobs tend to be very conservative. For example, if they need to stay just 10 minutes beyond the end of their shift, they often show little flexibility. Some may even leave work during the day without informing anyone.”

According to her, wages for these positions have risen by a larger percentage than salaries for many higher-skilled professions, including finance specialists and translators.

Working conditions are more attractive at foreign companies

Ilona Khachatryan is a logistics specialist. She now works for an American company and earns four times more than she did two years ago in the same role at a local firm. But salary is only part of the reason she left. She says unhealthy relations with management at her former company also played a major role. More broadly, she is critical of hiring practices and personnel management at many local organisations.

“At the company where I worked, it was extremely difficult to receive the bonuses that management itself had promised. To avoid paying them, they would even falsify hourly timesheets.

I applied for jobs at other local companies as well. I attended interviews and then waited for months without hearing back. Even if they decide not to hire you, shouldn’t they at least tell you? After all, you invest your time and effort preparing for those interviews. Foreign companies treat candidates much more fairly. They make transparent hiring decisions. If they decide not to hire someone, they explain in detail why they cannot move forward with the candidate.”

Ilona says her current employer hired her after the first interview. The company immediately explained the salary, holiday entitlement, employment rights and job responsibilities.

“Hearing the words ‘thank you for your work’ genuinely motivates me. It gives me energy and makes me work with greater enthusiasm and commitment. And when your employer also recognises your achievements, you realise just how undervalued professionals are in the local labour market.”

Analysis of labour market trends in Armenia

World.title: Azerbaijan changes status of internally displaced people: What do new rules provide?
World.content:
The status of internally displaced persons in Azerbaijan

On 23 July, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev signed into law amendments to the Law on the Status of Refugees and Internally Displaced Persons and the Law on the Social Protection of Internally Displaced Persons and Persons Equated with Them.

The amendments to the Housing Code provide for the creation of a Permanent Resettlement Fund in the territories liberated from occupation. Housing from the fund will be used to resettle internally displaced persons (IDPs) to the reclaimed territories and will later be transferred to them as private property.

The legislation also clarifies the grounds on which a person may lose IDP status. This applies to those who refuse housing offered by the state, as well as to those who are provided with alternative housing that meets the officially established housing standard for the relevant region instead of accommodation in their previous place of residence. At the same time, social protection measures will remain in place for three years after a person loses or voluntarily relinquishes their IDP status.

The changes are intended to strengthen the legal framework for the Great Return programme. In practice, however, they could significantly affect the lives of hundreds of thousands of people who have spent decades building their lives in Baku and other parts of Azerbaijan.

The purpose of the law and the benefits linked to IDP status

Under the previous legislation, internally displaced person (IDP) status entitled holders to a range of social benefits, including a monthly allowance of 60 manats (about $35) for each family member, state-funded tuition at fee-paying departments of public universities, and exemptions from certain government fees and utility payments.

For people forced to flee their homes in the early 1990s and who had spent decades living in dormitories, temporary housing units or other makeshift accommodation, these benefits represented a basic form of social support. The status also carried legal significance, as it formally recognised that they had been displaced against their will.

Under the new rules, the state is deemed to have fulfilled its obligations once it offers an internally displaced person permanent housing. If the person accepts the apartment, ownership is transferred to them, but they simultaneously lose their IDP status. Those who refuse the offer also lose their status and may forfeit the temporary accommodation provided to them in Baku or another city.

During a three-year transition period, only social support measures, including financial assistance and education benefits, will remain in place. The legal status itself, along with the other rights and guarantees associated with it, will cease to apply.

Freedom of choice and the problem of “any available housing”

The law refers to “alternative housing that complies with the standards established for the region of residence”. In practice, this means that internally displaced people are not necessarily offered housing in their native village or on their ancestral land.

For example, a person who owned several hectares of farmland before being displaced may now be offered a house in a newly built settlement with a plot of only 100–200 square metres. Ownership of their original land is not restored, as the state provides housing only. As a result, the concept of “returning home” is significantly narrowed.

According to dozens of families whose accounts have been shared on social media and in public appeals, many of the homes offered to them suffer from poor construction. They report leaking roofs during rainfall, flooded yards, and repeated disruptions to gas, water and electricity supplies. In some cases, applicants say they have been told verbally: “You’ve been given a house — be grateful, or you’ll lose that too.”

Similar complaints have also been submitted through official grievance mechanisms, although the issue has yet to generate wider public debate.

Life in Baku after three decades of integration

A large proportion of Azerbaijan’s internally displaced people have spent more than 30 years living in Baku and other major economic centres. Over that time, they have found employment, received an education, gained access to healthcare and established stable social networks. After losing their homes in the early 1990s, they were provided with temporary accommodation by the state, including places in dormitories, unfinished buildings and container settlements, as well as apartments in purpose-built residential complexes.

Under the new rules, however, this housing may be reclaimed once a person loses IDP status. As a result, many people face a difficult choice: accept an apartment in Karabakh and leave behind the life they have built in Baku, or lose both their IDP status and the accommodation provided to them by the state.

International human rights standards, including the UN Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement, require that return be voluntary, safe and carried out in dignity. These principles are based on freedom of choice, the provision of adequate housing and, wherever possible, the restoration of rights to former property. Under Azerbaijan’s new legislation, however, the state is considered to have fulfilled its obligations once it offers housing, while refusing that offer results in the loss of IDP status. This weakens the principle that return should be voluntary.

Official position and expert assessments

Pro-government media outlets, including Milli.az, Report.az and APA, have presented the amendments in a positive light, using phrases such as “restoring property rights”, “sustainable social support” and “providing a legal framework for the Great Return programme”.

MP Vugar Bayramov has also argued that the three-year transition period demonstrates the state’s continued commitment to social support. Official statements emphasise that the new housing is transferred into private ownership rather than provided on a rental basis, which the authorities say will encourage people to settle permanently in the region.

At the same time, independent observers and some human rights advocates argue that the changes restrict freedom of choice, fail to fully restore land rights and raise other concerns. They also point to the contrast between the urban lifestyles that many IDPs have built over the past three decades and the newly established rural settlements, as well as the risks of unemployment and inadequate infrastructure.

The status of internally displaced persons in Azerbaijan

World.title: EU’s 21st sanctions package targets Kulevi oil terminal and cryptocurrency platforms in Georgia
World.content:
Georgia in the EU’s 21st sanctions package

The European Union’s 21st package of sanctions against Russia includes an oil refinery in the Georgian town of Kulevi and several cryptocurrency platforms.

The sanctions against the Kulevi refinery, which processes and sells Russian oil, include a six-month grace period. The ban on transactions will take effect after six months unless the refinery changes its business practices.

The Kulevi refinery had previously been considered for inclusion in the EU’s 20th package of sanctions against Russia, but was ultimately removed from the sanctions list.

At the time, the EU said that “the Georgian authorities and the port operator had made positive commitments.” This was stated in a letter from the EU’s Special Envoy, David O’Sullivan, to Georgian Foreign Minister Maka Botchorishvili.

What does the new sanctions package include?

The EU’s 21st package of sanctions against Russia, which is expected to take effect shortly, was formally approved by the permanent representatives of the EU member states on 23 July 2026.

The sanctions are expected to enter into force on 23 July following approval by EU leaders and their publication in the Official Journal of the European Union.

The measures target sectors of the Russian economy that generate significant revenue for Moscow’s war in Ukraine, including energy, financial services and the cryptocurrency sector.

The package also imposes sanctions on more than 50 companies and organisations involved in supplying military goods and weapons to Russia.

It includes the EU’s largest-ever round of individual sanctions, targeting a total of 218 entities — 48 individuals and 170 legal entities.

It is one of the most significant expansions of the EU’s sanctions regime in the past four years.

Sanctions against the Kulevi refinery

“The package introduces the possibility of banning transactions with oil refineries listed in Russia and third countries that process Russian crude oil and petroleum products. Under these measures, the EU is imposing a ban on transactions with the Georgian oil refinery in Kulevi, which processes and trades Russian oil. The ban will take effect in six months,” the EU said in a statement.

According to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, citing a source familiar with the matter, the introduction of a six-month deadline is unprecedented in EU sanctions policy.

The same source said the decision reflected Tbilisi’s willingness to meet the EU’s requirements, which became apparent during discussions over sanctions related to the port.

This means that if the Kulevi refinery continues processing Russian oil over the next six months, it will become subject to EU sanctions. The refinery’s owner, Black Sea Petroleum, announced on 1 July 2026 that it would begin full-scale processing of non-Russian crude from August or September.

According to Georgia’s National Statistics Office, domestic exports rose sharply in January 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, driven largely by exports of petroleum products.

Petroleum and petroleum products ranked as Georgia’s second-largest export category in January 2026, with exports worth $58.7 million, accounting for 12.2% of the country’s total exports.

Cryptocurrency platforms added to the sanctions list

The EU has imposed transaction bans on 14 cryptocurrency platforms based in Georgia, Panama, the United Arab Emirates, Kyrgyzstan, Belarus and the Marshall Islands.

For the first time, the EU has introduced a mechanism allowing it to impose a complete ban on transactions between EU companies and cryptocurrency platforms that help Russia circumvent sanctions.

The measure also applies to crypto service providers operating in third countries if they facilitate activities that serve Russian interests.

What does the inclusion of Georgian companies in the sanctions package mean for Georgia?

The inclusion of the Kulevi refinery in the EU’s 21st sanctions package has already sparked debate in Georgia.

“The EU’s 21st sanctions package is a national disgrace: Georgian assets are being used as cannon fodder for Russia’s war machine. By allowing the Kremlin to circumvent sanctions, those in power are betraying our sovereignty. Georgia’s place is in Europe — we will never become a loophole for Russian aggression,” Georgia’s fifth president, Salome Zourabichvili, wrote on X.

Analyst Lela Djedjelava said sanctions against such an important economic asset would have an impact on the Georgian economy.

“The consequences will become increasingly visible over time. The reality is that the Kulevi refinery is probably not the only facility that could be exposed for cooperating with Russia. If other businesses in Georgia are also hit by sanctions, it will naturally have a very negative impact on the country.”

Gedevan Popkhadze, one of the leaders of the opposition Coalition for Change, said the EU sanctions against the Kulevi refinery were the result of the Georgian government’s inaction.

“If you are not helping Ukraine, why are you helping Russia? If you do not want war, why are you acting in favour of one of the parties to the conflict? We must clearly understand that these sanctions are not a message to the Kulevi refinery itself — they are a message to Georgia’s de facto government. It should realise that claiming to be neutral is hypocrisy.”

Georgia in the EU’s 21st sanctions package

World.title: Opinion: ‘There is no longer peace in Georgia’
World.content:
Opinion on the latest events in Georgia

Professor at Ilia State University and literary critic Zaal Andronikashvili comments on the events that unfolded in Georgia on 22 July 2026, including the arrest of a journalist, a shooting in central Tbilisi, and an attack on an opposition stand-up comedian.

He writes that there is no longer peace in Georgia and blames Bidzina Ivanishvili and his Georgian Dream party.

Journalist Vakho Sanaia was sentenced to 14 days of administrative detention over satirical social media posts about members of the Georgian Dream party. A shooting took place in central Tbilisi on 22 July, leaving four people injured, including two minors. One of the minors later died in hospital. Comedian Onise Okriashvili, a critic of the government, was brutally beaten at his home. Before the attack, he had been the target of a disinformation campaign on pro-government television channels.

Zaal Andronikashvili: “It is important to find the right name for what is happening in Georgia. The situation is new, and historical parallels apply only in part.

Since at least 2019, during the ‘Gavrilov Night’ protests, Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party have done everything possible to prevent a peaceful transfer of power. Some scholars describe this as a ‘coup from above’.”

This “coup from above” is not peaceful.

Anyone who believes that Georgia is at peace today is deeply mistaken. Beyond dragging Georgia into a geopolitical confrontation on Russia’s side — at an enormous cost to the country — Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party are waging an asymmetric, hybrid civil war against the overwhelming majority of the Georgian population.

Part of this hybrid civil war consists of unlawful restrictive legislation enforced only against certain groups of citizens and against civil society as a whole.

There is also financial repression aimed at depriving opponents of the regime of their livelihoods, as well as the deliberate destruction of education and culture. Alongside this come aggression, hopelessness, and an absence of love and empathy elevated to the level of state policy.

There is micro-level violence — encouraging crime and fostering a culture of impunity that ultimately erodes trust in the law, the justice system, and the very idea of justice. There is macro-level violence carried out by the police and special forces, along with many other elements.

“I repeat: this is not peace.

It is a hybrid civil war waged by a regime that controls the police, the legislature and the country’s financial resources against the majority of Georgia’s population, especially its most active citizens. Its goal is to suppress, subjugate and ultimately enslave them.

The other side has nothing but the truth and peaceful resistance. But the truth is a powerful, almost invincible weapon — and it can never truly be defeated.

Despite this asymmetric civil war, whose domestic objective is to cement the regime permanently in power and make the current government irreplaceable, while its foreign policy goal is to sever Georgia once and for all from the European values-based community and turn it into a banana republic under a quasi-colonial regime, Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party have failed to win this unequal conflict.

Peaceful resistance is alive. The people have not been broken. They have not been intimidated.

Those who support the regime today, or choose silent complicity, should look at Russia.

People there also believed that if they kept quiet and buried their heads in a bowl of caviar, none of it would affect them. Other people’s children would die, someone else would go to prison, someone else’s life would be ruined. Perhaps someone would stop greeting them, but they could live with that.

In reality, supporting injustice always comes at a price. Injustice and lawlessness may begin by targeting only selected groups, but they very quickly spread to everyone.

By supporting injustice, you create an environment in which that injustice will inevitably reach you in one form or another.

But people are willing to ignore it until it affects them personally. There is a powerful metaphor in the Gospel of Matthew (26:52): ‘All who draw the sword will die by the sword.’ This is not really about the sword itself, but more broadly about the laws of social reality and their universal nature.

There is no peace in Georgia. Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party are responsible for that.”

Opinion on the latest events in Georgia

World.title: Russia’s state Duma passes law targeting citizens abroad, restricting property rights and passport renewals
World.content:
Russia Passes Law Targeting Citizens Who Left the Country

Russian Embassy in Lisbon, Portugal. Photo: Antonio Pedro Santos / EPA

On July 22, Russia’s State Duma approved, in its second and third readings, a bill introducing what it calls “temporary restrictive measures.” The legislation targets people living outside Russia who are deemed to be evading criminal or administrative penalties.

The restrictions will apply to anyone convicted under any article of Russia’s Criminal Code. They will also affect people facing a range of administrative charges — many of them based on provisions that Russian authorities have increasingly used to prosecute political opponents and dissenters.

The law will take effect once it is officially published.

This article is based on reporting by Novaya Gazeta Europe.

What restrictions would the law introduce?

Authorities would be able to impose the following measures on people entered into the special registry:

freeze bank accounts and other assets;

block access to banking apps and online accounts;

redirect a person’s income into a special ruble-denominated account;

prohibit the sale of real estate and vehicles;

block the registration of property and automobiles;

suspend licenses, permits and accreditations;

bar individuals from registering as sole proprietors or self-employed workers;

restrict driving privileges;

deny access to government and consular services;

prohibit notarial services and transactions carried out through a power of attorney.

Before the vote, State Duma Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin said that Russians living abroad should be thinking about how to appear before a court.

“We are talking about people who are harming our country — extremists, traitors to our homeland. People who have spent years trying to do everything possible to destroy our state,” Volodin said.

How the registry will work

The government will create a state registry of people who are outside Russia and deemed to be evading criminal or administrative penalties. The registry will be maintained by the Justice Ministry, which already administers the country’s lists of “foreign agents” and “extremists.”

Information will be supplied to the Justice Ministry by the Interior Ministry, the Federal Security Service (FSB), the Prosecutor General’s Office, the Federal Bailiff Service and other government agencies.

To be entered into the registry, a person must meet three criteria:

have a criminal conviction or administrative penalty that has entered into legal force;

be officially deemed to be “evading” enforcement of that sentence or penalty;

be outside Russia.

The law, however, does not specify how authorities will determine whether someone is “evading” enforcement.

An interagency commission will be established to coordinate information sharing between the Justice Ministry and law enforcement bodies. It will also decide whether to impose the restrictions.

Lawyer Yevgeny Smirnov said he expects the registry to expand regularly, much like Russia’s list of “foreign agents.”

“I believe the mechanism will closely resemble the weekly expansion of the ‘foreign agents’ register. It will become a show of intimidation through the constant addition of new names,” he told Novaya Gazeta Europe.

Who could be affected?

Formally, the law applies to anyone outside Russia who has been convicted of a crime or an administrative offense and is deemed to be evading enforcement of the resulting sentence or penalty. The specific article under which a person was convicted does not matter.

In practice, however, those most at risk are people prosecuted for political reasons. According to lawyer Yevgeny Smirnov, this primarily includes journalists, politicians, human rights defenders and civic activists.

The law also applies to people facing administrative charges under six specific provisions:

failure to comply with Russia’s “foreign agents” law;

violations of regulations governing the activities of a “foreign agent”;

calls to violate Russia’s territorial integrity;

“discrediting” the Russian Armed Forces;

calls for sanctions against Russia;

participation in the activities of an “undesirable organization.”

Lawyer Anastasia Burakova said the legislation is primarily intended to intimidate Russians living abroad. Since the state cannot physically detain them, she argued, it is instead restricting their civil and property rights.

In her view, the authorities also aim to silence opponents of the war and spread fear among Russians who have left the country.

What happens to a person’s money and property?

The law allows authorities to freeze a person’s funds and other assets. Formally, this does not amount to confiscation, since ownership does not transfer to the state. In practice, however, it would make it much more difficult for people to manage or dispose of their property.

All payments, including pensions, would be redirected to a special ruble-denominated account. The rules governing access to and use of those funds will be determined later by the Central Bank of Russia. Court costs and other financial penalties could also be deducted directly from the same account.

People included in the registry would be barred from selling real estate or vehicles. They would also be unable to register ownership of newly acquired property or register a vehicle.

In addition, banks would block their access to mobile banking apps and online accounts, making routine bank transfers impossible. Banks would also be allowed to deny them loans and other forms of credit.

Lawyer Valeria Vetoshkina described the measures as a tool of financial pressure.

“It creates a paradoxical situation. A person is deprived of access to the very financial tools needed to fulfill the obligations that led to their inclusion in the registry,” she said.

Restrictions on business and employment

People included in the registry would be barred from registering as sole proprietors or self-employed workers.

If their profession requires a license, authorities would refuse to issue a new one. Existing licenses could also be suspended until the individual is removed from the registry.

The government would also be able to suspend permits and accreditations that have already been granted.

Driver’s licenses would not be revoked outright. However, the right to drive would be suspended until the person is removed from the registry.

Ban on powers of attorney and access to government services

People included in the registry would no longer be able to use an enhanced qualified electronic signature. Existing certificates could be revoked, and new ones would not be issued.

They would also lose access to Russia’s Gosuslugi online government services portal, making it impossible to submit applications, process official documents, or access federal and regional public services online.

Before carrying out any notarial act, Russian notaries would be required to check the registry. If a person’s name appears on the list, the notary would be obligated to refuse service.

The law would also prohibit anyone from carrying out transactions on behalf of a listed individual under a power of attorney. In practice, this would deprive Russians living abroad of one of the main ways to manage their property and handle legal matters in Russia remotely.

Which consular services would be denied?

One of the law’s most significant restrictions concerns Russian consulates abroad. People included in the registry would lose access to nearly all consular services.

They would no longer be able to:

obtain a new international passport;

notarize a power of attorney;

certify copies of documents or authenticate signatures;

obtain notarized consent required for legal transactions;

register a marriage or a legal name change through a consulate;

receive consular assistance if detained abroad;

rely on Russia for emergency consular assistance while overseas.

Lawyer Valeria Vetoshkina said the most consequential provisions are the ban on representation through a power of attorney and the restrictions on consular services. Those are the mechanisms that allow Russians living abroad to handle most legal matters remotely.

At present, even people held administratively liable can still obtain a new international passport through a Russian consulate. Those charged with or convicted of criminal offenses also retain access to some consular services.

Once the law takes effect, however, obtaining official documents without returning to Russia will become significantly more difficult.

Lawyer Yevgeny Smirnov described the initiative as a form of de facto deprivation of citizenship.

“Citizenship technically remains, but a person is no longer able to exercise the rights that come with being a citizen,” he said.

Lawyer Anastasia Burakova agreed with that assessment. In her view, the law would leave affected individuals in a situation approaching statelessness, as the Russian state would effectively cease providing them with documentation and legal assistance.

What is the “humanitarian allowance”?

The law provides for what it calls a humanitarian allowance. The payment may be granted if a person included in the registry has close relatives who are financially dependent on them.

Eligible relatives include parents, a spouse, or children who have no independent source of income. The allowance would be paid monthly using the person’s own frozen funds.

The decision to grant the payment would be made by the interagency commission, while the amount would be set by the Russian government in coordination with the Central Bank.

When would the restrictions take effect?

The restrictions would come into force the day after a person’s name is added to the registry.

In theory, a person could be removed from the registry in several circumstances:

if a court overturns or revises the underlying decision;

if the person begins serving their sentence or complies with the penalty;

if the person returns to Russia;

if the person dies.

If the Justice Ministry fails to remove someone from the registry without justification, that person may file a request for review. The ministry must issue a decision within 20 working days, and its refusal can be challenged in court.

In practice, however, not all penalties can be served remotely. For example, a prison sentence cannot be served from abroad. As a result, anyone convicted and sentenced to imprisonment would have no realistic way to be removed from the registry without returning to Russia.

Administrative penalties present a different paradox. A person on the registry would face restrictions on banking services while also being barred from appointing a representative under a power of attorney. It therefore remains unclear how they would be able to pay an administrative fine and secure their removal from the registry.

What do lawyers recommend for those at risk?

The law will take effect once it is officially published. Lawyers advise people who could potentially be affected to resolve key property and documentation issues before it comes into force.

In particular, they recommend:

settling matters related to real estate and vehicles in Russia in advance;

obtaining notarized copies of Russian documents;

securing apostilles for school certificates, university diplomas, and civil status documents;

renewing international passports while they can still obtain long-validity documents;

withdrawing funds from Russian bank accounts and deposits;

obtaining apostilled certificates confirming the absence of a criminal record and their driving history.

Once a person is added to the registry, many of these steps would no longer be possible.

exchange

World.title: Will Hobart ever see snow as it did 40 years ago?
World.content:
July 25, 1986, was a day Hobartians awoke to find, quite literally, that their streets had turned into a winter-sports wonderland overnight.

Bernadette recalls being drawn to her window because of the "silence".

"Because I'm used to the hum of the traffic, and it was so silent," she told 936 ABC Hobart this week.

"I went and looked out the window, and while I was standing there, a guy went down past my house on skis," she said.

About 8 centimetres of snow settled on Hobart rooftops in July 1986. (ABC News)

"Hey, somebody's just skied down the Southern Outlet!" she yelled to her family.

" And one of my kids goes: 'Mum, don't you think it's a bit early to be drinking in the morning?' "

Many of those who made it to work got creative in doing so. (ABC News)

The 1986 event was the heaviest snowfall in Hobart in 65 years, with 8 centimetres blanketing the city, only 4cm off the city's biggest snowfall on record.

There was talk of then-premier Robin Gray eating his words, after he brushed off criticisms of being a dictator by saying if he was, "there'd be snow on the steps of Hobart's post office".

Most shopkeepers decided that staying shut was the logical move. (ABC News)

But residents also remember the ensuing mayhem, with only 20 per cent of employees showing up to work.

On the Midland Highway, which connects the north to the south of the state, 29 semi-trailers jack-knifed as drivers attempted their normal commutes.

"It was hopeless trying to work because everyone was either not there or taking advantage of it. You couldn't get anything done," Mike told 936 ABC Hobart.

Malcolm, who was employed at the zinc works at the time, said the company, "to their great credit, paid everybody for the full day if they got there by lunchtime".

Loading...

Emergency services vehicles struggled in the conditions which they were not equipped to handle.

"It was very difficult for emergency services because most of the police cars were two-wheel drive, so they were actually putting out calls to borrow four-wheel drives from car outlets that sold them," Ian, then a park ranger, said.

Loading

One father said he won't live down the fact he tried to send his kids off to school, while other parents presumed school was cancelled.

Rod told local radio he made his kids trek to school that day despite the freezing cold. (ABC News)

"The children, well they're adults now, do not let me forget that I made them go to school, and they were the only ones at the school, and the poor little fellas had to walk home again," Rod said.

Hobart resident Grant said his sister rarely had birthday parties throughout the 70s.

Some residents lamented the less frequent low-level snowfall in Tasmania in recent years. (ABC News)

"My sister's birthday is in August, and we used to get snowed in virtually every year. And I remember she couldn't have a birthday party for three, four years in a row because we were snowed in," Grant said.

"But nothing happens like that anymore, and it's quite sad really, because the weather's certainly changing," he said.

On an August day in 2015, snow did fall to sea level in some parts of southern Tasmania.

That day, then-17-year-old Tabbi Fasnacht and her father Pat crossed snow instead of sand for their morning surf at Clifton Beach.

Tabbi Fasnacht and her father Pat surfed by a snow-covered beach on Hobart's eastern shore in 2015. (Supplied: Pat Fasnacht‎)

According to the Bureau of Meteorology, extreme low-level snow events are becoming less and less likely.

The view from Lewisham of a snow-covered Clifton Beach and surrounds in 2015. (Supplied: Christine Gaby)

So far, the winter of 2026 has made the top five warmest June-July periods on record, the BOM said.

"There is a long-term trend for a decrease in the number of 'low snow' events in Tasmania," it said in a statement.

A snow-capped Kunanyi/Mt Wellington seen from Bellerive, on Hobart's eastern shore, in August 2021. (Supplied: Nathalia Secco)

" There is very high confidence that as warming progresses, there will be very substantial decreases in snowfall, increase in melt and thus reduced snow cover. "

The BOM said while snow is not completely off the radar, the air is just too dry lately, with rainfall being about 20 per cent below average across Tasmania.

"In more recent years, there have been many events where snow to 300 metres has been possible, but more often than not, there is little moisture in the atmosphere at the same time.

"Moisture coincident with the cold air is required to have snow instead of just a cold day," the BOM said.

So for now, those days where Tasmanians wake up to a mountain top iced like a Boston bun, that might be as close as low-level city dwellers get to snow.

World.title: Langbroek under pressure over appointments to Qld Cultural Centre boards
World.content:
Queensland's arts minister is facing questions about a series of political appointments to the state's Cultural Centre boards, including former senators, veteran LNP politicians and advisers, in the latest chapter of the government's "jobs-for-mates" row.

John-Paul Langbroek's board appointments include Brisbane retiree Martine Whitton, who last worked as a part-time administration officer in the suburban office of a Liberal councillor.

Ms Whitton concluded her working life in December 2021, as a part-time ward officer, in the suburban office of Liberal Brisbane City Councillor Fiona Cunningham.

Martine Whitton, who retired in 2021, has been appointed to the Queensland Cultural Centre board. (LinkedIn)

In June, Ms Whitton took up a three-year appointment to the board of the Queensland Museum, one of the state's leading scientific and cultural institutions.

She is the daughter of the late Queensland Liberal senator Warwick Parer, a one-time Queensland Liberal Party president.

Ms Whitton, who describes herself on LinkedIn as a "retired political staffer" with a Bachelor of Arts in Art History, worked for many years as an executive assistant to both former Queensland Liberal senator George Brandis and then Queensland LNP leader Deb Frecklington.

"To be promoted from electorate office administrative duties to the board of a major statutory authority would surely invite closer scrutiny," said political commentator and Griffith University associate professor Paul Williams.

A Queensland Museum spokesperson said Ms Whitton brought extensive experience in public service, stakeholder engagement and community leadership, with a strong focus on philanthropy, partnerships and volunteer service.

"She has served in governance and leadership roles across community organisations and is an active volunteer in Queensland's arts sector," the spokesperson said.

A spokesperson for Mr Langbroek said: "These changes provide a balance of fresh ideas and experience, which is important to deliver the fresh start that Queenslanders voted for."

Board changes

The Crisafulli government is coming under increased pressure over "jobs-for-mates" appointments.

At budget estimates this week, Deputy Opposition Leader Cameron Dick questioned the appointment of former LNP minister Andrew Cripps to a newly created $300,000 taxpayer-funded role as special commissioner for rural and regional Queensland.

In April, former federal opposition leader Peter Dutton was appointed to the board of the Queensland Investment Corporation by the Crisafulli government.

FPeter Dutton now sits on the Queensland Investment Corporation board. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Also appointed to the Queensland Museum board is retired veteran LNP MP Mark Robinson, who was the long-time member for Oodgeroo.

Former Queensland Liberal senator Brett Mason is the new Queensland Museum chair.

Outside its governance role, the museum board oversees that organisation's major program of scientific research. It is also the lead agency for the repatriation of ancestral remains, sacred objects and burial goods from overseas and interstate museums to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities in Queensland.

Mr Langbroek has also overhauled the board of the State Library.

The overhaul of the State Library board came after fraught relations with the minister. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

Only one State Library board member remains from 2025, a year in which the ABC understands the minister clashed repeatedly with the former board over lucrative literary prizes and grants, awarded by the library.

Former Liberal senator and arts minister George Brandis was installed as the new chair in March for a three-year term.

Martine Whitton spent years as an executive assistant to former Liberal senator George Brandis. (Four Corners)

Ms Whitton's husband, mining executive Leigh Whitton, was also appointed to the library board in March, serving alongside his wife's former boss.

Mr Langbroek has also appointed two of his former ministerial staff members to the library board.

Former ABC journalist Fiona Crawford was Mr Langbroek's chief of staff from 2012 until 2015, during the Newman government. She was also an LNP senate candidate in 2016, and last year worked for the Queensland Tourism Minister Andrew Powell as his senior media adviser.

Gold Coast PR consultant Danyelle Britz worked alongside Ms Crawford as Mr Langbroek's senior media adviser between 2012 and 2014.

Both were appointed to the library board in March for a three-year term.

The State Library's biography for Ms Britz notes "she has produced lifestyle and sports television programs". Her LinkedIn profile reveals she has worked on The Boss is Coming to Dinner, Big Brother, I'm a Celebrity, Get Me Out of Here, and Dancing with the Stars.

"How these appointments are received depends on the political climate of the day," Mr Williams said.

"Because voters are overwhelmed with the very material concerns of the cost of living, these sorts of lower-level appointments will probably pass through with little notice or condemnation.

"The one element of these appointments that could stick in the public's craw, however, is that some appointees appear little qualified for their roles," he said.

Strained relations

The almost total overhaul of the board was achieved by declining to renew the terms of some existing members and sacking others.

Mr Langbroek removed three State Library board members from their positions, including two First Nations directors, part of a broader purge of experienced Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders from Cultural Centre boards.

The overhaul of the board came in the wake of fraught relations between the minister and the board in 2025.

Not only did the minister issue a formal direction to the board under the Libraries Act, ordering that the intended recipient of a $15,000 Indigenous fellowship to Martu writer K.A. Ren Wyld not be given the award, but sources say there was also tension over the Queensland Literary Awards.

The ABC understands the minister made a request to change the final list of award winners after taking issue with three particular authors.

In a high-stakes stand-off with the government, the board sought independent legal advice about the matter to establish whether complying with such a request would constitute a breach of the Queensland Human Rights Act.

Under the Libraries Act, if the minister issues a formal direction to the board and it refuses to comply, individual board members would contravene the Libraries Act and be guilty of an offence.

In the end, no such formal direction from the minister was issued.

Asked about the incident, Mr Langbroek confirmed in a written statement: "I gave no direction to change the recipients of the 2025 Queensland Literary Awards" but did not comment whether he made any informal approaches to the board.

The minister has also made prominent political appointments to the leadership of other cultural institutions.

Last October, former Queensland LNP minister for the arts Ian Walker was installed as QPAC's new chair.

He is well regarded in the arts and has served on the board of Queensland's Chamber Orchestra, Camerata, and is chair of Queensland Youth Orchestras.

While appointments to cultural centre boards are prestigious, fees are modest.

In 2024-2025, the annual fee for each member of the State Library board was $4,000 while the chair was paid $12,000.

Last financial year, each museum board member was paid $7,000 while the chair received $20,000.

"Despite the modest remuneration, most voters would question why important jobs are handed out without a transparent selection process, including meeting objective selection criteria," Mr Williams said.

World.title: ICC dismisses prosecutor Karim Khan for serious misconduct
World.content:
The International Criminal Court has voted to remove the global tribunal's chief prosecutor, nearly two years after sexual misconduct allegations against him first emerged.

British barrister Karim Khan was accused of sexual misconduct with a female aide, allegations he has steadfastly denied.

At an emergency session at the United Nations headquarters in New York on Friday, local time, the ICC's 125-member states ousted Mr Khan from his position, the first time a chief prosecutor has ever been removed from office.

ICC prosecutor suspended The International Criminal Court's chief prosecutor, Karim Khan, has been suspended pending a vote by member states on his fate.

The court's oversight body, the Assembly of States Parties, concluded that Mr Khan had committed "serious misconduct and serious breach of duty," Päivi Kaukoranta, the body's president, said.

Mr Khan was temporarily removed from his duties at the ICC in June, pending Friday's vote, after a report by the executive committee of the court's oversight body found he had committed "serious misconduct".

According to documents, Mr Khan engaged in a sexual relationship with the woman and tried to prevent her from pursuing her allegations.

Mr Khan, who had been elected to serve a nine-year term as the court's prosecutor in 2021, disputes those findings.

Challenges for ICC

Early in the session, a motion brought by Sierra Leone that would have made it harder to oust Mr Khan failed and diplomats quickly moved forward to vote on removal, several hours ahead of schedule, according to three diplomats familiar with the proceedings.

The lengthy and complicated process has pitted human rights advocates, staff and member states against one another at a time when the court is already facing daunting challenges, including a campaign by the United States to "dismantle" the ICC, which was established to prosecute people responsible for humanity's worst crimes.

In a statement last week, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US was launching a "sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court to US sovereignty".

Mr Rubio said he will pressure member states to withdraw from the institution, sanction organisations that work with the court and ban staff from travelling to the US.

In blowing up at a world court, Biden adopts a Trump tactic One of America's presidential candidates is notorious for attacking prosecutors and courts, undermining their decisions and disrespecting their independence.

Countries that "enjoy the benefits of the US security umbrella" will be called upon to reject the court's jurisdiction over US citizens.

Hours after the vote, Venezuela announced it would withdraw from the court.

"Venezuela considers that the court's actions reflect a demonstrated geographical bias, which has disproportionately concentrated its work on African and Latin American countries, to the detriment of the global south," Félix Plasencia, the country's Minister for Foreign Affairs, announced in a statement.

Karim Khan's removal from the ICC will have no immediate impact on the arrest warrant for Benjamin Netanyahu. (Reuters: Peter Dejong)

Earlier this year, prosecutors at the court announced they were dropping an investigation into whether US sanctions against Venezuela qualified as crimes against humanity, citing a lack of evidence.

A separate investigation into possible crimes committed by Venezuelan security forces under former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro will continue.

US President Donald Trump's administration has already brought sanctions against Mr Khan and a dozen other ICC staff in retaliation for warrants the court has issued for top Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, over the war in Gaza and investigations into US personnel in Afghanistan.

"Karim Khan believed that by launching a political witch hunt against Israel and issuing a politically motivated arrest warrant against Prime Minister Netanyahu, the world would ignore the grave sexual misconduct allegations against him. "He was wrong," Israel's ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, said in a statement.

The allegations have become entwined with the court's investigation into the war in Gaza, experts said.

"Political considerations have been folded into this, especially as it is the first time a prosecutor has pursued warrants against a Western ally," Iva Vukusic, a researcher at Utrecht University who has been following the process, told AP.

Netanyahu arrest warrant may affect Israel's allies but not change war While the chances of Benjamin Netanyahu travelling and being arrested are very low, an ICC arrest warrant will affect Israel's allies who now must consider whether their support for Israel is more important than their support of international institutions and treaties.

Mr Khan's removal will have no immediate impact on the arrest warrants in 2024 for Mr Netanyahu and former Israeli defence minister Yoav Gallant for crimes against humanity, which can only be withdrawn by ICC judges.

The ICC Assembly of States Parties will elect a new prosecutor shortly.

AP

World.title: Mynas were introduced to control pest insects. Now they are the pest
World.content:
There is one backyard bird nobody wants.

The Indian, or common, myna, Acridotheres tristis, has a dark brown body, black head and distinctive yellow features.

It was introduced to Australia in the 1860s to tackle insect pests. Now it has become the pest.

President of the Canberra Indian Myna Action Group (CIMAG), Bill Hanke, said the myna outcompeted native birds for food and nesting sites, destroying eggs and chicks.

"This is a highly invasive species, very aggressive to native birds," Mr Hanke said.

"It affects both large birds and small birds, particularly hollow nesting birds like crimson rosellas and eastern rosellas, but also the small little birds that people like in their gardens."

The Indian myna has been so successful as a species, breeding at a prolific rate, that it has spread up and down the east coast of Australia.

Tackling the cane toad of the sky

Bill Hanke says the species can be very aggressive to native birds. (ABC News: Dave Sciasci)

CIMAG formed in 2006 to raise awareness of the impact of the birds and offer a free backyard trap loan scheme.

Over the years, they have consulted with government, animal welfare groups and the community to deliver a control program.

They say more than 3,000 households across Canberra, Queanbeyan and Murrumbateman have been involved in trapping efforts, removing more than 80,000 birds.

"When we first started, they were the third most common bird in Canberra, according to the local birdwatcher's weekly surveys. And within a dozen years or so, we had them down to the 24th most common," Mr Hanke said.

But Mr Hanke said that progress has stalled, and the number of Indian mynas has "exploded".

"There's a huge backlog of people wanting traps, and that's an indication that mynas are on the way back," he said.

He said a recent survey placed mynas back at the 10th most common in the region.

Government support has 'waned'

The Indian myna was introduced to Australia in the 1860s to tackle insect pests. (Getty Images: Ronen Goldberg)

When mynas were declared a pest species in 2021, CIMAG hoped it would trigger a coordinated government control effort around public land including schools, hospitals and government-owned buildings.

"When [environment and heritage minister Rebecca Vassarotti] declared mynas as a pest animal in 2021, we thought that that would be the start of a major concerted effort by government to lend their hand to the control of this pest animal," Mr Hanke said.

"But it didn't happen, and it's a bit of a mystery.

" This is the real disappointment, that the ACT government isn't actively doing anything to control mynas. "

A 2023 petition to the ACT government, signed by more than 2,100 Canberrans, "went nowhere", he said.

"We're not getting the support that government should be providing, including controlling on public lands around public buildings, schools, hospitals, airports, stuff like that," Mr Hanke said.

An urban specialist bird

ACT Conservator of Flora and Fauna Bren Burkevics says common mynas are not a priority species to be managed. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

The ACT government does not dispute the myna is a pest, but ACT Conservator of Flora and Fauna Bren Burkevics said the species has adapted well to the urban environment and is not a priority species to manage.

"If there was a definite threat, there might be a need to take action," Mr Burkevics said.

" What we're not seeing is a threat to matters of national significance, our native birds, and particularly those in reserves. "

CIMAG challenge this.

"The environment is more than just a nature reserve," Mr Hanke said.

"The environment is where we live."

The ACT government declared Indian mynas a pest species in 2021, but did not introduce a control program for the species. (Source: Pexels)

CIMAG argue mynas outcompete native hollow-nesting birds, such as crimson and eastern rosellas, and prey on threatened invertebrates including the golden sun moth and the Canberra earless dragon.

"We've just culled some kangaroos to protect the grassland. And they were the animals, these little critters, that the kangaroo cull was to help," Mr Hanke said.

Changed advice on disposal

Part of the complexity hinges on the most humane method of trapping and disposing of the birds.

CIMAG's protocol uses carbon monoxide from a cold petrol engine, a technique Mr Hanke said was identified as the fastest, least stressful option available.

Carbon dioxide is now the preferred method of disposal.

Michelle Robertson says any potential myna population control would need a clear framework to ensure humane disposal. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

RSPCA ACT chief executive Michelle Robertson said the organisation was not opposed to managing myna numbers in principle.

"We're not saying you can't do any of these things," Ms Robertson said.

" We're just saying it needs to occur in a very carefully managed framework by qualified people so that it is humane. "

The ACT government has also taken this approach.

"The government supports the view of the RSPCA, their policy position that encouraging trapping and killing of common mynas should not be encouraged," Mr Burkevics said.

This problem is not unique to Canberra. In an effort to manage the birds, some councils provide disposal service at local depots.

Bill Hanke says CIMAG has encouraged the ACT government to provide a myna disposal service to the community. (ABC News: Dave Sciasci)

"We've suggested that to the government here, but it doesn't happen," Mr Hanke said.

"If they're concerned about the method of disposal, they should be providing a disposal service to the community."

Flying under the radar

Mr Hanke is calling on the government to act as a precautionary measure, saying without a sustained effort to manage the population the myna bird could become a major problem.

"It's a real shame that we've let, and by we, I mean the ACT government and the ACT Environment Directorate, have really let this opportunity that we provided initially with our massive control program, they've let that slip and we've now got mynas right across Canberra in very big numbers," Mr Hanke said.

The Office of the Conservator of Flora and Fauna said their work has not gone unnoticed.

"We absolutely respect their passion, but I think the likelihood of an all-in Canberra effort would be unlikely," Mr Burkevics said.

That leaves Canberra with a pest species everyone agrees is unwelcome, but no-one is sure exactly how to get rid of.

World.title: In a team full of towering trees, Forrester takes her chance to be seen
World.content:
Jenna Forrester wasn't even supposed to be there.

The 23-year-old travelled to Glasgow as a 400m freestyle and individual medley swimmer.

Then, when backstroke queen Kaylee McKeown succumbed to illness on the eve of the Commonwealth Games, selectors decided to throw Forrester in the 200m back too.

Such is the depth in Australian swimming, that's usually a pretty solid tactic to nab a podium double or even the vaunted sweep.

But usually it's not the afterthought climbing the top step.

"I really just went into tonight with a positive attitude," she said.

Swimmers spark medal rush on day one Lani Pallister wins Australia's first gold of these Commonwealth Games in the women's 400m freestyle, with more Aussies scooping up medals in the pool on the first full day of competition.

"I felt like I had nothing to lose and my family would have been really proud of me no matter what the result was. I feel like I really just took that in my stride."

At the trials in June, it was 20-year-old Iona Anderson who announced herself as a potential heir to McKeown's throne when she bettered her qualifying time.

McKeown, in the depths of glandular fever, responded in the final with a dominant victory, besting Anderson by almost four seconds in the final.

Hannah Fredericks was third and Forrester was more than five seconds behind McKeown in fourth.

For much of Saturday morning's final, it appeared something similar would repeat, albeit without the knowledge that everyone is racing for silver behind McKeown.

Fredericks was out fastest, while Forrester sat sixth at the first turn.

In fact, Fredericks led for the first three quarters of the race, before slowing in the last lap with only a 34-second split of the top six.

Meanwhile, Forrester was only getting stronger, saving her second-fastest 50 metres for last as she mowed down her compatriot, Scotland's Katie Shanahan, and Canadian Madison Kryger.

Forrester was a surprise gold medallist on night one. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

A veteran of three world championships, a Commonwealth Games and an Olympics before arriving in Glasgow, this marks her first gold medal at a major meet.

The stamina on display was remarkable for a woman who, only 15 minutes earlier, was standing on the podium celebrating her 400m freestyle bronze alongside champion teammate Lani Pallister.

Exactly how she managed to pull that off remains a mystery even to her.

"I honestly couldn't tell you, I am as shocked as you are," she said.

"I think my training this year has been really consistent and I have all of Swimming Australia and my coaches to thank for that.

"Honestly, I couldn't have done it without the help of a lot of others."

And on a night when 15 of her fellow Dolphins also won medals, there's plenty of help around.

World.title: Factory-built homes could help Australia reindustrialise, report says
World.content:
Australia could build more homes, in a radically faster way, to solve its housing crisis, a new report argues.

Putting the ambitious national strategy into action would also help Australia to rebuild its industrial base in a once-in-a-generation opportunity to reverse decades of deindustrialisation, it says.

The John Curtin Research Centre (JCRC), a Labor-aligned think tank, has released a new report, Manufacturing Homes: A National Strategy for Solving Australia's Housing Crisis.

Modular homes help housing crisis The modular home model would involve sections of rooms being constructed off-site in a dedicated facility before being transported to new developments across NSW.

Federal Housing Minister Clare O'Neil has launched the report at Labor's National Conference in Adelaide today.

The report warns that Australia has become the least manufacturing self-sufficient country in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), which has left critical sectors of the economy, including housing, exposed to supply chain shocks and cost volatility.

But it says if policymakers made Australian manufactured housing (AMH) a central pillar of Australia's housing system, it would offer Australia a pathway to re-industrialise while solving its housing crisis at the same time.

It says Australia's housing crisis is a consequence of how slowly and inefficiently we build houses, and the system needs overhauling.

"Australia's housing crisis is not only a shortage of dwellings. It is a crisis in how Australia builds," the report argues.

"While right-populists blame immigrants for the current housing shortage, the fact is Australia saw far higher immigration and population growth in the 1950s and 1960s — during which housing was cheap and abundant.

"One of the reasons Australia was able to deliver abundant and affordable housing throughout the biggest population boom in our history was because we used prefab housing and had a high-productivity housing sector.

"The current housing shortage is fundamentally a productivity problem," it says.

A new industrial strategy and a solution to the housing crisis

The 84-page report was written by the JCRC's chief economist, Lachlan Kerwood-McCall, and executive director, Nick Dyrenfurth.

It says manufactured housing, delivered with Modern Methods of Construction (MMC) and industrialised building systems, would provide an Australian-made, productivity-driven pathway out of our housing crisis.

Labor conference to debate gas and gambling The fiery debates of years gone by may not be as public as they once were, but Labor's conference still gives rank-and-file ALP members a say.

At the moment, only around 5 to 8 per cent of total construction activity in Australia incorporates modular or manufactured methods, compared with vastly higher adoption rates in countries like Sweden, Germany, Japan and Singapore.

And to help Australia's MMC sector transition from early-stage adoption to a scaling phase, it will require collaboration between government, industry, and finance, the report says.

It says the Australian government should set a 10-year target of lifting the Australian manufactured housing (AMH) industry's share of total new housing construction to 35 per cent by 2036-37, with a longer-term target of 50 per cent.

"Achieving such a share would position AMH as a mainstream delivery model across multiple housing typologies and procurement streams," it says.

See the graph below from the report.

It also argues that by making manufactured housing a central pillar of Australia's housing system, it could be used as an industrial strategy to rebuild Australia's manufacturing industry after decades of deindustrialisation.

"The closure of Australia's automotive industry and the decline of complex manufacturing removed the very industrial ecosystems, precision engineering, systems integration, advanced materials, that typically underpin modern manufactured housing sectors," it says.

"[But] the pandemic, geopolitical tensions, and supply chain disruptions have exposed the risks of over-reliance on offshore production.

"Reindustrialisation is ultimately a choice about the kind of country Australia wants to be," it says.

Clare O'Neil launched the John Curtin Research Centre's manufactured housing report at Labor's National Conference on Saturday. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Recommendations to achieve a home building revolution

The report makes 12 recommendations, structured around five key pillars.

A National Strategy for Solving Australia's Housing Crisis, by Lachlan Kerwood-McCall and Nick Dyrenfurth (July 2026)

First, it says governments should help the MMC and AMH sector create economies of scale.

"Unlike traditional on-site methods of construction, where higher output involves higher costs and requires higher prices, manufactured housing becomes cheaper the more we build," it says.

"Public sector demand does not push up prices and crowd out private sector demand; it pushes down prices and crowds in private sector demand.

"Aligning government procurement and social housing policies to the MMC industry lowers costs and prices for private sector buyers, as well as getting Housing Accord and Housing Australia Future Fund (HAFF) home-building targets back on track thanks to higher productivity."

It says policy levers could include procurement, HAFF reform, and reforms to Defence Housing Australia.

Second, it says an Australian manufactured housing industry should not be overly dependent on imports.

Rather, it says, it could be underpinned by Australia's substantial timber plantations, wood processing and emerging engineered wood product manufacturing sectors.

Are 'flatpack' homes Australia's future? From early colonial settlers to the post-war construction boom, prefabricated and modular housing has a long history in Australia. Can factory-built homes fix our housing woes and help the climate?

"Reforms must ensure that the domestic industry can rapidly scale up to meet substantially higher demand long-term without supply-side bottlenecks and cost pressures emerging," it says.

"Policy levers include local content requirements and reforms to the National Reconstruction Fund."

Third, it says Australia's entire housing system has been designed and built around the assumption that houses are built on-site, but that is extremely costly and inefficient.

It says a change of national building culture will require system-wide change using policy levers like planning, certification, and finance.

Fourth, it says an AMH industry would need an abundant supply of young workers to prevent skills and labour shortages.

"Policy levers include expanding and building on trade and apprentice pathways and aligning the TAFE, VET and broader training system and the Australian government’s Key Apprenticeships Program (particularly the Housing Construction Apprenticeship stream) with MMC industry requirements," it says.

Fifth, it says demo projects and regional manufacturing hubs would be essential to prove the model at scale, build public confidence, and anchor industrial capability in the regions that stand to benefit most.

World.title: Pogačar claims stunning victory in stage 19 of the Tour de France
World.content:
Tadej Pogačar launched a stunning solo attack from the foot of the iconic Alpe d'Huez to win the 19th stage of the Tour de France and extend his overall lead overnight.

Even by the four-time Tour champion's lofty standards, it was up there with his best wins as he was more than 3 minutes behind with 12km remaining.

Riding without a teammate for the last section, he caught Ecuadorian rider Richard Carapaz and Frenchman Lenny Martinez with 1.5km left and then surged ahead for his fifth stage win of this year's race and 26th overall.

"It's very cool to win up here," Pogačar said. "I'm super happy to take the win."

Martinez finished six seconds behind and Carapaz — who won the 18th stage with a brilliant breakaway win of his own — nine seconds back. American Sepp Kuss, who faded in the closing stages, was 1 minute, 14 seconds adrift.

With a lead of 7 minutes, 11 seconds over Remco Evenepoel in the overall standings, and two stages remaining, Pogačar is on the brink of joining Eddy Merckx, Miguel Indurain, Jacques Anquetil and Bernard Hinault as the only men to win five Tours.

Barring mishap or accident, the Slovenian star will be crowned when the race ends on Sunday on the Champs-Élysées in Paris.

Rated as an HC mountain pass, the hardest category in the race, Alpe d'Huez is arguably the most famed climb in cycling and has near-mythical status on the Tour. Swarms of fans, many camping overnight and carrying flags of several nations, screamed encouragement on each of the 21 hairpins.

"It was a crazy atmosphere on the whole climb," Pogačar said.

He kept his focus as the public got perilously close to his face and, at one stage, he had limited visibility due to smoke from flares being lit by spectators.

But as impressive as Pogačar's win was, it also came about because Carapaz, Kuss and Martinez did not work together properly to distance Pogačar when he was lower down.

"I had to fight against super good riders," Pogačar said. "But they were playing against each other a bit so it helped me to catch up."

Perhaps thinking he could benefit from others fading and get the stage win, Martinez kept sitting on Carapaz's wheel, which was very much to Carapaz's annoyance and meant the veteran had too much work to do alone.

He kept trying to accelerate while Martinez — 10 years his junior — did less work and a tired-looking Kuss generally sat back too much before drifting away.

With 900m left, Carapaz was showing phenomenal stamina to stay with Pogačar, but he was finally undone by a brutal acceleration and could not follow as the yellow jersey rolled past him.

Saturday's mammoth 171m Alpine stage could be epic.

It features three HC climbs — Col de la Croix de Fer, Col du Galibier and Col de Sarenne — and one Category 1 climb up Col du Télégraphe before a hilly finish to Alpe d'Huez.

Pogačar does not need to go for victory and can safely hang back and protect his lead.

But will he?

There are 66m of pure climbing, and that may be too much for him to resist.

"Tomorrow is the Queen stage of the Tour," Pogačar said. "[It] is the hardest day of the Tour. We'll follow our own plan, our own rhythm. We don't care about anything else."
