World.title: Beefed-up brekkie rolls to golden boreks: Sydney’s best cafes with exceptional food
World.content:
Eating outEssential cafes and bakeries Beefed-up brekkie rolls to golden boreks: Sydney’s best cafes with exceptional food The commitment to detail and sheer deliciousness of every dish make these cafes really stand out. All hail the very best cafe food of 2026. Good Food Guide reviewers July 25, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cafe food has long been associated with simplicity and speed. Granola with a scoop of Greek yoghurt, fried eggs, a chicken sandwich to-go. If you didn’t know any better, you might think it’s the same deal at cafes like Serva in Seaforth, Ellenin Alexandria or Angus in Marrickville. What’s the big deal about a cheese toastie, after all? Well, maybe you haven’t tried Serva’s: filled with maple-glazed mushrooms, house made mushroom XO sauce, kombu butter and three types of cheese, with a side of syrupy thick blueberry chutney (also made in-house). It’s delicious, textural and entirely singular in Sydney. This list is part of the 100 Essential Sydney Cafes and Bakeries of 2026, a celebration of the cafes with that kind of exceptional attention to detail, from a fish sandwich at Angus that takes three days to make, to a slice of sourdough toast with snapper pate and pickled fennel at Sway in Manly (everything made from scratch). Angus’ brekkie roll with corned beef, cheddar and house relish is also worth a look. Dion Georgopoulos Angus



Angus is the sleeper hit of Marrickville cafes. It launched quietly as Agnes in 2023, then gradually changed its name, ownership and opening hours. The menu kept improving, strengthened by ties to cult-favourite Kirrawee bakery Thoroughbread and a commitment to deceptively labour-intense dishes. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Did you know that making their bestselling crumbed fish sandwich requires three days of steaming fish, creating stock, making sauce and baking bread? That they cure the salmon to make gravlax for their Scandi-style brekkie plate? Or that they poach the rhubarb for each rhubarb matcha matte? No wonder it’s getting tough to score a table. 69 Meeks Road, Marrickville, angusmarrickville.com.au Co-owner Jovan Radevski stocks the cabinet at Burek Brothers. Sitthixay Ditthavong Burek Brothers



It’s one of the most underrated snacks in Sydney: a single, handheld slice of filo pastry pie filled with fresh ricotta and feta cheese, or maybe a lightly spiced mixture of minced beef and caramelised onion, and then baked until golden. Some call it borek, but brothers Nikola and Jovan Radevski use its Balkan name, burek, and each morning they draw upon their Macedonian great-grandfather’s 100-year-old recipe to make seven savoury and sweet varieties from scratch, using dairy from Vannella, and meat from Lebanese butcher The Butcher Boys in Rockdale. 162 Bay Street, Rockdale, burekbrothers.com.au Dogs and humans enjoying the Cafe Cressida courtyard. Jennifer Soo Cafe Cressida



Chef Phil Wood and Lis Davies are the couple behind Cressida, which is named after their daughter and is fundamentally a nice place to drink coffee and read the paper. Cushioned seats are upholstered in marigold stripes, water is poured in Maison Balzac glasses and illustrations of a prancing burger decorate the exterior walls. The real-life cheeseburger is a fun time too, featuring a beefy medium-rare patty on a squishy potato bun. Fresh produce is a cut-above across the board and the kitchen will send out a terrific version of eggs any way you like them with Iggy’s sourdough. Later, enjoy that same crusty sourdough with Charentes-Poitou butter, oysters and champagne in the courtyard, which is what life is all about at the end of the day. Must order: The Sicilian-style orange cake made famous by Margie Agostini when she ran her own cafe at the site in the 90s. 118 Queen Street, Woollahra, cafecressida.com.au Cafe Lewi



It took three years for fine-dining chefs John and Leva Laureti to transform a suburban corner store into the elegant cafe of their dreams. People wander in from the street, lured by a counter display of desserts – none so beautiful as the miniature marjolaine, frosted with the flourish of a vintage wedding cake. The brunch menu convinces them to stay, making the tough call between salmon confit on a crunchy potato base with whipped avo, or the abundantly yolky, teriyaki breakfast bun. This one was worth the wait. Good to know: Dinner service has started on Wednesday and Friday nights, the former dedicated to steak frites. 8A Victoria Street, Lewisham, cafelewi.com.au Cafe Monaka



Look around at the tables at Cafe Monaka and you’ll notice everyone has ordered the same thing: a plump pink cutlet of shio-koji marinated salmon, rolled tamagoyaki egg omelette, soy-simmered green beans and a bowl of miso soup. It’s the asagohan, a well-portioned Japanese breakfast plate built on the ichiju-sansai principle of “one soup, three dishes”. Green tea is the traditional accompaniment, and Cafe Monaka imports its sencha, matcha and hojicha straight from Japan. 2/24 Waratah Street, Mona Vale, cafemonaka.com.au Cafe Baby Finger Two blocks from Parramatta Road, the mood is serene at Baby Finger, with simple decor and a cooling through-breeze. Owner-chef John Jeong welcomes every customer with a lilting “Helloo” and a menu that – from glazed French toast ladled with plump strawberry coulis, citrus mascarpone and macerated balsamic berries to fried eggplant and charred bush tomato curry topped with a poached egg – is not usual cafe fare.



Jeong also bakes his own focaccia, sourdough and brioche, and is the kind of accommodating guy who will still make scrambled eggs if you ask for it. Good to know: Cafe Baby Finger (named after Jeong’s habit of taking photos accidentally featuring his little finger) is also a top destination for anyone with a pram. Unit 27/12 Layton Street, Camperdown The pork banh mi at Ca Phe Mai Parker Blain Ca Phe Mai



From banh mi filled with bacon and soft steamed egg, to brekkie muffins served with lemongrass pork sausage patties, Ca Phe Mai combines Vietnamese flavours with Australian cafe favourites to create a menu unlike anywhere else in Sydney. The ca phe muoi (Single O espresso sweetened with condensed milk and thick, salted coconut cream) is dangerously good with a thick slice of toasted banana bread, spread with Vietnamese coffee butter, but chicken broth dishes like pho ga and laksa are the real must-tries, made with a 40-year-old secret family recipe. Good to know: This is a day-to-night venue, transforming into a wine bar after dark. 377 New South Head Road (enter via Kiaora Lane), Double Bay, caphemai.com.au Yu Ozone and her husband Masa at Comeco. Edwina Pickles



Comeco Foods This organic Japanese cafe will change how you think about gluten-free and plant-based food. Stop by for a matcha latte sweetened with house made strawberry puree, or one of those revelatory “sourdoughnuts”, filled and fried to order. Nourishment is the express goal here, and it’s done with deceptive deliciousness – who would have known the katsu curry roux is made with 11 vegetables if it weren’t on the menu? Try a bite of (almost) everything with the tempura and onigiri plate, then return at dinnertime for the colourful sushi platter that might include grilled capsicum nigiri and aburi eggplant rolls. Good to know: The new dinner service features specialty Japanese alcohol like yuzushu, available by the glass. 524A King Street, Newtown, comecofoods.com.au



The famous fish burger at Ellen. Ellen It’s difficult to make muesli exciting, but at Ellen it’s a textural delight of puffed rice, yoghurt and crunch, served with pistachio cream and fresh strawberries. It’s that kind of commitment to the small things which makes this place special. It recently became the go-to for fish burgers in Sydney – they’re generously portioned, carefully wrapped and full of acidity and heat from pickles and seeded mustard. But that’s only the start – the kitchen goes beyond typical cafe fare with specials like poached Queensland grouper, served with fish bone broth, chives and a paper-thin slice of pancetta. Good to know: About half of the seating is outside (and dog-friendly) – lovely on a sunny day, less so when it rains.



Unit 153/18 Huntley Street, Alexandria Haven, Rosebery. Haven Specialty Coffee Whichever of Haven’s five locations you visit, expect Scandi-minamilist lines and a menu that squeezes hits into every square inch. Owners Kit Tran and Herman Chiu roast coffee beans in house, and all the staples are present and correct, but next-wave drinkers can expect the lychee coconut water under cold matcha foam or cold brew topped with peach-infused cream to hit the spot. Food? Pandan-coconut French toast and Mont Blanc cake are standouts on an inventive Asian-inspired brunch menu.



Must order: Chilli scramble with roasted peanuts. 7 Crewe Place, Rosebery, havencoffee.com.au The new kaisendon filled with fresh quality seafood at Kurumac. Kurumac Owners Eugene Leung and Dika Brianata’s Marrickville cafe Kurumac set a new standard for Japanese cafe fare in 2019, but the menu revamp in July took it to another level of authenticity and innovation.



In the morning, go for a soft egg sando with curry mayo on fluffy shokupan bread from nearby Azuki bakery. For a lunch that’s substantial, yet balanced, try the teishoku set, featuring a soft omelette spiked with salty mentaiko (pollock roe), grilled salmon, slices of poached chicken, clam miso soup, pickled daikon, sauteed spinach and rice. House special drinks include the hoji-sso, where an iced hojicha latte is combined with black sugar and topped with espresso cream. 107 Addison Road, Marrickville, kurumac.com Pina Don’t be deterred by the ever-present queues crowding the laneway – Pina is worth the wait. Service remains friendly under pressure, moving efficiently through the cafe’s blushed industrial interiors to deliver a vast menu of classic brunch fare, made better.



Sourdough pancakes become supersized, with sweet or savoury toppings to choose from; a massive, crisp potato rosti is piled with chunks of cucumber and herb-flecked creme fraiche. And it’s all adaptable, with more than 15 sides, spanning haloumi to kimchi. Good to know: Pina is licensed, with a short selection of Australian wines. All of the condiments are made in house at Serva. Dylan Coker Serva Serva, a bright orange cafe in the Northern Beaches, is where owner-chef Miles Ackermans shows off his vast range of pickles and preserves – sold retail, or served in sandwiches, toasties, muffins and salads.



Join his growing group of customers-turned-mates, and start swooning over umami-rich mushroom toasties, laced with kombu butter and served with zucchini pickle; and marvelling at the meaty, crunchy, melty Reuben with apple and celery kraut. A Freshwater location has been announced to open sometime in winter 2026, too. Good to know: Need a last-minute birthday gift? Pick up a pickle jar and locally crafted ceramics here. Suite 1/538 Sydney Road, Seaforth, servasyd.com.au SIT in Marrickville. Dion Georgopoulos SIT



First, there was Baba’s Place: a hatted Marrickville restaurant where Eastern Europe meets Western Sydney. Now, from the same team, there is SIT: a cafe with intentional eclecticism and Mediterranean-ish food, like Baba’s well-travelled grandchild with a penchant for freddo espressos. There are two absolute must-tries: the pot-set yoghurt with honey and walnuts, and the pancakes. The former is a textural joy so delicious you’ll question everything you knew about yoghurt; the latter, a perfectly cooked vehicle for maple syrup and a paper-thin sheet of butter that slowly, theatrically, melts in. 387 Illawarra Road, Marrickville, comesit.com.au Even the sourdough bread is made from scratch at Sway. Dion Georgopoulos Sway Manly



Sway has a warmth that extends from the sunlit footpath to the service. Look beyond the car park views to a menu that evokes the spirit of Manly: a bright take on Aussie brunch, lush with salads and hearty with house-made sourdough, each dish deeply considered. Take the honey-roasted pear and seed porridge, painted with blueberry and orange blossom compote, or the light pâté made of local snapper, creme fraiche and dill, slathered thickly on toast with lemony fennel salad. The specialty coffee is notably good, but the peach and Earl Grey iced tea can’t be beaten. Shop C, 1/13 The Corso, Manly Taguan Cafe Taguan promises a “home away from home” for the Filipino diaspora, but everyone’s welcome. In November, the cafe moved into a two-storey terrace with a cheerfully lived-in feel – mementos on the walls, golden pothos trailing the ceiling, trays of warm pandesal rolls lining the counter.



Brunch here blends tradition, innovation and fun: toasties pull apart in streaks of purple ube halaya and molten cheese; queso fundido, warm in the iron skillet, leans into richness with crumbled longganisa sausage; and pork adobo, from a family recipe, is the comforting signature dish, tart and tender, on a bed of garlic rice. Good to know: The ube matcha might be the most expensive drink, but it’s worth every dollar. 274 Abercrombie Street, Darlington Tento specialises in ramen and ochazuke. TenTo



The courtyard restaurant-cafe is hemmed in by concrete and humming with morning energy, steam rolling off hand-built clay bowls of rich tonkotsu ramen and salmon ochazuke dressed in a delicate blend of green tea and dashi. This is TenTo’s high-impact take on Japanese brunch fare, informed by its mastery of soup stocks, specialty coffee and hand-whisked matcha. Try the snack menu with crisp katsu eggplant and house made miso cheese; opt for the minimalist Mont Blanc, finished with clouds of Hokkaido-style vanilla cream; and return for dinner (with sake) when you invariably want more. Good to know: Co-owner Ryota Kumasaka makes those gorgeous rough-hewn ceramics, and you can purchase them to take home. 3/8 Hill St, Surry Hills , tento.com.au Yum Yum Bakery



It’s not often a cafe can celebrate its 35th birthday, but family owned Yum Yum Bakery is one of the exceptional few. The milestone prompted big moves – a second location in Concord, a new contemporary look in Guildford – and though there’s more seating than ever, they’re all taken come lunchtime. It could be its food, a joyous expression of wood-fired Lebanese brunch fare. It could be its evolution, embracing modernity while maintaining tradition. But more than anything, it’s the warmth of its people – no matter who you are, you are welcome. Good to know: The hospitality is as outstanding as the food at this 2026 Good Food Guide cafe of the year winner. 273 Guildford Road, Guildford, yumyumbakery.com.au Related Collection Explore Good Food’s Essential Sydney Cafes and Bakeries 2026



Good Food reviews are visited anonymously and paid independently. A restaurant can’t pay for a review or inclusion in the 100 Essential Cafes and Bakeries guide. Can’t see your favourite cafe? Chances are it’s in another category. Explore the full list of the 100 Essential Cafes and Bakeries of 2026 in the Good Food app.

World.title: 'Severe' magnitude 5.9 quake hits North Island
World.content:
A strong earthquake jolted the central North Island early on Saturday.

GeoNet said the 'severe' magnitude 5.9 quake happened around five kilometres southwest of Taumarunui at 4.51am.

The earthquake was nine kilometres deep and the intensity was severe.

The quake was reportedly felt across much of the North Island, including Auckland, and as far as the top of the South.

By 6am, nearly 23,000 'felt reports' had been filed to GeoNet. At least 11 aftershocks, ranging between magnitudes 2.2 and 3.7, followed.

Fire and Emergency (FENZ) said there were no quake-related callouts at all.

Aftershocks could go on for a week or longer - seismologist

A seismologist told RNZ the earthquake was the first ever recorded in that spot.

While Earth Sciences New Zealand duty seismologist Sam Taylor-Offord said it was a normal faulting earthquake, so not unexpected, and could have occurred on one of the few mapped faults in the area. It was the first to strike since records began in the early 1800s.

Taylor-Offord said larger earthquakes were not common in the wider area.

"The nearest earthquake in the country was in 1946, south of Te Kūiti, magnitude 5.4.

"But I would remind people who might have felt them, there was an earthquake in 2023 in Te Aroha, magnitude 5.1, which is very similar to this, smaller. There was also a deep earthquake in the region in October 2018, which was a 6.2, and that was felt down to Otago.

"So they do happen in the region. They're just much less frequent than other parts of the country."

Taylor-Offord said there had been more than 50 aftershocks, up to 3.7 in magnitude, within three hours.

"It could go on for a week, more or less, regularly... and then we expect things would taper off. But we could still be seeing earthquakes here in years to come that are associated with this one, just much, much smaller."

While nearly 23,000 'felt reports' had been filed to GeoNet, Taylor-Offord said it only recorded the first five minutes.

"So that 23,000 is the people that woke up and reported it, and I could not tell you how many more have been reporting it in the hours since, so it could be in the high tens of thousands."

Minor damage in Taumarunui

The mayor of the Ruapehu District confirmed there had been some minor damage in Taumarunui.

Weston Kirton told Saturday Morning one or two commercial buildings had been affected, "glass broken and the like".

There had also been minor slips on the roading network, including one blockage where someone could not get out.

Quake Update - Weston Kirton Saturday Morning Download MP3 4m

Kirton, who lived just three kilometres south of the epicentre, described the earthquake as traumatic.

"My bedroom has got lights that were shaking, and I thought things were going to start falling over. We did have photos, and what have you, fall over, but it was one of those moments where you don't know whether it's going to get worse, but as it turned out, it was five or 10 seconds of, just, trauma, and then of course it quietened down.

"It certainly was traumatic. I've lived here all my life and it certainly was the largest I've experienced in my lifetime."

Minor slips reported

Manawatū-Whanganui Emergency Management Group urged motorists to take care while driving after minor slips were reported in the area.

"Emergency services and roading crews are assessing the situation, but a fuller view of any impacts is unlikely to be available until daylight," it said.

No injuries or other damage had been reported.

The Emergency Management Group expected aftershocks to continue throughout the morning.

"If people feel them, they should drop, cover, and hold. If you are in bed, the best thing to do is to stay there and cover your head and neck with a pillow."

'Strong and long' in the lower North Island

The earthquake felt like it would not end in Whanganui, according to a resident in the suburb of Springvale.

Cushela Robson described the tremor as a very strong, prolonged rolling motion.

"I thought, should I get out of bed? And if I did, could I stand? So I thought, no, probably, because I grew up in Wellington, I thought, no, I think it's probably better to stay in bed."

World.title: Wellington under severe thunderstorm warning
World.content:
Wellington city and airport are under a severe thunderstorm warning, with torrential rain also expected.

MetService issued the warning at 9.20am Saturday, valid until just before 11am.

It said its weather radar had detected severe thunderstorms moving east-northeast.

It expected the thunderstorms to be accompanied by torrential rain.

The MetService warned that such rain could cause surface and/or flash flooding about streams, gullies and urban areas, and make driving conditions extremely hazardous.

The National Emergency Management Agency advises that as storms approach you should:

Take shelter, preferably indoors away from windows

Avoid sheltering under trees, if outside

Get back to land, if outdoors on the water

Move cars under cover or away from trees

Secure any loose objects around your property

Check that drains and gutters are clear

Be ready to slow down or stop, if driving

During and after the storm, you should also:

World.title: Lewis  Clareburt celebrates in and out of Commonwealth Games pool
World.content:
Fresh off winning a Commonwealth Games silver medal, Lewis Clareburt says meeting his baby nephew for the first time made the moment even sweeter.

Clareburt, alongside Erika Fairweather, claimed the country's first podium finishes with a pair of silver medals on the opening night of finals in Glasgow.

Delivering one of the races of the night, Clareburt stormed home in a thrilling men's 200m individual medley to claim silver in 1m 56.77s, half a second behind crowd favourite Scotland's Duncan Scott.

"To be able to do a personal best on this stage is such a good feeling. I've been on the 1.57 mark for eight years, so to dip under that today and to get a silver on top is a cool feeling," Clareburt told reporters following the race.

The 27-year-old was the fourth fastest qualifier during the earlier heats.

Clutching his silver medal after the medal ceremony, Clareburt was asked whether a silver medal or a personal best was more important to him.

Lewis Clareburt (L) celebrates with winner Duncan Scott (SCO) after claiming silver in the men's 200m Individual Medley Swimming at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games. Photosport

It turns out another special moment meant most.

"A PB (personal best), actually meeting my nephew for the first time, not going to lie, that was better than all of that. That was pretty cool," he said.

"My sister has had a child since the last time I saw her, seven weeks old and got to see the little man for the first time. I think he was asleep.

"It was a pretty special feeling. I'm pretty proud of my sister."

Although a first meeting was accompanied by a Commonwealth Games medal, the new uncle chuckled that his nephew probably would not remember the occasion.

The silver was Clareburt's fifth Commonwealth Games medal, adding to the two gold medals and bronze he won in Birmingham in 2022, as well as bronze on the Gold Coast in 2018.

Clareburt also claimed bragging rights over his training partner Australian William Petrick who touched fourth, 1.1 seconds behind the Kiwi.

The pair train together at the Nunawading Swimming Club in Melbourne.

"One-nil so far. We're versing each other once more so hopefully I can double that."

World.title: Country Life: "Why not llamas?"
World.content:
Already addicted to llamas' yarn, Janette Buckingham thought she'd give farming the animals a spin.

That was over 30 years ago and in that time her herd of camelids has grown to include a few ovine cousins - Gotland sheep - also raised for their fibre which she spins and sells from her home studio in Southland's Waikawa Valley.

"For me, I like just being able to turn fibres over to people who will use them, and certainly the money's good too," she told Country Life.

It was a high school friend who first got her wheels spinning - literally.

Addicted to yarn: Llama herd follows love of fibre Country Life Download MP3 13m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

Buckingham has been spinning since 1973 when she was first introduced to the craft.

"I was terribly uncoordinated, but I just stuck with it," she said.

"Nobody showed me what to do. I just felt my way sitting up 'til God knows what time at night, trying too hard, but eventually ... I got the hang of it and could even spin a lumpy yarn. Anyone will tell you that's the breakthrough."

Since then she's taught a few people to spin herself. The trick is in knowing how to coordinate one's hands and feet.

Janette Buckingham at her home in the Waikawa Valley. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

It was a high school friend that got her interested in spinning in the 1970s. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

She looked quite at ease, tucked up by the fire on a squally afternoon, working away on her electric spinning wheel - a massive timesaver which helps when she's trying to rapidly replenish her stock of yarns.

Her love of spinning is what got her started on the llama farming. She'd bought a packet of caramel-coloured alpaca fibre in the 1980s which she "fell in love with".

"It was absolutely beautiful, like nothing I'd ever spun before, just sort of buttery smooth. I became addicted to it."

It was a time when many farmers were looking to diversify their farming operations, and the llama's cousin, the alpaca, was starting to become more well-known.

A love of fibres saw a Southland woman build her own herd of llama, Guanaco and Gotland sheep. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

However, it was a herd off llamas near Canterbury that caught her eye.

"We managed to get three, and one was a guanaco male. The fine-fibred guanaco is also a cousin to the llama.

"They weren't as popular then because people just wanted alpacas or llamas. The guanaco was something else again."

The Gotland sheep came later, a breed popular for their dark and grey-toned wool. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Crossed with a llama, she said they can produce "very fine fibre".

"They're a bit more of a challenge to handle, but they're something that perhaps make my business a little bit different from a lot of other people's."

Today she has about 40 llama and guanaco which she runs alongside the Gotland sheep on her 25-acres in the Catlins.

The Gotland sheep came later, a breed popular for their dark and grey-toned wool and originally from the Gotland Islands off the coast of Sweden.

"There seemed to be a lot of interest in the Gotland wool because of its lustre, its colour, not much crimp in it, but it's just got certain characteristics that appeal to people."

The studio is stocked with a range of finished products. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

She sells the skeins from her home studio. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

World.title: Country Life: Celery, butterflies and Travis the goat
World.content:
Please publish to Country page and Country Life page (CLI) by ****** Saturday 8AM *********

"Six days a week, rain or shine, hail, sideways, wind, lightning ... put a raincoat on and carry on."

That's Luke Franklin, standing in a field of celery on a grey winter's day, describing the almost daily harvest which has been going on in the Franklin family for 120 years.

The present owner of Franklin Farm is the fifth generation in the business and the third at this 28-hectare site near Waimauku, north-east of Auckland.

It was 1906 when Sid Roskill first planted celery in Mount Roskill. Fifty six years later, Luke's grandfather Graham moved the Franklin legacy to Waimauku. He and wife Lucy started off with just 2.4ha before gradually buying up neighbouring farms.

Graham Franklin RNZ/Sally Round

Celery has been harvested by the Franklins for 120 years Supplied

The 85-year-old is still on the tools, driving the forklift and helping around the packing shed.

Big celery bunches are out these days, neatly trimmed and packed stalks are in, Graham told Country Life. And of course there's no horse and cart to take the crop to market.

"Things have changed, but not a hang of a lot. We still cut by hand, we still bring it all up, pack it much the same."

Celery, butterflies and Travis the goat Country Life Download MP3 18m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

Graham's son Alan is standing at one of the benches packing, alongside workers from the Philippines and Tuvalu.

"I think with the amount of hard work that we do and the long hours that we do, it makes it sustainable. I think there's no member of the family that's a shirker," Alan said.

Solokiala Manulele in the packhouse RNZ/Sally Round

The Franklin family have been growing celery for 120 years RNZ/Sally Round

"There's times where there's more competition comes into the market and there's times when you're having weather events or disease events.

"It can wipe out the crop, but you've just got to see past it and just enjoy the job and hopefully your bank account lasts long enough to come out the other side."

Alan's been out in the celery fields since he was a baby, when his mother Lucy would be out helping her husband Graham.

"Oh, my goodness me, you get up and it's freezing cold or it's pouring with rain, you still had to go out there," Lucy said.

Lucy RNZ/Sally Round

"No babysitters in those days. The children come out with you. Yes, one in a pushchair, one in a pram.

"They were raised on slugs and snails," she laughed. "It doesn't really hurt children to be out in the soil."

Peak celery season is October until Christmas and when that winds down, the visitor experience winds up.

Families can visit from Boxing Day during the summer to visit the Franklin's butterfly house and experience the release of thousands of butterflies, wander through sunflower fields and visit a farmyard of small animals.

When she's not in the packing shed, Alan's wife Monique can be found in the paddocks with small goats, a flock of chickens laying different coloured eggs and a "micro miniature" cow called Bubba Gump.

"I find the little children really can connect with them because they're a nice size."

She said many children are surprised to find eggs are laid by chickens and don't just come in cartons at the supermarket.

Travis, an energetic pygmy goat, was one of the stars last summer, "Chewing people's bags, their flowers, he's hopping in kids' prams, chewing ladies' dresses. He was just getting into everything, and everyone just loved it."

Jasmine Franklin with Sarge and Travis RNZ/Sally Round

sign RNZ/Sally Round

Opening Franklin Farm to visitors is a great way to connect farming with the public, Luke's wife Jasmine said.

"People enjoy the raw, honest truth. So sharing crop failures or sharing animals that we can't contain, people love that because it's genuine and real, and they find it quite entertaining, and people like to come along and see, for example, our goat Travis that we struggle to contain.

"In a way, sharing our problems and failures keeps us real and relatable, and people like to come along and check that out as well."

"They're entertained, they're getting lots of exercise, just connecting back to nature and our roots. Yeah, it's like a big YouTube."

World.title: Country Life: What NZ can learn from a US farmer who coped with H5N1
World.content:
Disbelief and a sense of failure swirled through Georgie Cartanza's mind as she found more and more dead birds at her broiler chicken farm on the eastern coast of the United States last year.

In January 2025, the Delmarva Peninsula - where many migratory birds converge - had already had seven cases of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) and her "angst" was building.

"Over the 20 years that I've grown chickens, I'd never observed a dead snow goose on my property, but [...] I found eight dead snow geese in close proximity to the poultry houses," she told Country Life.

What New Zealand can learn from a farmer who lived through H5N1 Country Life Download MP3 11m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

Cartanza is not only an experienced chicken farmer, she also educates poultry farmers on good practice as extension agent for the University of Delaware's Cooperative Extension programme.

She had noticed water and feed levels were a little off in one of her four chicken houses, each housing 37,000 birds.

"My mortality started to pick up, but it wasn't tremendous. It wasn't anything that would have been earth shattering, but I really started feeling uneasy on a Friday evening."

By 2 o'clock on Saturday afternoon HPAI was confirmed.

"I think it's, it's a little bit of disbelief. I think it's a little bit of, 'you know, I've done everything I can. I've done everything I know to do.' It's an overwhelming feeling because it's a sense of failure."

All farms within a three kilometre radius were quarantined.

"You're thinking, 'what did I do wrong? This is impacting me, but it's now impacting my neighbour as well.' It's a pretty traumatic experience to go through and so it's changed me as a human being."

The houses were then "depopulated" - the chickens euthanised in situ via "ventilation shutdown plus heat" overseen by state agricultural authorities and a vet.

"They actually didn't expect me to be present during the process itself, and that's good because you've invested yourself into a flock of chickens and it's hard regardless."

The hardest time for Cartanza was going in the next day to deal with the remaining feed, surrounded by dead chickens.

"It's a really bad feeling to have to do that. I wouldn't wish it on anybody for certain."

Then came the composting process - the bedding, chickens and other material decomposing within the chicken houses for 14 days to contain the virus, subjected to heat with the temperature monitored, deemed virus free after 28 days.

"Then the cleaning process starts - to get the house cleaned up and disinfected."

Changing the way she farms

After the initial shock, Cartanza wanted to figure out where the virus had come in.

"So I kind of put my extension hat on and really started trying to think about that as far as what could I do to help somebody else."

Still poultry farming, she said she has changed a number of things, aside from maintaining a line of separation between clean and dirty.

"Anything outside of where the chickens are is considered dirty. And then once you come into the area where you cross that threshold where the chickens are present, that's now your clean area."

Aside from footbaths, dedicated footwear, hand sanitizer and signs, each chicken house now has its own tool box and other equipment.

"There's no reason you're going to bring something from the outside into this house. It's all about touch points and opportunities where, whether it's your feet, your hands, or an inanimate object, that virus could be carried into your house."

Snow geese Wikimedia Commons, credit: Bruce Hallman, BLM

Cartanza grows organic broilers and said certifiers had allowed them to keep them indoors when they deem the risk is greatest - during peak wild bird migration times.

"What tends to happen is people almost get burned out and they're like, 'well, nothing's happened, you know, it's no big deal', and they let their guard down."

It was an "odds game," she said, and a clearly defined high level biosecurity plan implemented consistently was key to lowering the odds of getting the virus, noting New Zealand's "phenomenal biosecurity system".

"I've been to New Zealand, I went through the airport, I saw what they did to my shoes, but the (wild migratory) birds, they're not going through that.

"So we have to do whatever we can to prevent that from getting into our poultry houses."

World.title: Five London police injured as boat hits bridge
World.content:
Five British police officers were injured after a Metropolitan Police boat struck Westminster Bridge in central London on Friday, the force said.

The vessel, from the Met's Marine Policing Unit, hit the bridge at about 1440 GMT, the police said. It added that a number of officers had entered the water but were rescued, with additional police responding along with other emergency services.

"We understand five officers were injured and are receiving treatment," the police statement said. "We await an update on the extent of their injuries."

It added it did not believe any members of the public were involved or injured and said the circumstances of the incident would be "thoroughly reviewed".

The incident occurred close to the Houses of Parliament with crowds of onlookers watching on from the bridge. The Port of London Authority said it was also supporting the response.

World.title: Commonwealth Games: Erika Fairweather wins NZ's first medal of the 2026 Games, silver in the women's 400m freestyle
World.content:
New Zealand's medal campaign at the 2026 Commonwealth Games is underway after swimmers Erika Fairweather and Lewis Clareburt claimed the country's first podium finishes with a pair of silver medals on the opening night of finals in Glasgow.

Fairweather collected the first medal of the Glasgow Games for New Zealand with silver in the women's 400m freestyle, before Clareburt backed it up minutes later with a thrilling runner-up finish in a gripping final of the men's 200m individual medley.

Australia's Lani Pallister dominated the women's 400m freestyle, pulling away over the closing stages to win in 3m 59.56a. Fairweather finished second in 4m 2.65s, more than three seconds behind, having stayed in touch with the Australian through the opening 300m before fading over the final 100m.

"It was definitely to stay as close to her as possible," Fairweather said of her race plan.

"It wasn't my best performance today, but you can't be mad with the outcome that I got."

Fairweather appeared disappointed with her performance in her favoured event. Michael Steele/Getty Images

Despite appearing frustrated after the race, Fairweather said finally winning a Commonwealth Games medal after missing the podium in Birmingham four years ago was a special moment.

"I was gutted last time when I didn't get one, to know I'm going home with one in my suitcase now is super special."

New Zealand teammates Caitlin Deans and Eve Thomas also featured in the final, finishing sixth and eighth respectively.

Clareburt then produced one of the races of the night, storming home over the freestyle leg to claim silver behind Scotland's Duncan Scott in front of a vocal home crowd.

Scott successfully defended his Commonwealth title in a Games record time of 1m 56.38s, with Clareburt touching second after sitting third at the final turn before producing a blistering finish. England's Tom Dean claimed bronze in 1m 57.22a.

The silver was Clareburt's fifth Commonwealth Games medal, adding to the two gold medals and bronze he won in Birmingham in 2022, as well as bronze on the Gold Coast in 2018.

More importantly for the 26-year-old, the performance delivered a long-awaited personal milestone.

"The medal didn't mean as much to me as the time," Clareburt said.

"To be able to do a personal best on this stage is such a good feeling. I've been on the 1.57 mark for eight years, so to dip under that today and to get a silver on top is a cool feeling."

Clareburt finished second to local favourite Duncan Scott, and England's Tom Dean. Michael Steele/Getty Images

Clareburt admitted he had little idea where he was positioned over the closing stages of the race.

"To be honest I was breathing the wrong way and I couldn't see anyone. I knew that I was probably going to be close and I sort of had a glimpse and at some point I saw the TV, and all I could see was blue, which was what Duncan was wearing, so I knew he was ahead, but I had no idea where I was."

He also had no idea Fairweather had already opened New Zealand's medal tally.

World.title: Quick hits: Aussie's dash to glory, Englishman drops his lollies
World.content:
A broken lane rope holds up the swimming program, an Australian wins gold after a mad dash from the medal podium and an Englishman drops his lollies.

Here are the quick hits from day one of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Broken lane rope

A broken lane rope delayed a heat of the men's 100m breaststroke. (Getty Images: PA Images/Owen Humphreys)

There is a whole host of things you probably do not want to see when you are about to dive into the pool ahead of a major championship.

One of them faced Zac Stubblety-Cook ahead of the 100-metre breaststroke heat, when he saw the lane rope had popped out of its holder.

"I was a bit worried, and nobody noticed. It was in my lane," Stubblety-Cook told the Seven Network.

Stubblety-Cook backed away from his block and alerted the authorities, who initially seemed to make things worse, with part of the rope falling into the pool as an official precariously reached for it pool side.

His attempts were unsuccessful at first, as the swimmers sat back down for what felt like an indeterminable wait (ultimately about 15 minutes).

"I've never had a delay that long," Stubblety-Cook said.

"That's just sport. You have to roll with it."

Easily done, perhaps, for a 27-year-old four-time Olympic medallist and former world champion, but what about if you are 23-years-old and making your major championship debut?

"I think it's expected to expect the unexpected," Bailey Lello said.

Well said young man, and well swam too. He made it to the semifinals alongside Stubblety-Cook and Sam Williamson.

2. All in a day's (or hour's) work

Jenna Forrester shows off her gold medal after winning the women's 200m backstroke final. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

In the space of an hour, Australia's Jenna Forrester mastered multi-tasking.

After finishing third behind fellow Australian Lani Pallister in the women's 400m freestyle final, Forrester took part in the medal ceremony and the photo opportunities that come with that ritual.

She then raced to the call room, needing to back up for the women's 200m backstroke final.

Forrester could be forgiven if she was out of breath but managed to win gold in astonishing fashion.

What made her victory even more remarkable was the fact she initially missed qualifying for the event after placing fourth at last month's selection trials in Sydney.

She only got a berth in the 200m backstroke when Australia's backstroke great Kaylee McKeown withdrew from the Games with glandular fever.

"I don't know what to say and didn't expect it to happen," Forrester told the Seven Network.

"I gave it my all and I'm so proud of myself. I am shocked."

3. Englishman drops his lollies

The pause button was hit on Australia's clash with England in the men's 3x3 wheelchair basketball competition for an unusual reason: one of the England players dropped his lollies.

Play was halted after lollies fell from the pocket of England captain Peter Cusack.

Officials asked staff for some assistance clearing the court surface, but Cusack waved them away.

He politely scooped up the fallen cargo and took them to the side of court before re-joining the game.

4. Sister rivalry either side of Hadrian's wall

Astrid Carroll (left) represents Scotland, while younger sister Ursula Carroll represents England. (Getty Images)

The single heat of the women's 100m S13 freestyle event had something of an unusual quirk in it.

Teenage sisters Ursula and Astrid Carroll were both making their international debuts, but for different countries.

The reason is not quite as spicy as one might hope, even with the countries at stake being Auld Enemies England and Scotland.

Astrid, 17, was born in Edinburgh, so she swims for Scotland, while her 14-year-old sister Ursula was born in Halifax, the people's republic of Yorkshire, so she swims for England.

The pair both live with Stargardt disease, a rare, inherited eye condition that causes progressive, central vision loss, "basically like seeing through a doughnut" Astrid told the BBC.

"It'll be nice walking out and just seeing you," Astrid added in that same interview.

Ursula simply responded the only way she could have, as an Englishwoman: "Scottish, unbelievable."

In the heats, Ursula got the win over her big sister, swimming 1:05.25 to Astrid's 1:05.84.

5. It's all in a name

De Niro Pao (right) took on Pooana Khoahli in the men's 65kg class. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

Did Niue's De Niro Pao chose boxing or did boxing choose De Niro Pao?

If you are wondering where we are going here, let's hear from Pao himself.

"Robert De Niro is my mum's favourite actor, so she named me after him," Pao said.

"That's my grandad's favourite actor too."

Of course, De Niro won an Oscar for his portrayal of boxer Jake LaMotta in the 1980 film Raging Bull.

Given Pao competed in the men's boxing in Glasgow, perhaps he psyched himself up with a viewing of Martin Scorsese's classic?

Perhaps not.

"My grandad always tells me about Raging Bull, but I've never seen it," Pao admits.

For the record, Pao was eliminated via a points decision in the men's 65kg class, going down to Lesotho's Pooana Khoahli.

World.title: How Hani harnessed mum and mana to go 'balls out' for bronze
World.content:
There is a two-minute countdown clock when para powerlifters enter the arena.

In that time they have to settle on the bench, most get their legs strapped down, align their back and shoulders under the bar, get their grip perfect, then lift.

Eventually, the pump-up music fades out when the lifter is finally ready, usually about halfway through the time.

Not Australia's Hani Watson, though.

For the first 30-40 seconds of her time on the bench, Watson, an effusive and effervescent athlete who loves a chat, takes a moment of supreme stillness.

As trusted coach Simon Bergner hurriedly organises straps and chalk with arena staff, he at no point rushes his charge.

As the crowd nervously watches the seconds tick down, Watson sits, eyes closed, breath steady, mind awash with the words of her late mum.

"You got this darlin'."

Hani Watson manages rogue bones and a body on fire When Hani Watson settles under the barbell at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, she will be lifting more than just the plates on the bar.

Watson credits mother Laurita June "Bub" Rayward, who died in 2023, for "creating the strong woman" she has become.

"I believe in having that spirit, that energy, that mana, my culture that's within me, the Australian spirit and just sitting there and calming myself down and listening to that internal voice," she said after winning a second straight women's heavyweight Commonwealth Games bronze medal.

"As kids we don't listen to our parents, but I'm listening to them now. And they told me, 'This is your superpower, this is what you can do, this is what you need to focus on.'"

She was plenty strong enough in 2022 to win bronze with a best lift of 127 kilograms, and shattered that number with a final re-rack of 147kg in Glasgow on Saturday morning AEST.

"I didn't actually think I was going to hit the numbers coach was gonna ask me to hit," she said.

"But I just blocked it out, I didn't wanna know. I just went balls out and just hit it."

A "wild" crowd at Glasgow's Armadillo was enraptured by the ease with which she completed her lifts — although the third took some shifting.

But the loudest moments were reserved for the Nigerians, who collected silver through Rita Ferdinard and gold courtesy of the all-conquering Folashade Oluwafemiayo, who shattered the 86kg+ world record with a final lift of 175kg for a second straight Commonwealth gold.

Folashade Oluwafemiayo (centre) is seemingly untouchable, but Watson is chasing. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot)

Watson is chasing her, and is hoping to have closed the gap by the time the 2028 Los Angeles Paralympics roll around.

"It's nice to have someone to chase and I keep chasing her, I keep looking up to her," she said.

"I think it's important to have mentors in the game. She's been doing it since she was a teenager so she's got a lot of years on me — maybe about 30 years in the game — and I've been doing it for five, so I've got a lot to learn from her."

Oluwafemiayo also broke her own Games record score of 134.8 points despite weighing 15kg less than Watson (Commonwealth Games scores are calculated by comparing body weight to weight on the bar).

Swimmers spark medal rush on day one Lani Pallister wins Australia's first gold of these Commonwealth Games in the women's 400m freestyle, with more Aussies scooping up medals in the pool on the first full day of competition.

Both athletes had added 20kg of apparently pure muscle since Birmingham.

"Every time I see her it's like she's become this big chunky cow that she's eaten or something. It's muscle upon muscle on that woman," Watson said with pure admiration.

"I just watch her in awe. I ask her what's changed, what do you bench, what are you eating, and she tells me everything.

"I need someone to look up to because the sport's always changing, the goalposts are always changing.

"As long as she's there I've gotta keep watching her and she's watching me too. She knows I'm on her tail."

World.title: What it feels like to have your sport dumped from the Comm Games
World.content:
As the Commonwealth Games kicked off on its first full day of competition, plenty more sat at at home, many wishing it could be them.

Organisers in 2026 ditched badminton, hockey, wrestling, road cycling, mountain biking, rhythmic gymnastics, rugby sevens, squash, table tennis, triathlon, beach volleyball, cricket and, the most storied of all, diving.

It has been held at every edition since the first Empire Games in 1930, until this year.

Of the 22 Commonwealth Games diving events, Anabelle Smith went to the past four, including Glasgow 2014.

Twelve years ago she won bronze in the women's synchronised 3m springboard with Maddison Keeney, but not in Glasgow like the rest of her team.

This dive for Smith (left) and Keeney was at Glasgow 2014 in name only. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The Scottish capital did not have a facility to allow for diving, so Smith, Keeney and Co were shipped to Edinburgh, the site of the 1970 and 1986 Games.

"[There was] obvious disappointment from the divers … but also an understanding," Smith told ABC Sport.

"It made sense they weren't just gonna ship the divers up to Edinburgh, disappointing but they'll power on and look ahead now."

The 33-year-old had not been planning to defend her 3m synchro gold medal from Birmingham 2022, but is instead attending her fifth Games as a spectator and part of the Australian team's connection and belonging squad.

How we got to Glasgow 2026 The bumpy road to Glasgow 2026 has produced a Commonwealth Games that will look a little different than the ones that came before.

She's joined by other athletes who have seen their sports axed, including beach volleyballer Chris McHugh and Melissa 'Milly' Tapper.

Her sport of table tennis was also axed after being included in six straight Games from 2002 to 2022.

Tapper, an Olympian and Paralympian, embodies the inclusive and integrated nature of the Games perhaps better than anyone.

She won team bronze at Glasgow 2014 and singles gold on home soil on the Gold Coast in 2018, and is still getting the chance to flash her skills in the team lounge at the decked-out Glasgow Argyle Hotel.

Loading Instagram content

"I've got a little bit of a call-up having the table tennis table in there," she said.

"We've had plenty of athletes and even some staff come through and challenge. Being around athletes everyone's competitive. It's a lot of fun.

"So even though table tennis isn't technically in the Games, it's still a part of the Games."

Table tennis was a "core sport" for the Commonwealth Games and falls into the category of many of the 2026 events, in that it could be held in existing halls.

Melissa Tapper has represented Australia at the Olympics, Paralympics and Commonwealth Games. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

Field hockey, however, requires a bit more space and bespoke facilities. Its history in the Commonwealth Games is not quite as long as diving's, but it had an elevated status as a "core sport".

In 2014, it was held at the Glasgow National Hockey Centre, which remains operational and is located along the River Clyde, within the 13-kilometre corridor of the pared-back 2026 Games.

When cuts were being made for 2026, the International Hockey Federation (FIH) and Commonwealth member nations lobbied for the sport's inclusion, but they missed out as organisers opted largely for indoor sports with athletics the only outdoor event.

Glasgow 2026 events 3x3 basketball/wheelchair basketball

Artistic gymnastics

Athletics

Bowls

Boxing

Judo

Netball

Para powerlifting and weightlifting

Swimming

Track cycling

The Kookaburras have won all seven men's gold medals since 1998, while the Hockeyroos have also never missed the podium, boasting four gold, two silver and a bronze.

Kookaburras captain Eddie Ockenden carried the flag in the Birmingham 2022 opening ceremony, as evidence of the sport's standing in Australia's Commonwealth Games movement, so Hockey Australia was "naturally disappointed" to miss out in 2026.

"Our national teams only play a finite number of international tournaments, making every opportunity to compete in one incredibly valuable," high performance director Bernard Savage said.

"The Commonwealth Games have always been one of those opportunities that our teams have genuinely looked forward to. Beyond the competition itself, the Commonwealth Games provide a unique multi-sport environment that our athletes look forward to and aspire to be a part of.

"The broader interest in the Games has provided an opportunity for our athletes and teams to inspire the next generation of hockey players across Australia and the Commonwealth.

"While this has been disappointing news, our focus remains firmly on our preparation for the 2026 FIH Hockey World Cup."

The World Cup will be played in Belgium and The Netherlands from August 15-30, shortly after the end of the Glasgow Games.

World.title: Cats down Dees, Dockers flex muscle against Eagles in derby
World.content:
Jye Amiss has kicked five goals and Murphy Reid produced a third-quarter clinic as Fremantle continued their western derby dominance with a 70-point win over West Coast at Perth Stadium.

The Dockers led by just eight points at half-time of Friday night's match before kicking 11 goals to one in the second half to race out easy 16.16 (112) to 6.6 (42) winners.

(Getty Images)

Amiss took seven marks inside 50m on the way to 5.1, while last year's Rising Star winner Murphy Reid (26 disposals, one goal) snared the Glendinning-Allan medal as best afield after turning the contest on its head with a mesmerising nine-possession third quarter.

Matthew Johnson (29 disposals, six clearances) and Caleb Serong (26 disposals, seven clearances) also had big games in front of 56,616 fans — a record home crowd for a Fremantle regular-season game.

There was late concern for West Coast mid-season recruit Oliver Francou when his right knee was gashed open after sliding over the studs of Andrew Brayshaw during a tackle.

Eagles players immediately signalled to the bench for help as Francou lay on his back and lifted his leg high in the air to stop blood from gushing out.

Star West Coast midfielder Harley Reid battled hard on the way to 30 disposals, 12 clearances, while Tim Kelly (31 disposals, 603m gained) and defender Marcus Herbert (36 disposals) were prominent.

The Dockers have now won five derbies on the trot — and 10 of the past 11 — to close to within three in the overall head-to-head ledger (33-30).

The result means Fremantle (17-2) will finish the round at least three wins clear on top of the table with just four rounds remaining, putting them in an excellent position to snare just their second minor premiership.

World.title: Have the AFL's rule changes worked? Not exactly
World.content:
There is nothing more constant than change.

People have argued about the future of football for as long as the game has existed.

Every year players, fans and football staffers await the new direction or interpretations handed down from high.

Some changes are winners and stand the test of time — such as the 50 metre arc and the centre square.

Others are destined for the dustbin of history, such as the flick pass and around the ground bounces.

Regardless, change is never far from sporting administrators of different codes and sports. The AFL is not immune from this want to improve the sport.

Rule changes among what's new in the AFL for 2026 The new AFL season is only days away, and there are plenty of new things to get your head around. Get up to speed before Thursday night's opener.

Ahead of the 2026 season seven rule changes and interpretation shifts were heralded as being common sense solutions to perceived long-standing problems surrounding the sport.

Changes to the centre bounce, kick-ins, shrugs, the "stand" rule and last disposal out of bounds were implemented. Some elements of the footy fan base were excited by the changes, others horrified.

"We have consulted clubs and other industry stakeholders over the past six months and taken on board their feedback and ideas, and we believe these changes will make a positive impact on the game," AFL executive general manager Football Performance Greg Swann said before the commencement of the season.

The aims of each change were varied but aligned to increase scoring, reduce game time and improve the look and feel of the game.

So far scoring has increased about 3.5 points per game compared to last year.

Scoreboard operators haven't been this busy since the 2017 season, with early season scoring rates threatening to push the clock back even further.

But that number alone may not tell the whole story.

With the season winding towards finals, research undertaken by the ABC and Andrew Whelan of Wheelo Ratings looks at whether the changes have had their intended impact.

Centring the truth

Rule changes around centre ball-ups have increased the numbers of ruckmen leaping for the ball. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

To the casual fan there were few more iconic parts of the Australian game than the centre bounce. The biggest optical change to the game in 2026 was the removal of the centre bounce and changes to how rucks engaged at the restart.

The bounce had been the start of each game since its formal introduction in 1887.

For many the bounce was integral to the look and feel of the sport — a unique element that set the native code away from the other global codes of football.

AFL rule change injury fears Geelong's Shannon Neale might have escaped a serious injury, but coaches and players are beginning to voice concerns the AFL's rule changes could lead to more rucks getting hurt.

But it had become untenable in the face of umpire injuries and skill barriers, seen to reduce the ranks of vital recruits.

"Currently, umpire pathways are being narrowed by the requirement of the bounce. By removing the skill aspect of bouncing the ball, umpires can focus their energy on adjudicating the game and consistency of decision-making," Swann stated.

At the same time that they removed the bounce, the league also instituted a change to encourage more rucks to leap at centre ball-ups.

According to the AFL, just 21 per cent of centre bounce ruck contests had at least one ruck leaping last year. That's down from about two-thirds just two years prior.

After the preseason Swann was keen to sell the success of both changes.

"The unintended consequences from a good perspective is scores out of the centre bounces have gone up. It's a very small sample size, but the things that we wanted — the game length has gone back, the scoring has gone up, scoring from centre bounces has gone up, so we're hopeful that goes into the season proper as well."

At face value the rule changes — in combination — have delivered in spades. Scoring from centre bounces are at their highest level for at least 20 years.

Digging a little deeper presents more questions as to its impact.

While scoring is up from centre bounces, the major reason why they are up is a little more unconventional.

Instead of fast flowing play from the restart the biggest contributor to the jump are scores from free kicks.

Free kicks at the restart have surged in 2026, perhaps sparked by confusion around the new rules.

More points are being put on the scoreboard from these free kicks than in recent years.

Instead of the dynamic future promised from the new ruck set up, the reality is more of the same buttressed by a surge in indiscretions.

With more centre ball-ups overall, teams are scoring 0.96 points per live ball centre clearance, up just 0.02 points per clearance on last year.

There's also been a subtle tactical evolution as the season has progressed.

As teams have become accustomed to the new rules, scoring from centre bounce has also dropped.

The predictable new ball-up has become easier to defend as winter has gone deeper and teams have become better equipped at limiting damage from the middle.

In the last five weeks teams have averaged just 10.6 points per game from the middle — a big drop on the fast start to the year and the past three full seasons.

While centre bounce scoring is up about 12 per cent on last season, it still only makes up around 14.5 per cent of all scoring. That's only 1 per cent more than the contribution last year.

Teams are better at getting the ball inside 50 from centre bounces this year than years past however, contributing to the territory game so important to many teams.

While rule changes often take a season or two to fully bed down, it appears the early optimism for increased centre restart scoring may be diminishing.

The new centre bounce revolution may be more a minor change in the grand scheme of football things.

Where do I stand?

Far more contentious has been the introduction of the "stand" rule six years ago.

For a sizeable cohort of fans across the league it is the single most hated rule in the AFL rule book.

Some of the rule changes have allowed teams to move the ball easier with limits on defenders' encroachment. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Designed to anchor the mark to a single spot, and prevent the creep of defenders, it aimed to open up aggressive ball use into the middle of the ground.

This year the rule has been slightly tightened to prevent a nearby player retreating "outside 5", instead requiring them to remain in place or to head to the actual spot of the mark or free kick.

Since 2021, many have attributed improved transition success from defence to the new rule. The accepted wisdom is that there has been at least a small improvement in the ability to move the ball due to 'stand'.

This trend has continued through 2026 so far, with a bump in both categories so far. But much like the centre bounce successes, there's more than meets the eye initially.

The increase in transition from defence to attack is largely down to stoppage and kick-in transitions. This matters because these areas are less impacted — or not impacted at all — by the 'stand' rule.

Teams usually escape the contest via broken (not set) play from stoppages.

The 'stand' rule has the biggest impact in set play in the back half of the ground. With the ball already entering in pressurised general play, the 'stand' rule has a far smaller impact on play than in the intercept game — if it has any real impact at all.

The rise in kick-in transition is even more fascinating to consider.

The introduction of a reduced time limit for restarting play has seemingly led teams to becoming more aggressive when bringing the ball back in after a behind.

With teams taking more direct kick-ins, there is more risk of defence's being caught if the ball is turned over. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Matt Roberts)

The average length of kick-ins is about 3 metres longer in 2026 than three years ago. Kick in targets have also gone more central, with about 40 per cent this year heading up the corridor versus about 25 per cent in 2023.

This has led to a rise in full field transition, and an increased risk of the ball going back the other way.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

By contrast, the ability to move the ball after intercepting has actually declined from last year.

Despite a rash of teams focusing on overlap handball, the overall trend has seen a decline in success of this type of movement.

There's also been a slight decline overall in the ability to move the ball from defensive 50 to the front half of the ground.

This is usually seen as the break-even success measure for teams to achieve in transition.

While the changes to 'stand' may look dramatic, the ability for defenders to trail overlap runners has not changed, nor has the ability for sides to zone off defensively up the ground.

Many of the scintillating highlights that are attributed to stand are more down to poor defending than the "intrusive" new rule.

What hasn't changed dramatically is the number of 50m penalties called due to stand infractions, or general unhappiness with the rule from some quarters of football fandom.

For these people, the only solution is complete overhaul.

In the balance the reality probably sits somewhere in the middle — not truly transformative, nor game destroying.

Stopping the stoppages

This season also brings about a radical change to the game's out of bounds laws. Following the lead of the SANFL and AFLW, the league introduced a "last disposal" rule to encourage play through the corridor and away from the boundaries.

The rule provides a free kick to the opposition where a side clearly disposes the ball via kick or handball before it passes over the boundary line — regardless of intent or whether it is on the full.

The impact of this rule change has been clear — but again with an interesting caveat.

Throw-ins are unsurprisingly down, with approximately five fewer boundary umpire overheads per game. Far more surprising is the drop in ball-ups per game.

The number of around the ground ball-ups has fallen by almost the same amount as throw ins.

The effect for both is quite dramatic through the middle of the ground. For the first time since the start of COVID there have been more stoppages in each arc than outside them.

This has led to individual stoppages being more threatening than ever before.

But as a result of the reduced volume, the stoppage game has also contributed less to the overall scoreboard than ever.

The intercept game remains the bedrock of football, despite the focus of media and fans on the dead-ball contest.

This reduction in stoppages has likely had the biggest impact on the reduction of game time.

Around two and a half minutes on average, or about two minutes on median, has been reduced from game lengths in 2026.

While better than nothing, for most fans this difference would barely be noticeable.

Next changes up?

While length of games is the hot topic of conversation, there is still more to do in trying to prevent head knocks and concussions. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Jason McCawley)

Already focus has begun to turn to the next wave of rule changes.

Chief amongst them is the length of the game.

"We've knocked off 3 minutes per game but is it enough? Probably not," Swann told Channel 7 this week.

More radical options have been tabled to further reduce game time. The most radical of these appears to be a reduction in the length of games to 16 or 18 minutes plus time on — similar to the COVID-impacted 2020 season.

This would likely occur when the league expands its home and away schedule to 24 games per team once Tasmania enters the competition in 2028.

Such a change is popular amongst many football people, but is a harder sell to a cynical and change-fatigued public.

"The COVID quarter (length) felt about right. Now maybe (that's) too short — I don't know. But it keeps the game close. You know I think we want close games," GWS coach Adam Kingsley told the ABC earlier this year.

Kingsley is far from alone in this desire, with premiership coaches Chris Fagan and Chris Scott — as well as former AFLPA president Patrick Dangerfield — calling for similar reforms in previous years.

The unspoken part of these continuous sets of rule changes and interpretation amendments are the bigger fish that are yet to be fried.

For too long the AFL have seemingly been unwilling to substantially address the elephant in the room — that of player safety and head trauma.

For example, when introducing the changes to the ruck engagement rule, Greg Swann was clear about the risks, specifically around PCL injuries to rucks.

"I think you'd be naive to say it's not going to happen — it'll happen," Swann acknowledged at the start of the year.

"If there was a pandemic of them you might change it back."

This approach appears to run contrary to much of the rhetoric around the importance of player safety in the modern game.

When limits to run up and changes of engagement at centre bounces were originally introduced they were backed by a robust base of evidence including academic research.

Instead of leaning on this, the league appears to be throwing caution to the wind for little real gain.

As a whole, injuries still are prevalent across the league, and still often affect the best of the best.

This carries through to the biggest challenge currently facing the sport.

There is still an uneasy tension between the potential for traumatic brain injuries to occur as a result of the sport that players and fans love and the enjoyment of the sport itself.

The AFL and clubs are facing class action suits over past responses to these risks.

As of next season clubs will have mandated limits around contact training following a recommendation from the Victoria State Coroner's inquest into the death of former AFL player Shane Tuck in 2023.

In that inquest the AFL provided a submission that they were considering a limitation at that time as to be guided by medical evidence.

That inquest recommended that the AFL should implement contact training rule restrictions by the commencement of the 2025 AFL/W preseason.

These rules are still yet to come into force.

While there has been a focus on training, there are also the on-field rule-based elements that seemingly have not been publicly considered by recent administrations.

Since the AFL changed the "prior opportunity" element of the holding the ball rule to better reward tacklers in 1996 the number of tackles per game has increased sharply.

In this time there has been a sharp rise in tackles per game and direct contact pressure. Tackle coaches have been introduced across the league, and an intense focus developed on locking the ball in during tackles.

In addition, the evolution of the game has meant that there is an increase of contested marking events — particularly with a third or fourth player present to spoil the ball.

Prior research funded by Monash University and the AFL suggests that these two situations account for the vast majority of head acceleration events in a game of football.

This research suggests that men's AFL players face 5.7 head acceleration events per game, and women's players 3 per game, on average. While this is less than other sports such as American football and rugby union, a reduction of these events should be a priority for the league.

Until these issues are substantively addressed the biggest need for reform will still be on the table, while much of the football landscape is inundated by relatively benign, minor changes.

One can hope that commonsense can be found soon.

World.title: Twin thrillers and key injuries in crazy NRL double-header
World.content:
Some of the NRL's biggest names will be missing for the run to the finals after injuries struck in two Friday night thrillers.

Newcastle will likely be without Dylan Lucas and Dylan Brown for the rest of the season after the Newcastle duo suffered ankle and knee injuries in their 23-22 loss to the Roosters which was sealed by a late Daly Cherry-Evans field goal.

Lucas was injured in the first half after twisting awkwardly in a tackle and was later transported to hospital with a broken and dislocated ankle.

The severity of Brown's injury is yet to be confirmed but there are fears the million-dollar halfback has torn his ACL after going down without contact in the second half.

"That's tough at the moment," Newcastle coach Justin Holbrook said.

"It could have been one of one of our best wins tonight with what we had to deal with ... and that's why it's so devastating for myself to sit here now with a side that you can be so close to being so happy and yet we're not.

"The docs, physio is not thinking it's good (on Brown), but cross my fingers and hope we get some good news with the scans.

"(With Lucas) he's dislocation straight away, and so that's back in, which is good. But just got to see how much damage around that's been done as well."

A James Tedesco hattrick was the highlight for the visiting Roosters, who claimed their fifth-straight win to secure their place in the top four but they didn't escape unscathed with veteran winger Daniel Tupou facing further time on the sidelines with a shoulder problem.

Meanwhile, Melbourne captain Harry Grant has suffered a hamstring injury in a 28-26 loss to South Sydney that leaves the depleted Storm's NRL finals aspirations hanging by a thread.

Grant's hamstring injury turned the course of the match. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

Their hopes of a 16th consecutive finals berth now hinge on five consecutive wins to finish the regular season and even that may not be enough.

"I don't know whether he's torn the hammy or if it's a bad strain but the way he came off, we're hopeful to see him as the year goes on but we might not see him again," said Melbourne coach Craig Bellamy.

"He'll go for a scan some time this weekend and we'll find out how bad it is and what the plan will be.

"I can't remember the last time we had as bad a run as we've had with injuries but having said that there's a few teams. I'm not sure why that is."

Grant is set to miss at least some of the fight for Melbourne's season, joining big names Cameron Munster, Xavier Coates, Eli Katoa, Tui Kamikamica and Will Warbrick on the pine.

The Queensland hooker pulled up sore popping a pass up for Trent Loiero just before halftime in Friday's clash at Stadium Australia.

He limped to the sidelines and threw his headgear to the ground in frustration.

After a torrid week that claimed David Fifita (suspension), Cam Murray (calf) and Tallis Duncan (hamstring), the Rabbitohs lost their own hooker Brandon Smith (calf) to injury.

But the victory was crucial to South Sydney's own finals hopes, which had been thrown into jeopardy with two losses from their previous four games.

A Campbell Graham try in the 76th minute off a fine pass from Ashton Ward proved the difference in an 11-try thriller.

ABC/AAP
